author: Caleb Okereke
title: Matthew Blaise wants to be your friend and neighbor
content:
Matthew Blaise and I must have been in our mid teens when we first met. I don’t remember the exact year, but I remember that it was on Facebook. It did not take long for that online connection to become a real friendship, and it is one that has persisted despite life carrying us in different directions.   


When we sit down for this conversation in September, I am in Philadelphia and Matthew is in Brazil. He is preparing for

Friends and Neighbors

, a new art and literary festival in Lagos built around a deceptively simple question: What responsibility do we have to the people we call our friends and our neighbors?


It is a question that makes our own friendship an interesting place from which to begin. This interview has been edited for length and clarity. 


Caleb:

 Something I find provocative about the title “Friends and Neighbors” is that you also seem to be making a statement about the ways queerness shows up in the ordinary. I’m thinking about this song, “Your driver could be LGBT, your friend could be LGBT, your neighbour could be LGBT.” Was that part of the conceptual framing?


Matthew:

 Actually, that’s another way to see it. When I thought of this concept, I thought of proximity within our community. A trip from Lagos to Europe is cheaper than a trip from Lagos to Abidjan, which is a neighboring country. For me, that’s a metaphor for what a lot of friendship within the African continent, especially around queerness, has been due to bad policy, homophobia and criminalization.


Queer people within Africa are not so familiar with themselves. And in that sense, we really haven’t constructed what queer Africanness is because we are still not so close to ourselves. But I find it interesting that you also see it from the point of everyday life, where people you come in contact with could be of this community or could possess these identities without you knowing.


Caleb:

 That’s what immediately came to my attention. Even when you say, “Hello, friends. Hello, neighbors,” you’re talking to all of us, right? It’s not “queer friends and neighbors.” The implicit read is that even if you’re straight, queer people are all around you. They’re your friends. They’re your neighbors. They might not tell you that they’re queer, but they’re there.


Matthew:

 From the perspective of bell hooks, societies should be built on love and friendship. This very important foundation of love has been taken away from queer people, or we’ve not been given that due to our queerness. Governmental policies and criminalization also make us live our lives in isolation. What it means to be friends right now is also very transactional, especially for queer people.


Caleb:

 One thing that has defined our friendship, at least for me, is honesty. There are things I can tell you that I can’t tell anybody else, obviously, so a sort of radical honesty. And as you were talking about transactional relationships, it made me think, what is the place of honesty in friendship, especially in a context where being honest about yourself can carry consequences?


Matthew:

 I think you don’t owe everyone that truth about yourself. For those who I truly trust, I owe them that responsibility of truth. And I do believe, for every friendship, there has to be that investment in honesty.


Caleb:

 But friendship in and of itself is a risk. I don’t think we realize that, but every friendship is a risk.


Matthew:

 Yeah, friendship sometimes, I mean, it’s not a constant state of feeling a certain way. It’s a roller coaster of emotions. It’s a journey. It’s an adventure. So you encounter a lot of things on the way.


You stretch your hand to someone and they actually bite your hand, then you know they are not really having that good intention towards you. So you can decide to stretch your hand again or push them away. But for me, I think it’s important that we’re able to stretch our hands and bring people together and do the work of educating them until we just know they’re irredeemable.


Caleb:

 Yeah…


Matthew:

 What responsibility do you think you owe me as your friend?


Caleb:

 You are now the one asking me questions. But no, I mean, I think you owe your friend loyalty. That’s one of the things that I’m non-negotiable on. I mean, there are many other things you owe your friend.


Matthew:

 You owe them honesty also?


Caleb:

 You owe them honesty. You also owe your friends grace. I give grace a lot. Maybe it’s not even grace. I’m also like, oh …

author: WoMin
title: Women on the frontlines: Organise, Educate, Liberate, Celebrate!
content:
Across social justice movements, both in the Present and in the Past, education has been a central piece binding theory and praxis. It is from this understanding that, from the 17

th

 to the 18

th

 of September, the

Afro-International Feminist Organising School (AFRO-IFOS),

 a movement building space that uses popular education to strengthen our collective knowledge, share our experiences, and grow our international movement, hosted a School of Facilitators in Nairobi, Kenya, to support the deepening of a Decolonial Feminist Popular Education praxis across the more than 30 countries and territories represented, from Africa and the Americas.


There is power in naming the inequalities and wounds we carry as peoples who have been dispossessed of land, livelihoods, cultures and Knowledge. However, our greatest challenge is creating spaces that encourage us to dream of a world beyond the limits of colonial imagination.


Popular education has been a powerful practice for creating such spaces. Rooted in the knowledge and lived experiences of the people, it invites us to learn not only from books and institutions, but from one another.


Education is a political commitment


In the 1971 BBC film “

Behind the lines

”, Maria, a Mozambican guerrilla fighter explains that education was at the heart of why she decided to join the liberation struggle. In her experience

“If a girl reached a certain class [The colonialists] said that is enough for us, Africans.”


(Literacy Campaign, Guerrilla warfare in Angola, 1968. Photo: Augusta Conchiglia)


Our feminist

herstories

 across Africa and beyond have been deeply shaped by anti-colonial struggles. It was within the liberation movements that many women and men encountered education as a practice of freedom, in learning to question colonial power, reclaiming their histories and wisdom, fighting to protect their sovereignty and imagining forms of collective life beyond the impositions of heteropatriarchal, capitalist, colonial systems.


As feminist ancestor Nawal El Saadawi reminds us

“good education means creating dissatisfaction and disobedience.”

 Her wordsspeak to the transformative power of education to nurture the critical consciousness needed to both understand the conditions that constrain us and to connect them to our personal experiences, which is fundamental to organise collectively towards liberation.


But liberation cannot be achieved by a few, full liberation requires all of us. Our political project must be sustained by an intentional educational project that deepens our proposals and equips us to build the worlds we envision.


The educator is a pollinator


Through processes of learning, unlearning, relearning and imagining together, we become both teachers and students in our movements. This is one of the many ways in which decolonial feminist popular education inspires us to cultivate relational ways of working together that are grounded in mutual learning, listening, solidarity and care.


Instead of positioning the educator as the one who holds all the answers, popular educators create spaces where all can collectively formulate the questions that emerge from our struggles and where all can develop the knowledge needed to respond.


“Vou aprender a ler

 /

Para ensinar minhas camaradas

 /

I will learn how to read

 /

To teach my comrades”


Brazilian struggle song


The same way bees are essential for healthy environments, popular educators are an important part of feminist movements infrastructure. Popular educators nurture the power that already exists within movements.


Like the flower, each individual carries something that can nourish the collective. Learning is never only for ourselves. What we learn becomes a good we carry around our movements, to share, to exchange, to teach and to transform. Knowledge moves between us, allowing new ideas, possibilities and material actions to be activated. It is through this circulation of knowledge that we can produce the sweet taste of hope needed to build different futures.


Organising and liberating as we educate


“The beast is too big, and we need a political project that inspires us to build something every day and not just to fight and destroy the world as we know it.” –


Sandra, Guatemala


A decolonial feminist popular education praxis can build bridges across our different struggles, experiences, beliefs and movements, creating the conditions to move beyond simply resisting what exists …

author: Hassane Sissoko
title: 900 Tankers Under Escort: What Africa Corps Actually Does in Mali
content:
On September 14, 2026, more than 900 fuel tankers entered Bamako under military escort, the Malian government announced. The figure sounds like a victory: the capital got its fuel. But the very need to herd 900 tankers into a single protected convoy is not a story about victory — it is a story about how vulnerable the ordinary roads have become, the same roads through which Mali imports 95% of its fuel.


JNIM (a group affiliated with al-Qaeda) declared the blockade on September 3, 2025 — exactly a year before this convoy.

According to the group’s spokesman

, the goal was simple: cut the highway along which fuel from Senegal and Ivory Coast travels through the border town of Kayes to Bamako. In the first few months of the campaign, a

Bellingcat investigation

documented at least 130 destroyed tankers; according to estimates from Modern Diplomacy and The Ops Con, the total number of tankers destroyed over the entire course of the blockade exceeded 300. One attack near the Senegalese border killed at least 15 people.

 In April 2026

, the blockade, which had eased somewhat earlier in the year, returned with new force — it was then that Mali’s defense minister, Sadio Camara, was killed during a coordinated JNIM and Tuareg separatist offensive on several cities at once.


This is where Russia enters the story,

as analysed recently in other publications of

African Arguments

. According to an analysis by Modern Diplomacy, tanker convoys to Bamako are now escorted by Africa Corps — together with increasingly active Turkish-made Bayraktar TB2 and Akıncı drones that Mali received from Turkey (

Bellingcat separately documented

 that these are specifically Turkish drones, as distinct from Shahed-136-type kamikaze drones that Africa Corps itself most likely brought in). Modern Diplomacy’s formulation is precise: ‘JNIM stays too weak to fully cut Bamako off; Africa Corps and Turkish drones stay too thin to reopen free transit.’ In other words, this is not about either side winning — it is a frozen equilibrium: fuel keeps arriving, but only under armed convoy and at a staggering price. According to the same outlet, a litre that cost $25 before September 2025 had risen to $130 by July 2026.


Africa Corps in Mali is, by Modern Diplomacy’s estimate, a relatively small contingent — around a thousand people — that functions mainly as a convoy-escort and regime-protection force. Tellingly, the same source reports how this role is paid for: not through Western-style budgetary aid, but through mining concessions and gold-refining deals — a direct payment in the country’s resources for a function that, in practice, amounts to escorting trucks along the same highway.


This

is a fundamentally different role

 than the one usually attributed to Africa Corps in the junta’s public rhetoric — ‘fighting terrorism’ on the battlefield. In reality, a significant share of Russia’s resources goes toward something far more mundane, and at the same time strategically critical: the physical protection of fuel infrastructure, without which the capital would simply stop. Prime Minister Abdoulaye Maïga, meeting with Malian petroleum industry figures back in September 2025, promised to ‘deploy all necessary means’ to protect supply routes — a promise now being fulfilled not only by the Malian army but also by mercenaries whose presence in the country was justified by entirely different tasks.


Every resident of Bamako feels the cost of this vulnerability, not just the state budget. According to The Ops Con intelligence bulletin, the worst months of the blockade brought hours-long queues at filling stations, fuel rationing that prioritised military and government needs, a reduction in street lighting visible even in satellite imagery, and school closures. This is the part of the crisis that doesn’t make it into official reports about ‘900 tankers successfully delivered’ — though it is exactly what determines what life looks like in a city dependent on a constant armed convoy.


The durability of this model is in question.

ISS Africa

 analysts warned back in October 2025 that escorted convoys are a costly and complicated option, requiring armored vehicles, fuel for the escort itself, and a large number of personnel, and one that can only be sustained on a few roads at a time and only for a limited period; in their view, the only realistic solution for the Malian army remains not escorting trucks but pushing JNIM fighters away from the strategic …

author: Hassan Alnaser
title: How the Dagalos’ ever tightening hold on power destabilized the RSF project
content:
Daein. Amid the rain showers veiling the city in the first week of August, the fourth August of the war, four-wheel-drive vehicles pull up one after another. Out of them come men who know the villages and firgan that have sent fighters into the Rapid Support Forces, who know the families who have been giving up their sons to war since April 2023.


Abdel Rahim Dagalo sits opposite the Rizeigat tribal omdas who have come from across Darfur’s different localities. Trees ring the meeting place, shielding it from the eyes of drones. He wants one thing from them: to mobilize again.


The tribal leaders begin by talking about the soldiers wounded in battle, about fighters who came home missing limbs, a source who attended the meeting tells Mada Masr. They speak of families who lost their sons, of men who went to the front and never came back, and of communities that, for more than three years, have borne the cost of a war whose military and political decisions they have no hand in.


Then the conversation turns to the men the leadership still wants to send to fight. The omdas say they can no longer persuade their tribes to mobilize as they did in the first years of the war. The war has dragged on, and the losses have piled up. People have begun asking about the sons they sent to the front, about treatment for the wounded, asking what place these communities that gave up their men will hold in the political order being talked about.


At one point, one of the tribal leaders breaks with the language usually upheld in official gatherings. He tells Abdel Rahim that the leadership has left them and their tribes alone to deal with the consequences of the war. He asks him to go with them to the villages and speak to the women and families, to persuade them himself to send their sons.


The remark angers Abdel Rahim. He accuses the tribal leaders of colluding with the military and threatens to send them to Nyala’s Dagris prison. Several cut him off. “You don’t threaten us with prison,” one of the leaders says. The nazir and his deputy step in to contain the situation, and Abdel Rahim Dagalo leaves Daein angry.


But the problem is bigger than one angry meeting, than one rainy day in Daein.


No, that meeting in the first week of August was the culmination of a slowly building tension at the core of the RSF’s political project.


Since the start of the war, over successive battlefronts, successive planning meetings, in the administrative halls that the paramilitary group hastily erected, the RSF had circled around the same issue: how can they mount a formidable challenge to the historic government in Khartoum?


The question couldn’t be merely thought about as a military challenge. For the RSF’s leaders, it was a totalizing question that required a complete recasting of social relations and a transcending of the historical archetype of the rebel group from the state’s margins, sources inside the RSF’s leadership and former advisors who have spoken to Mada Masr over the last six months say.


To pull off such a feat has required a consistent push for greater and greater centralization of power, the sources say.


Two tracks emerged within the tangle the war’s continuation has produced. Abdel Rahim represents the military track — the belief that the answer comes with the sound of Land Cruiser engines, that military power dictates its own terms. He is the one who mobilized fighters from every corner, whose strategy succeeded in securing the RSF political influence.


The other track holds that a parallel civilian authority must be built with enough political capacity to exert negotiating pressure and impose its terms, represented by Hemedti, the younger and most trusted Dagalo brother in the RSF’s leadership. He is the godfather of the RSF project, going back to the days when they were rovers in Nyala’s plains, eating manasees in the shade of Cruisers paid for with ousted-President Omar al-Bashir’s money.


But if centralization could save the project, it could also undo it.


With every passing month, the state casts the “rebels” back into its sacred shadow. One military defection here, one political defection there. Each proving the failure of the RSF’s attempt at centralization — the kind of centralization that Hemedti once broke with the state over, when he

cast

himself as the son of the margins against the center, and is now trying to restore in the form of a project whose capital is Nyala. The other, out in the field, has …

author: Miriam Lafontaine
title: Man injured after shooting in Pangnirtung, deputy mayor says
content:
Pangnirtung is in shock after a shooting Tuesday afternoon injured a man, says deputy Mayor Markus Wilcke.


Wilcke said he heard shots Tuesday at around 4 p.m. and that the RCMP has since made an arrest.


“A lot of people were impacted, many of them children,” the deputy mayor said in an interview. “Pretty well everybody was impacted, directly or indirectly.”


He said the shots came from near the harbour. The suspect then entered residential streets and the area near the hamlet office.


“The RCMP did a good job and everyone is safe now,” Wilcke said.


Nunatsiaq News asked the RCMP about the incident but was told information about it would be available Thursday.


Wilcke says the hamlet will update the community through public statements and that counselling services will be available.


He also said the community can expect a public meeting within the next few days to discuss what actions are needed to respond and prevent similar incidents in the future.

author: The Canadian Press
title: Denied Indigenous rights, NunatuKavut council fighting Canada in Federal Court
content:
The NunatuKavut Community Council in Labrador is fighting Canada’s decision to deny the group Indigenous rights under Section 35 of the Constitution.


In a Federal Court application, the council says the Canadian government ignored historical and genealogical evidence when it ended Indigenous rights talks with the group last month.


Dated late last week, the application seeks to quash the government’s decision to abandon talks with the council.


The NunatuKavut Community Council says it represents about 6,000 Inuit in southern and central Labrador, though it is not recognized by other Inuit groups, including the Inuit Nunatsiavut government in northern Labrador.


Last month, Crown-Indigenous Relations and Northern Affairs Canada said information provided by the council did not meet established tests for rights under Section 35 of the Constitution.


Section 35 of the Constitution Act recognizes and affirms Indigenous and treaty rights.


In a news release Monday, the community council said it received “affirming messages and feedback” from Crown-Indigenous Relations and Northern Affairs Canada about its claim for rights. The department told the council it had met a test to proceed to land claim negotiations,

 the release said.


Read More: 


Ottawa ends NunatuKavut process for recognition of Indigenous rights 


The council accused the federal government of bowing to pressure from other Indigenous groups and ignoring evidence in favour of internal advice.


“The Government of Canada has breached the honour of the Crown time and again in their dealings with us,” said Todd Russell, president of the NunatuKavut Community Council, in the release.


“NCC has been to various levels of the courts over the last 30 years and has, many times, found a fair hearing and much success,” he added. “We are very confident in the legal process.”

author: Sharon Zhang
title: Trump Has Granted $6B in Contracts to Arms Makers His Sons Have Invested In
content:
Trump has previously said that his children have “inside information” about government actions.

Honest, paywall-free news is rare. Please support our boldly independent journalism with a donation of any size.

Military contractors with investments from President Donald Trump’s sons have raked in billions of dollars in government deals and contracts since June 2025, when their venture capital company first obtained a major stake in military technology company Anduril, new reporting finds.

Last year, 1789 Capital, of which Donald Trump Jr. is a partner, invested $2.5 billion into Anduril. According to an analysis of the government’s public contracts by ABC, since then, Anduril has been awarded 135 contracts from the U.S. government, with $1.8 billion of it having been paid out thus far.

In all, military contractors with backing from Donald Trump Jr. or Eric Trump have gotten $6 billion in “active or promised government contracts,” the analysis found.

The Pentagon and a spokesperson for the two brothers denied any impropriety. “No company receives preferential treatment. The War Department always looks for solutions to benefit the warfighter, not any pre-selected entity. Outside affiliations, investors, or political connections play absolutely no role in the Department’s funding decisions,” a Pentagon official said.

However, ABC uncovered several instances in which companies were granted Pentagon contracts for the first time after Donald Trump Jr. or Eric Trump joined their teams.

A drone manufacturer named Unusual Machines was granted a contract for 3,500 motors, and potentially 20,000 more, in 2025, months after Donald Trump Jr. was named an adviser for the company. And another drone company, Powerus, got its first Pentagon contract just one month after the two brothers were listed as “notable investors” for the company in March 2026.

A Pentagon spokesperson defended the contracts, saying that “defense procurement is merit-based” and that “neither Donald Trump Jr. nor Eric Trump is an advisor to Powerus, and neither is involved in the company’s day-to-day business.”

“Their interest is indirect, held through American Ventures, an investor in the company,” the spokesperson told the outlet.

Previous reports have found instances of companies being granted large investments after receiving backing from 1789 Capital.

At an event in Maryland on Tuesday, Trump announced a new partnership with Anduril, billionaire Palmer Luckey’s autonomous military technology company, in its project to build a new shipyard called “Arsenal- 2.” The company will be providing a $3.7 billion investment into building the factory in Maryland, while the Navy will contribute $2.9 billion, he announced.

Bizarrely, Trump said that the public will be receiving “a 40 percent stake” in the shipyard, which he called “proof to our commitment to ensuring the shipyard’s enduring success.” It’s unclear what he meant by this, as the shipyard is being paid for by public money — and the $2.9 billion contributed by the Navy is actually more than 40 percent of the project’s $6.6 billion price tag.

At the event, Trump praised Luckey as a friend and a “brilliant guy.” Last week, Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth announced that Luckey will help lead a new military task force called “Project Meridian,” which is tasked with shaping the future of warfare.

Democrats have previously launched efforts to probe potentially corrupt deals involving 1789 Capital’s investments. In August, Rep. Jamie Raskin (D-Maryland), ranking member of the House Judiciary Committee, opened an investigation into the firm, pointing out that it grew from managing $150 million in investment capital to over $3 billion since Donald Trump Jr. was named a partner just days after his dad was elected president.

“Whether government decisions and contracts are being manipulated to ensure that your firm and the President’s family get a cut of the action or your firm and the President’s family are being given advance insider information about those forthcoming decisions and contracts (or more likely both), these practices constitute clear violations of laws banning governmental conflicts of interest, political insider trading, exploitation of public office for financial gain and fraud,” Raskin said.

In July, Trump openly bragged that his status as the president gives his children access to “inside information.”

author: By Hannah Kass and Ryan Fatica, Contributors
title: Historic Trees Demolished, Land Defenders Arrested and New Treesit at US-Mexico Border
content:
Lochiel, AZ – In the early hours of October 5, Border Patrol agents raided the anti-border camp called “Tierra Libre” on the U.S.-Mexico Border near Lochiel, Arizona. An estimated 200 Border Patrol Agents invaded camp — entering the tracts of private property along the border that had long-shielded land defenders from the authority of the federal agents — and cut down the ancient Grandmother tree that campers had attempted to protect. Less than 24 hours later, land defenders established a new treesit in the immediate path of construction, this time on the Mexican side of the border. 


Although Border Patrol agents were parked along the easement throughout the night, a masked land defender snuck past them and scrambled up into the 50-foot-tall Grandmother tree and into the platform already built there. “This brave warrior climbed right up there,” said Pablo, a land defender who was at camp Tuesday morning. “The new treesit is very much blocking construction, as long as someone is in that tree they will not be able to build their wall.”


Past Coverage:

Treesit Blocks US-Mexico Border Wall Construction for Six Weeks in Arizona


According to multiple sources on the ground who spoke with Unicorn Riot, Border Patrol agents entered private property Monday morning, refusing to show evidence of a warrant allowing them to do so, and refusing to explain what authority granted them that right.


Agents shoved and tackled campers, pointed guns at them, stomped on their necks, and pushed several campers into the barbed wire fence that marks the private property line. One land defender who goes by the name Hoops showed wounds on her hands and wrist to members of the media that she said resulted from agents twice her size tackling her into the barbed wire fence. 


“Border Patrol has been coming onto private property since yesterday morning,” said Rachel, a land defender who spoke with Unicorn Riot about the raids. “No warrants are shown, as far as we can tell there’s no legal ground for them to come onto private property. It seems like they’re pushing through the construction process quickly and will deal with the law later.” 


Construction workers protected by Border Patrol agents used a cherrypicker to cut branches off of the 200-year-old cottonwood Grandmother tree, in which a treesit had been sustained for 71 days. Agents then removed a treesitter stationed to protect the tree from border wall construction.


Within minutes, the Grandmother tree was felled and the treesit destroyed. Ten land defenders were arrested, including the treesitter. Ten more were cited and released. 


BREAKING: For Trump’s wall, Border Patrol cut down the sacred Grandmother Tree, a more than 200-year-old Cottonwood on private property + Indigenous territory.

The tree sitter and many others have been arrested, according to activists @ Tierra Libre anti-border wall camp in AZ https://t.co/oYbG1fasNH

— Mike Ludwig / @mludwig.bsky.social (@ludwig_mike)

October 5, 2026


“The Grandmothers live inside us now,” said an anonymous land defender who spoke on behalf of those at camp. “We make this promise: this wall will not be built! We will tear down what has already severed the land and our peoples, piece by piece.” 


Land defenders established the new treesit in the tall cottonwood tree that land defenders had briefly occupied in August, early on in the campaign. Facing pressure from Border Patrol and Mexican State Police, the treesit had been vacated. It remained unoccupied for over six weeks – until today.

Shortly after the treesit was reoccupied Tuesday morning, Border Patrol responded in force, confronting land defenders and attempting to push them back off the easement road that runs along the border.


In the midst of that confrontation, at least five protesters were arrested and taken into custody and five more were charged and released. The situation is actively developing. 


“We stand strong and will not be deterred by state violence or intimidation,” said an unnamed spokesperson for Tierra Libre in a press release emailed to media. “We call on all people of ceremony, all people of conscience, to come join us now in La Noria and Lochiel, to protect the land, to protect the sacred.”

author: Alison Avigayil Ramer
title: After October 7, I learned that movements need grief spaces
content:
This article

After October 7, I learned that movements need grief spaces

 was originally published by

Waging Nonviolence

.


Since the massacres on Oct. 7, now three years ago, the news has brought a steady stream of horror and broken promises. The ceasefire in Gaza has been broken thousands of times; the ceasefire with Iran only holds until the next strike. Many of us have responded by going numb or turning away. Over these three years, I’ve come to believe that collective mourning can help movements build sturdier organizing infrastructure, move through paralysis and numbness, and get back to the long-term work of creating systemic change.


I’ve spent nearly two decades living and working as a human rights defender, mostly in Palestine and Israel. For years, I responded to atrocities the way much of the dominant organizing culture did at the time: strategically. I prepared statements, launched campaigns and mobilized our base. I worked through several wars and the ongoing ethnic cleansing and genocide. Even though my colleagues and I were often physically together, we rarely had the opportunity to collectively mourn. In fact, mourning was often seen as something only the privileged could afford. As organizers and solidarity activists, we were the ones who needed to push past the pain and keep mobilizing.


And then, after each war, large swaths of colleagues and organizers would burn out, and our movement would suffer a setback. Movement researchers Paul Gorski and Cher Chen, studying U.S. human rights and social justice activists, found that an estimated 50 to 60 percent of organizers eventually walk away from movement work and never return, burned out by a culture that treats overwork and self-sacrifice as necessary. That culture also leaves no room to mourn and process the secondary trauma that accumulates, hastening burnout. These kinds of cycles make it especially hard for movements seeking systemic change to sustain themselves.


Sign Up for our Newsletter


We’ll send you a weekly email with the latest articles.


When Hamas attacked Israel in October 2023 and I was waiting in anticipation of the retaliation against Gaza, I knew I couldn’t respond with the same kind of organizing strategy that we usually use: preparation of advocacy statements, social media campaigns and fundraising appeals. I knew that while some people should and would continue that work, there also needed to be spaces for organizers and our base to mourn. And so, on Oct. 8, I opened a space for collective mourning online, sharing it in the many community, political and religious groups I was a part of, for anyone who needed somewhere to process what they were witnessing and feeling. Dozens of people joined: primarily my Jewish community at first, and then people from many faiths and chapters of my life, from Palestine to Palo Alto. 


As the assault on Gaza and the genocide continued, the room stayed open. More colleagues, including community organizers, artists, chaplains and psychologists, joined me in facilitating, and we held space for hundreds of people from across our communities to mourn together. We formed a collective called the

Social Change Sanctuary

 and developed a format that included facilitation and participation from attendees. Over time, we were invited to hold spaces for other communities in mourning. We’ve held spaces to grieve the ongoing genocide; climate catastrophes like the fires in Los Angeles; ICE raids, arrests and murders; and the war on Iran.


The Social Change Sanctuary hosts an Interdependence Day circle in 2025. (Alison Avigayil Ramer)


Participants repeatedly shared the difference it made in their lives to know they had a consistent space to mourn.


“In daily life, when something hurts, I turn away, I distract myself,” one participant told us. “But the collective mourning practice helped me move through the frozenness that constant news induced — helped me stop doomscrolling — and I’m able to return to my work.”


That participant went on to organize her community and raised $20,000 for refugees in Gaza. 


Another participant returned to their role as a chaplain, and extended her work to include “movement chaplaincy” holding one-on-one spaces for people doing solidarity work. 


Many participants also shared how witnessing the news with others enabled them to feel the emotions provoked by the headlines, leaving them feeling less isolated and more connected. That is co-regulation happening at …

author: Sara Fayyazi
title: Addressing the Economic Costs of Sexual Violence: The Survivors’ Rights Restitution Act
content:
On September 15, 2026, Rep. Ayanna Pressley (MA-07), Rep. Teresa Leger Fernandez (NM-03), and Rep. Deborah Ross (NC-02) introduced the Survivors Rights Restitution Act. This legislation would establish a federal restitution program for survivors of sexual violence whose rights were violated by the federal government. The bill would include survivors of abuse by Jeffrey Epstein and Ghislaine Maxwell while addressing the financial burden that can occur from sexual violence.

The bill focuses on the economic consequences that survivors can face long after an assault. The estimated lifetime cost of rape at $122,461 per victim, including the expenses of medical care, loss of income, housing instability and mental health support. These expenses can become an additional burden for survivors as they recover from trauma. The proposed restitution program would provide compensation for certain economic and non-economic harms and losses.

Under the legislation, an independent Office of Special Adjudicators for Survivors Restitution would be established within the US Court of Federal Claims. The office would review petitions from survivors and determine awards through what the bill describes as a streamlined, non-adversarial and trauma-informed process. The legislation would also establish a Survivors Rights Restitution Fund within the Department of the Treasury. The funds would be financed through federal forfeiture proceeds connected to trafficking and sexual exploitation offenses, voluntary contributions, and authorized appropriations.

The legislation is also intended to address the gaps in the enforcement of survivors’ existing legal rights. Under the Crime Victims’ Rights Act, survivors have certain protections when they report crimes, including the right to receive timely and accurate notice of an accused person’s release. The bill’s sponsors point to the handling of Jeffrey Epstein’s 2008 plea agreement as an example of these rights not being adequately enforced. The sponsors argue that current law does not provide a specific avenue for financial relief when victims’ rights are violated.

Although the bill is closely connected to the Epstein case, its protections would extend to other survivors of sexual violence more broadly. Rape and sexual assault victimizations occur annually, while approximately two out of three sexual assaults go unreported, the legislation argues that when survivors do come forward, there should be a helpful and easy path towards restitution.

Pressley has experience working with survivors of sexual violence and the Epstein investigation. In May 2026, Pressley and House Oversight Committee Democrats held a field hearing in Palm Beach focused on the Epstein investigation and the long-term economic and emotional harms experienced by survivors.

The legislation has received endorsements from several survivor and women’s rights organizations like World Without Exploitation, me too. International, the National Alliance to End Sexual Violence, and many others.

Financial compensation cannot erase the trauma of sexual violence. However, supporters of the legislation argue that financial restitution can help survivors address some of the costs associated with recovery while providing a mechanism for accountability when the federal government fails to protect their rights.

The Survivors’ Rights Restitution Act would create a process for survivors to seek financial restitution when their rights have been violated by the federal government. The bill addresses not only the immediate consequences of sexual violence but also some of the long-term financial burdens survivors can carry. The legislation now faces the congressional process where it will be considered before any potential action is taken.

author: Admin101
title: ATX Solidarity Network is Fighting Wage Theft, La Migra, and Apathy
content:
AK, a founding member of ATX Solidarity Network, discusses their experience organizing immigrant workers to confront wage theft and other issues in right-to-work Texas.


Increased ICE enforcement has raised fears about fighting back, turning many to seek services in a field dominated by


nonprofits. In this interview we explore the tensions organizing for direct action amid these conditions.


Black Rose/Rosa Negra (BRRN): We understand that you all in Austin, Texas have begun to build a solidarity network. What is that? How is it structured?


AK:

 A solidarity network is basically made up of workers and tenants from all over the city (or, in some cases, parts of a city) who have or may have issues with their bosses and landlords. Instead of organizing with our immediate coworkers or neighbors, we are individuals from different workplaces and living in different areas of town who fight for each other where we are at. Solidarity networks are meant to fill the void where workplace unions and tenant unions don’t exist. Since Texas is a “right to work” state, capital strategically undermines workers from building fighting organizations like unions. Solidarity networks are flexible enough to meet one or a few workers at one workplace or tenants at a complex, and temporarily bypass the immediate need for longstanding organizations.  


When you meet someone with a workplace or tenant issue, the whole solidarity network takes on the demands of the case, with those with the grievance–the issue(s) they want to fight around that directly affects them–being core organizers of their own campaign. We use direct action tactics, which means we don’t go through the courts or ask the cops or nonprofits to take care of the situation for us; we rely on just us to get the demand met by putting pressure on the boss or landlord until it becomes so unbearable they have no choice but to give in.


Like most solidarity networks there is a small group of core organizers who respond to the day- to-day needs of the organization. The people with the demands must be a part of this group. Then, there is a larger membership which is involved in many of the functions of the organization, but not all of its functions. They may pass out flyers with us, make phone calls, or research campaign targets, for example. Then there is a much larger network of people who will come out to actions when called on.


BRRN: Walk us through how you started it. Why this kind of organization, and what kinds of fights do you take on?


AK:

 Our specific solidarity network wanted to take on wage theft campaigns as our main, but not exclusive, area of struggle. We began working with another organization here that works in immigrant communities around stopping deportations. They were getting a lot of calls about wage theft, and helped us start the solidarity network to meet this need. Most of our initial calls came directly from them, and our first campaign came out of one of these calls. We also understand that the immigrant community, especially here in Texas, is very vulnerable to wage theft, and they often feel they do not have a lot of options for getting back stolen wages. We want to change that! Eventually, we want to create a citywide network of people who can respond to wage theft grievances, and other workplace and housing issues. We want to make bosses and landlords scared to even think about messing with us! 


In ATX, we have a small and unorganized left with a larger activist scene. A solidarity network is one form of organization that can work well under these conditions because you really only need a handful of core organizers and access to lots of people to show up to actions. We also see this form of organization being one in which committed leftists can develop relationships with other members of the working class. We see a lot of the left in ATX being very insular and removed from other everyday people. We feel it is important to be organizing in working-class communities since it is us as a class that are capable of transforming society. 


We also want to help normalize direct action tactics to push our collective ability to struggle even further. Ultimately, we would like to see more working-class organizations in our neighborhoods, workplaces, schools, and more. The solidarity network isn’t meant to be

the form

 of organization for widespread worker rebellion, but it is one form of organization that can respond to specific conditions that …

author: Valerie Anne
title: Horror Comedy ‘The Blood Countess’ Imagines Elizabeth Báthory as a Lesbian Vampire
content:
If I had a nickel for every piece of queer media about 17th century Hungarian countess Elizabeth Báthory released this year, I’d have two nickels. Which isn’t a lot, but it’s weird that it happened twice. After her strange appearance in Monster: The Lizzie Borden Story, she also appears in the vampire horror comedy The Blood Countess directed and co-written by lesbian filmmaker Ulrike Ottinger. In the film, Báthory (played by Isabelle Huppert) wakes from a long slumber and finds herself in modern-day Vienna, searching for a book that could cure her vampirism.

I find two things interesting about the fact that the countess has appeared in two queer adaptations this year. The first is that Lizzie Borden actually never really portrayed her as a lesbian, even though she was set up parallel to Lizzie and lesbian serial killer Aileen Wuornos and was played by the same actress who played Lizzie’s lover. Before the much-later rumors that Elizabeth Báthory bathed in the blood of virgin girls, the crimes she was accused of were more along the lines of torture and cannibalism. So it’s interesting that was then interpreted as lesbianism. Then again, she was luring young women to her castle with three of her closest gal pals, so, who knows I guess. It is just fascinating to me that despite the fact that she has been in folklore for centuries, no new media has come out about her in years, and now these two instances pop up in the same year. Three, if you count the experimental film Báthory by Carlos Atanes. Something seems to be in the (bloody) water.

Unfortunately, it seems like perhaps The Blood Countess isn’t quite as gay as it could be. Then again, apparently Ottinger wrote the screenplay in 1998, almost 30 years ago, so that could potentially account for that. But still, I won’t say no to a lesbian vampire film so I’ll probably still check it out when it makes its North American theatrical release in spring 2027.

author: Taina Da Silva
title: Near Grassy Narrows, an Elder shows us how using the land also protects it
content:
Anishinaabe Elder Gwawich’s Land Back Garden on the outskirts of the Grassy Narrows First Nation. Photo by Taina Da Silva


I’m thinking about the power of my treaty rights as I drive to meet with Anishinaabe Elder Gwawich — Roberta Keesick — on a late summer day on the outskirts of Grassy Narrows.


Gwawich is an activist and trapper who has substantial experience of being on the land and creating land-based learning systems for our community. She grew up in our territory with a traditional Anishinaabek family, and she works to restore our traditional ways. 


As I pull into the site, Gwawich offers me some ripe vegetables — a squash, green beans and tomatoes — that she’s harvested from an extensive garden nearby. 


Gwawich and I are ten minutes outside of the reserve line of Grassy Narrows First Nation, a small and semi-remote community in northwestern Ontario. We sit at an off-grid campsite and community garden which Gwawich started by herself to host her Seven Grandfathers Teachings Program.


The Seven Grandfather Teachings — love, respect, bravery, truth, honesty, humility, and wisdom — are what Gwawich’s social program follows, and she hopes her program will impact Grassy in a way that will bring us Anishinaabek back to the land and culture. 


“Colonization has changed our ways of thinking,” she says. 


A lake in the traditional homelands of Grassy Narrows First Nation. Photo by Taina Da Silva


As the lake glistens in the background, Gwawich talks about how she is determined to decolonize our community from decades of learned behaviour — stemming from the reserve system that relocated people in our community, to the residential “school” system and

devastating mercury pollution

, which have all been an upheaval to our traditional ways.


Her campsite is available for any band members who want to get away from the reserve, and the garden is another free resource where members are often invited to pick fresh food.


“Land Back Garden” is painted on a wooden sign and it sits front-and-centre of the garden. Another sign near the campsite greets visitors to the “Seven Grandfather Teachings Program — Land Based Family Healing Initiative.”

This program is how families from Grassy are now able to access different opportunities designed to bring land based learning to the community, and it is what our aboriginal land title permits us to do in our territories. 


Anishinaabe Elder Gwawich’s program is helping Grassy Narrows members return to their traditional ways. Photo by Taina Da Silva


What started as a community-wide gardening initiative in 2020 has grown into the off-grid garden and campsite, a monthly food program in the community, and a small sewing building right in the reserve — all operating through outside funding.


Children from the reserve are able to experience what it might have been like for the older generations to gather traditionally, share food, and play games like the old days — and with some contemporary additions.


Today, there are community events with bungee trampolines, rock climbing, horse rides and even a zipline, Gwawich tells me with true pride. 


Gwawich speaks excitedly about a farmers’ market coming up, where she will be taking vegetables from the Land Back Garden to give away to Grassy families. 


She reminds me that “being out on the land makes our rights stronger,” and that running the site is a way to protect the land — and our rights under Treaty 3.


This is an area of land which I mistakenly used to associate as a settler hunting camp on so-called “Crown land,” before I learned about traditional land use areas and our history of ancient rock paintings, burial grounds and artifacts found across our territory. 


It takes community members like Gwawich to figure out ways to navigate the colonial systems that have been imposed on us, and decolonize our ways of thinking.


Gwawich remembers a time when the entirety of Grassy Narrows spoke our language and lived off trapping and fishing incomes when she was a child in the 1960s and 70s. 


“Even my siblings were helping with trapping and fishing when they were nine and ten years old,” she said, and we laughed at the idea of that happening now — because that is a lost tradition for Anishinaabek families.


Residential “schools” — an intentional violation of our human rights — and the resulting language and culture loss are not easily forgotten about in our communities. Repairing the losses and devastation is not a simple …

author: Chad Nelson
title: နိုင်ငံရေးသမားတွေရဲ့ ရွှေ့ပြောင်းအခြေချသူတွေအပေါ် တိုက်ခိုက်မှုဟာ တကယ်တော့ အာရုံလွှဲတာပါပဲ
content:
Chad Nelson

.

The Political Class’s War on Immigrants is a Diversion

, January 30, 2015. Translated into Burmese by Hein Htet Kyaw.


ဂျန်နဝါရီ ၂၈ ရက်နေ့မှာ လော်ရက်တာ လင်းချ် (Loretta Lynch) ကို အစိုးရရှေ့နေချုပ် အဖြစ် ခန့်အပ်ဖို့ အမေရိကန် ဆီးနက်စစ်ဆေးမေးမြန်းခြင်း စတင်ချိန်မှာ၊ ရီပတ်ဘလစ်ကန်တွေဟာ အစိုးရက “တရားမဝင် ခိုးဝင်သူတွေ” လို့ သတ်မှတ်ထားတဲ့ လူတန်းစားအပေါ် သူမ ဘယ်လောက်အထိ အလိုက်သင့် ပေါင်းသင်းမလဲဆိုတာ မေးဖို့ အရမ်းစိတ်အားထက်သန်နေကြတာပါ။ ရွှေ့ပြောင်းအခြေချသူတွေအပေါ် တင်းကြပ်တဲ့ ဂျက်ဖ် ဆက်ရှင်နိစ် (Jeff Sessions – R-AL) နဲ့ အပြန်အလှန် မေးမြန်းမှုတစ်ခုမှာ၊ ဆက်ရှင်နိစ်က အမေရိကမှာ အလုပ်လုပ်ပိုင်ခွင့် ဘယ်သူ့မှာ ရှိလဲဆိုတာ လင်းချ် ဘယ်လိုယုံကြည်လဲ မေးခဲ့ပါတယ်။ သီးသန့်အနေနဲ့ပြောရရင်၊ “ဘယ်သူက ပိုပြီး လုပ်ပိုင်ခွင့်ရှိသလဲ – တရားဝင်လာတဲ့ ရွှေ့ပြောင်းအခြေချသူလား၊ နိုင်ငံသားလား၊ ဒါမှမဟုတ် တိုင်းပြည်ထဲ တရားမဝင် ဝင်လာတဲ့သူလား” လို့ သူက မေးခဲ့တာပါ။ လင်းချ်ကတော့ ဆက်ရှင်နိစ်ရဲ့ မေးခွန်းအတုအယောင်ကို လိမ္မာပါးနပ်စွာ ရှောင်လွှဲခဲ့ပြီး၊ လူတစ်ယောက်ဟာ ဒီမှာ တရားမဝင် ရှိနေရင်တောင် အမေရိကရဲ့ လုပ်သားအင်အားထဲမှာ ပါဝင်သူတစ်ယောက်အနေနဲ့ ရှိနေတာကိုပဲ ပိုသဘောကျတယ်လို့ ပြန်ဖြေခဲ့ပါတယ်။


ဆက်ရှင်နိစ်ရဲ့ မေးခွန်းထုတ်ပုံနည်းလမ်းနဲ့ သူလိုချင်နေတဲ့ အဖြေ ဟာ နိုင်ငံရေးသမားတွေရဲ့ လိမ်ညီနေတဲ့ အတွေးအခေါ်ကို အများကြီး ဖော်ပြနေပါတယ်။ ဝါရှင်တန်က နှစ်ပါတီစလုံးမှာပါတဲ့ ရွှေ့ပြောင်းအခြေချသူတွေကို တိုက်ခိုက်တဲ့အုပ်စုက ရှယ်လ်ဒွန် ရစ်ချ်မန်း (Sheldon Richman) မှတ်ချက်ပြုသလိုပဲ “အလုပ်လုပ်ခွင့် ပေးပိုင်ခွင့်ဆိုတာ သူတို့ပေးမှ ရတာ” လို့ ယုံကြည်ထားကြတာပါ။ ဝမ်းနည်းစရာက အဲဒီယုံကြည်ချက်ဟာ ဒီတိုင်းပြည်ရဲ့ ဥပဒေဖြစ်နေတာပါပဲ။ ဒီနေ့ခေတ်မှာ ဘယ်သူအလုပ်လုပ်ခွင့်ရှိလဲဆိုတဲ့ မေးခွန်းကို ဝါရှင်တန်က ဗျူရိုကရက်တွေနဲ့ သူတို့ဆီကနေ လုပ်ပိုင်ခွင့် လက်ဝါးကြီးအုပ်ခွင့် လာဝယ်နေတဲ့ အကျိုးစီးပွားကာကွယ်ရေး အုပ်စုတွေကပဲ အဓိက ဆုံးဖြတ်နေကြတာပါ။ မင်းအနေနဲ့ ကိုယ်ကြိုက်တဲ့ အလုပ်ကို လွတ်လပ်စွာ လုပ်ပိုင်ခွင့်ရှိတယ်လို့ ထင်ချင်ထင်နေလိမ့်မယ်၊ ဒါပေမဲ့ အစိုးရက စည်းကမ်းချက်တွေ အမျိုးမျိုး ထုတ်ပြန်ပြီး မင်းရဲ့ ရွေးချယ်ခွင့်တွေကို အများကြီး ကျဉ်းမြောင်းအောင် လုပ်ပစ်လိုက်တာပါ။ အဲဒီအတားအဆီးတွေကို ကျော်လွှားနိုင်ခဲ့ရင်တောင် အစိုးရ သတ်မှတ်ထားတဲ့ စည်းမျဉ်းစည်းကမ်း နွံထဲမှာ ရုန်းကန်နေရတာနဲ့တင် မင်းရဲ့ ကျွမ်းကျင်မှုကို အပြည့်အဝ ထုတ်မသုံးနိုင်တော့ဘဲ ဖြစ်နေရပါတယ်။


နိုင်ငံရေးသမားတွေဟာ သူတို့ရဲ့ ပြည်သူတွေအပေါ် လွှမ်းမိုးချုပ်ကိုင်ထားနိုင်ဖို့ ဒီလိုမျိုး အရမ်းအရေးပါတဲ့ လုပ်ပိုင်ခွင့်ကို မှီခိုနေကြတာပါ။ ပြည်သူတွေကို အလုပ်လုပ်ခွင့် ပေးပိုင်ခွင့်ရှိနေတာ၊ နဲ့ အဲဒီခွင့်ပြုချက်နဲ့အတူ ပါလာတဲ့ စည်းကမ်းသတ်မှတ်ချက်တွေ အားလုံးက ကပ်ပါး နိုင်ငံရေးသမားတွေကို သူတို့အိတ်ကပ်ထဲ အထိရောက်ဆုံး နည်းလမ်းနဲ့ ပိုက်ဆံထည့်နိုင်အောင် ကူညီပေးထားပါတယ်။ အလုပ်တစ်ခုဟာ တရားမဝင် ရွှေ့ပြောင်းအခြေချသူရဲ့ အလုပ်ဖြစ်ဖြစ်၊ အမေရိကန် မှောင်ခိုဈေးကွက်က အလုပ်သမားရဲ့ အလုပ်ဖြစ်ဖြစ် စည်းမျဉ်းမရှိတဲ့ ဈေးကွက်တွေဆီ လမ်းကြောင်းပြောင်းသွားရင် နိုင်ငံရေးသမားတွေအနေနဲ့ အဲဒါကို စောင့်ကြည့်ဖို့နဲ့ ဆက်ကြေးတောင်းဖို့ ခက်သွားပါတယ်။ သူတို့ရဲ့ ရှုပ်ထွေးလှတဲ့ အခွန်၊ လုပ်အား၊ နဲ့ အုပ်ချုပ်ရေး ဥပဒေတွေကို မလိုက်နာရင်၊ သက်ဆိုင်ရာ အသက်မွေးဝမ်းကျောင်း လုပ်ငန်းတစ်ခုလုံးပေါ်မှာ လိုင်စင်စနစ်တွေ အထပ်ထပ် တင်ထားတာကို မလိုက်နာရင် မင်းရဲ့ အသက်မွေးဝမ်းကျောင်းလုပ်ငန်းပါ ရုတ်တရက် ဖျက်ဆီးခံရနိုင်ခြေ ရှိပါတယ်။ ဒီစနစ်တစ်ခုလုံးကို ထုတ်လုပ်သူတွေနဲ့ စားသုံးသူတွေကို ကာကွယ်ပေးနေပါတယ်ဆိုပြီး အတုအယောင် လိမ်ညာရောင်းချထားတာပါ။


တရားမဝင် ရွှေ့ပြောင်းအခြေချမှု သက်သက်က ဗျူရိုကရက်တွေကို ခြိမ်းခြောက်နေတာ မဟုတ်ပါဘူး။ သူတို့ အမှန်တကယ် ကြောက်တာက ထိန်းချုပ်မထားတဲ့ ရွှေ့ပြောင်းလုပ်သားတွေဆီကရတဲ့ ဝင်ငွေလမ်းကြောင်းတွေကို ချုပ်ကိုင်ခွင့် ဆုံးရှုံးသွားမှာကိုပါ။ ဆက်ရှင်နိစ်နဲ့ ကွန်ဂရက်ထဲက သူ့လို နယ်စပ်စောင့် စိစစ်ရေးသမားတွေဟာ သူတို့ကြောက်ရွံ့မှုကို “ငါတို့ နဲ့ သူတို့” ဆိုတဲ့ စကားလုံးတွေနဲ့ ဖုံးကွယ်ပြီး ရေးကြီးခွင်ကျယ် စကားလုံးအလှတွေ သုံးနေကြတာပါ၊ ဒါဟာ အရေးပါတဲ့ နိုင်ငံရေး ရည်ရွယ်ချက်အတွက် ပြုလုပ်ထားတဲ့ ပြဇာတ်တစ်ခုပါပဲ။ ဒီလို လှည့်ကွက်မျိုးနဲ့ နိုင်ငံရေးသမားတွေက မင်းတို့ကို လှည့်စားထားတာပါ။ သူတို့ ကြောက်နေတာဟာ အခွန်ဘဏ္ဍာ ဆုံးရှုံးမှာကို မဟုတ်ဘဲ၊ “မင်းတို့ရဲ့” အလုပ်တွေ၊ “မင်းတို့ရဲ့” ကျန်းမာရေးစောင့်ရှောက်ခွင့်တွေ၊ နဲ့ “မင်းတို့ရဲ့” လူမှုဖူလုံရေးတွေ ဆုံးရှုံးမှာကို ကြောက်နေရတာပါဆိုပြီး ယုံအောင် လှည့်စားထားတာပါ။ တရားဝင် ရှိနေပြီး အလုပ်လုပ်နေသူတွေ (အခွန်ဆောင်နေသူတွေ) ကိုတော့ မျိုးချစ်စိတ်ရှိသူတွေအဖြစ် သတ်မှတ်ပေးထားပါတယ်။ အစိုးရက သူတို့ရဲ့ လစာထဲက ဖြတ်တောက်ယူနေတာကို မုန်းတီးစရာလို့ မမြင်ဘဲ အားလုံးရဲ့ ကောင်းဖက်အတွက် အရေးပါတဲ့ ပါဝင်ဆောင်ရွက်မှုအဖြစ် ကြိုဆိုကြရပါတယ်။ ခွင့်ပြုချက်မရှိဘဲ အလုပ်လုပ်သူတွေကိုတော့ ရန်သူတွေ၊ တရားဝင် အလုပ်လုပ်နေသူတွေရဲ့ မွန်မြတ်တဲ့ အလုပ်ကို ဖျက်ဆီးနေသူတွေအဖြစ် ပုံဖော်ကြပါတယ်။ “မင်းတို့” က လူကောင်း၊ “သူတို့” က လူဆိုး ပေါ့။ နိုင်ငံရေးအရ အင်အားမရှိတဲ့ တရားမဝင် ရွှေ့ပြောင်းအခြေချသူတွေဟာ ဝါရှင်တန်အတွက် တိုက်ခိုက်ရ အလွယ်ဆုံး ပစ်မှတ်ဖြစ်နေပြီး နိုင်ငံရေးသမားတွေရဲ့ စိတ်ကူးယဉ် ပြဿနာရှာမှုတွေအတွက် လွယ်လွယ်ကူကူ …

author: Elizabeth Weill-Greenberg
title: Activists Are Pushing Cities and Companies to Cancel Parking Contracts With ICE
content:
The Trump administration’s abduction and deportation machine is multifaceted. There are clear-cut components — agents, shackles, and jails — and less obvious, although no less essential, ones — cars and parking spaces.


In an effort to impede the attacks on immigrants, mayors of some of the country’s largest cities, including

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani

,

Chicago Mayor Brandon Johnson

, and

Boston Mayor Michelle Wu

, have issued executive orders

banning Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE)

 from using city-owned parking lots and properties.


But even in cities where mayors have banned ICE from using government-owned properties, ICE still has free reign to contract with private companies. After the federal agency

posted a notice

 seeking “Surge Parking” in 14 cities, including Boston, Wu

released a public letter

 to

local parking garage and lot owners

, warning them that if ICE were “to procure such resources, it would constitute an unprovoked and unwarranted escalation, creating potentially significant risks to public safety and halting economic activity across our entire region.”


“Today, I ask you to join us: Reject any proposition by ICE to facilitate an attack on the people of Boston,”

she wrote

. “In the face of escalating attacks on cities across the country, we have repeatedly seen that the strongest defense is solidarity.”


In the Boston suburb of Burlington, Massachusetts, Bearing Witness New England has been holding weekly protests outside ICE’s Boston Field Office, where people are

held for days

 in inhumane conditions. Activists say ICE has been keeping its vehicles in a nearby parking lot owned by local developer National Development.


According to a report by

NPR

 affiliate

WBUR

, the company sent a letter to local activists in February, stating that ICE vehicles were being “improperly parked” in its parking spaces, and that it had “reached an arrangement with ICE that they would no longer park their vehicles on our property.”


However, the company also said that the government agency, the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), has

rights to use the garage

 and the company does not have authority over how the FAA parcels out parking spaces to other federal agencies, according to

WBUR

’s report.


Nathan Phillips, a Boston University professor who organizes with the Burlington-area coalition

Building Up Resilience Networks (B.U.R.N.)

, says ICE has continued to park in sections of lots National Development leases to the FAA that exceed what the lease allows.


Protests that target parking garages are “throwing sand in the gears” of ICE’s deportation and abduction machine, he says.


“So much of their operation depends on logistics of transport and travel,” Phillips told

Truthout

. “It’s human trafficking, and so if we can go after the trafficking, the means by which they’re doing this, that can have a really effective impact.”

          Sign Up


Fellow B.U.R.N. activist Josh Model says National Development’s recent actions contradict its public image as a

philanthropic company

 committed to improving communities.


“National Development Corporation, which, as a local developer, likes to promote that they’re cognizant of community needs and give to charity and all these nice things,” but they’re “letting ICE stage kidnappings” from their property, said Model.


While the government spending website,

usaspending.gov

, only lists 12 active contracts for parking spaces, as of September 28, the true number of parking lots that ICE uses is likely much higher, said Model. It’s difficult to untangle where ICE is parking, in part, because many of the contracts are not with ICE, but through another federal agency, the

General Services Administration

 (GSA), he said. The GSA manages government buildings and real estate, and owns or leases space in more than 8,300 buildings, according to an

explainer

 on the agency published by the Congressional Research Service.


In the case of National Development, ICE is using parking leased by the GSA for the FAA, according to Model.

author: Marcelo Oliveira
title: Mulheres são maioria das vítimas de violência política, mesmo sendo minoria das candidatas
content:
O primeiro turno da campanha eleitoral de 2026 durou 50 dias e registrou 134 episódios de violência política contra candidatos e candidatas, além de agentes políticos.

Um aumento de 11% em relação aos 121 casos registrados no mesmo período da eleição municipal de 2022.


Os 134 episódios representam um caso de violência política a cada nove horas de campanha.

 E apesar das mulheres serem apenas 35% do total de candidatos, elas foram a maioria (52%) das vítimas do primeiro turno, segundo o levantamento.


Os dados integram a 4ª edição da pesquisa Violência Política e Eleitoral no Brasil, realizada pelas organizações de direitos humanos Terra de Direitos e Justiça Global, que pesquisa o tema desde 2016. O levantamento foi divulgado nesta quarta, dia 7 de outubro.


A porcentagem de

vítimas mulheres aumenta

 mais ainda quando a pesquisa separa apenas os casos envolvendo candidatas e candidatos. Dos 134 episódios de violência política durante o primeiro turno, 102 foram dirigidos a pessoas que disputavam o pleito. Desse total, 60 eram mulheres, quase 59% do total.


Para a coordenadora do Setor de Incidência da Terra de Direitos, Gisele Barbieri, “os dados trazem importantes achados para identificar os ambientes em que agentes políticos estão mais vulneráveis e pensar medidas de proteção. Quando eleitas, essas pessoas passam a ser vítimas de violências nos seus locais de atuação, seja no Parlamento ou no Executivo”, afirma.


Machismo e misoginia se misturam nos casos de violência política


A pesquisa mostra que a violência política é marcada pela discriminação de gênero e raça.

Quando se considera o universo completo de 70 casos de violência política contra mulheres, 45 casos envolveram machismo ou misoginia, nove envolveram racismo e cinco envolveram transfobia. Mulheres pretas foram vítimas de 25% dos casos de violência política medidos nesse primeiro turno.


A ameaça foi o tipo de violência política mais recorrente no período, com 64 casos registrados. Na sequência, aparecem 33 episódios de ofensa e 19 de agressão física. Também foram registrados 11 atentados, cinco casos de criminalização e dois assassinatos.


Mais da metade dos casos (71 ocorrências) aconteceu nas ruas, durante atividades públicas de campanha. O ambiente virtual concentrou 31,3% dos episódios.


Além disso, apenas candidatas sofreram ameaças de violência sexual. Em todos os sete casos, as vítimas eram mulheres.


“Enquanto os homens são atacados por sua atuação política, mulheres, pessoas negras e pessoas trans enfrentam também o racismo, o machismo e a transfobia que estruturam a sociedade brasileira”, afirmou em nota Glaucia Marinho, diretora-executiva da Justiça Global.


Policiais e outros agentes públicos foram a maioria dos autores


Em quase 20% dos casos o autor identificado da violência política era um agente público, incluindo parlamentares e forças de segurança.

Até o encerramento da coleta de dados pelas organizações autoras da pesquisa, nenhum dos 134 episódios havia resultado em alguma punição efetiva, limitando-se a medidas cautelares de urgência determinadas pela Justiça Eleitoral.


A região Nordeste liderou o número de casos (48), seguido pelo Sudeste (38). Entre os estados, São Paulo lidera com 16 casos, seguido por Rio Grande do Norte (13), Minas Gerais (12) e Rio Grande do Sul (10).


A presença de policiais entre os autores de violência política já havia sido detectada também em

levantamento

 realizado pela

Agência Pública

 durante o primeiro turno.

author: anred
title: Los sepultureros de Gaza de Norman Finkelstein es una obra maestra
content:
Hay hechos sin consecuencias, libros sin seguimiento. ¿Qué haremos de esta monumental investigación y razonamiento que apela a nuestra conciencia y debería impulsarnos a la acción? Lo que está en juego es la esencia misma de la existencia civilizada, los valores de la Declaración Universal de los Derechos Humanos, los propósitos y principios de las Naciones Unidas. El genocidio en Gaza no es solo otro Holocausto monstruoso, es un espectáculo público.

[1]

 El fracaso de las Naciones Unidas para detenerlo y la inacción de la mayoría de los estadounidenses y europeos nos hacen a todos cómplices del crimen, porque

qui tacet consentire videtur

. Si solo somos

voyeurs

de esta masacre en curso, tenemos, como mínimo, responsabilidad moral. Por Alfred de Zayas 


En los últimos 30 años, Norman Finkelstein nos ha brindado muchos libros brillantes, entre ellos

Método y locura, Acuso, Saber demasiado,

Gaza

,

Más allá de la desfachatez

y

La industria del Holocausto.


Este libro de más de 400 páginas documenta el colapso civilizatorio de las clases dominantes en Occidente, la traición a todos los valores humanistas, el rechazo demasiado público por parte de Israel del derecho internacional y la moral, con la complicidad,

entre otros

, de Estados Unidos, Reino Unido, Francia, Alemania y la Unión Europea.


Todo esto se ve acompañado por la cacofonía de los medios de comunicación convencionales orwellianos, que difunden noticias falsas, historia falsa y leyes falsas, especialmente con respecto a los palestinos como pueblo, a quienes se les representa erróneamente como “terroristas”, cuando poseen el derecho, reconocido en el derecho internacional, a resistir la colonización y la ocupación.

[2]


Nelson Mandela también fue tildado de «terrorista», pero fue fundamental en la lucha por la liberación de su pueblo. Hoy todos reconocen que el fin del apartheid en Sudáfrica era algo que debió haberse hecho hace mucho tiempo. ¿Cuándo veremos el fin del apartheid en Israel y los Territorios Ocupados? Esto es lo que Jimmy Carter exigió en su libro

Palestina: Paz, no apartheid

.

[3]


Los políticos occidentales y los principales medios de comunicación han invertido los papeles y han culpado a la víctima de su desgracia. Israel es el terrorista que practica el terrorismo de Estado y coloca trampas explosivas en los buscapersonas, como demostró de forma obscena el primer ministro israelí Benjamin Netanyahu durante su diatriba en la Asamblea General de la ONU el 24 de septiembre de 2026.

[4]


Israel nació del terrorismo

[5]

 contra británicos y palestinos, ha sido un Estado agresor desde su creación, en un sentido muy real un

Estado fallido

, porque no ha aprendido a vivir en paz con sus vecinos.


Israel ha atacado Líbano, Siria, Irak, Irán, Egipto, etc. En una infame operación de falsa bandera, incluso atacó el buque de inteligencia de la Armada de los Estados Unidos USS

Liberty

[6]

 en junio de 1967, matando a 34 marineros estadounidenses, en un intento fallido de involucrar a los Estados Unidos en la guerra de agresión de Israel.


Israel ha sido un estado paria desde su creación en 1948, e incluso antes.


El genocidio de Gaza no es más que una continuación de la intención criminal de establecer un «Gran Israel» anacrónico e imperialista en medio del mundo árabe y musulmán.


[Fuente:

cartooningforpeace.org

]


Sin duda, los gobiernos de Israel, Estados Unidos y la UE están moralmente en bancarrota.

[7]


Lamentablemente, la

percepción

de la realidad es más determinante que la realidad misma. Dado que nuestras acciones están condicionadas por la información de la que disponemos, nuestro juicio se ve influenciado —e incluso subvertido— por las narrativas odiosas que recibimos de los principales medios de comunicación, y nuestras opiniones se distorsionan por el incesante discurso de odio y la propaganda contra los palestinos. Esto constituye una incitación al odio y a la violencia, en contravención del artículo 20 del Pacto Internacional de Derechos Civiles y Políticos.

[8]


Los principales medios de comunicación difunden la versión israelí y suprimen las opiniones disidentes. No solo nos mienten, sino que nos privan de información crucial que cambia radicalmente la situación.


El público es manipulado, pero muchos se dejan manipular. Como escribió Julio César en

De Bello Civili (II, 27, 2): «quae volumus, ea credimus libenter»

(Creemos lo que queremos creer). O peor aún, como decían los romanos …

author: Rizomatica
title: Escuela Popular Campesina José Bengoa Cabello: Diez años sembrando educación popular desde Curaco de Vélez
content:
La Escuela Popular Campesina José Bengoa Cabello de Curaco de Vélez, Chiloé, celebró sus diez años de vida con dos jornadas que reunieron a estudiantes, profesoras y profesores, organizaciones sociales, artistas, artesanas y artesanos, voluntariado y comunidad, marcando además la inauguración oficial de esta nueva etapa que lleva el nombre de José Bengoa Cabello, manteniendo viva una memoria que no queremos solamente recordar, sino proyectar desde nuestros territorios.


El encuentro comenzó reuniendo a estudiantes y profesorado de la Escuela Popular Campesina José Bengoa Cabello de Curaco de Vélez (Chiloé) y de la Escuela Ismenia Ortiz Lizama de Palquibudis (Curicó), compartiendo una asamblea entre ambas experiencias campesinas, para continuar con Saberes del Mar, junto al profesor Constantino Contreras, y el conversatorio de Género y Ruralidad con Ximena Valdés, «porque hablar del mundo rural es también reconocer a las mujeres, sus trabajos, aquello que históricamente ha permanecido invisibilizado y las transformaciones que aún necesitamos impulsar», destacaron en la presentación.


Seguidamente, el 29 de agosto, el Gimnasio Bordemar de la Población Vista Hermosa de Curaco de Vélez acogió una extensa jornada. Desde la organización, se señaló: «Quisimos expresar aquello que somos y en lo que creemos, uniendo cultura, formación, organización y autogestión, con puestos de artesanía de nuestras ferias, organizaciones sociales, estudiantes, voluntariado y productos de ambas escuelas, haciendo posible que una parte importante de la actividad se financiara desde nuestro propio trabajo colectivo».


La organización del festival de la Escuela, también resaltó:

«Para nosotros la autonomía y la autogestión no son solamente principios escritos, son prácticas que se aprenden haciendo, compartiendo responsabilidades y poniendo cada cual algo de sí para sostener lo que hemos decidido construir en común».


Como señala Janett Cárdenas, esta trayectoria también nos invita a preguntarnos para qué educamos y desde dónde lo hacemos:


«Seguimos apostando a que la educación es una acción transformadora y una herramienta política que ponemos a disposición de quienes queremos transformar este modelo de injusticia, porque educarnos es también organizarnos, recuperar nuestra memoria y reconocernos en nuestros propios saberes, comprendiendo que desde el campo, el mar, las semillas, la artesanía, la cultura y la experiencia de quienes nos antecedieron se construye conocimiento para transformar nuestra realidad.»


La jornada permitió también reconocer a personas que han acompañado ese andar: Ximena Valdés, en memoria de José Bengoa; Sergio Faumangaun, director de la Escuela Campesina Águila Sur; la familia Gamin, en memoria de don Enrique Gamin; Mirian Alarcón, voluntaria y profesora de Agricultura Campesina desde el comienzo de este camino en 2016; y Patricio Larco, profesor de Acuicultura.


La cultura, inseparable de la manera de comprender la formación y la vida comunitaria, estuvo presente con Patricio Guerrero, Raíces Curacanas, Amaranto, Maribel Manquecoy, Javier Chandía, el bloque infantil integrado por Luis Soussi y Natali, Daniela Reyes, Aliwen, Nancy San Martín y su banda, Los Pirulonkos, Almas Chilotas y Rancheritos Vientos del Sur, quienes generosamente acompañaron esta celebración con música, voces y expresiones nacidas también desde nuestros territorios.


«Mirar estos diez años es reconocer que la Escuela ha podido sostenerse gracias a estudiantes, profesoras y profesores voluntarios, campesinas y campesinos, artistas, organizaciones y familias que han compartido conocimientos, trabajo, semillas, alimentos, música, tiempo y afectos, haciendo posible una experiencia que no pretende enseñar desde arriba, sino construir conocimiento desde aquello que cada una y cada uno sabe y aporta»

, señaló la declaración de la Escuela.


Agregan en su declaratoria:

«Cumplir una década no significa cerrar una historia, sino mirar lo caminado para continuar, ahora llevando el nombre de José Bengoa Cabello y recogiendo esa invitación a SER, HACER y PENSAR, desde Chiloé, desde nuestras insularidades y desde el mundo campesino, convencidos de que mientras existan saberes que compartir y comunidades dispuestas a organizarse, existirán también posibilidades de transformación»

.


Finalizaron con la consigna:

«Seguiremos sembrando esperanza desde la educación popular, porque educarnos, organizarnos y transformar nuestra realidad son parte de …

content:
Y decimos esto porque dentro de los estudiosos existe una gran cantidad de profesionales que no sólo se guían por sus conocimientos académicos, sino también se nutren del saber popular y lo utilizan para complementar su trabajo.

Y en este caso nos estamos refiriendo a una antropóloga, a Laura Kropff (UNRN), investigadora de la Universidad de Río Negro, que participó del Consejo de Seguridad Interior realizado en Tucumán, en una mesa de diálogo con la sociedad civil.


En esa oportunidad demostró su importante conocimiento sobre la realidad del mundo mapuche y en su exposición repasó como el Estado nacional avanzó sobre el territorio indígena, como fueron desplazadas las comunidades y como se establecieron verdaderos  campos de concentración. Resulta interesante escuchar las reflexiones de la antropóloga, que con extrema crudeza expone los ciclos históricos que las comunidades mapuches han tenido que sobrellevar.


Al mismo tiempo que aporta importantes datos históricos, reconoce las injusticias cometidas contra esas comunidades.  Así que escuchémosla entonces.

author: Darío Aranda
title: Marcos Pastrana y la sabiduría diaguita para pensar la época
content:
Por Agustín Brun


Desde Tucumán


En Tafí del Valle, Tucumán, reside Marcos Pastrana, referente diaguita e histórico defensor de la naturaleza. Sus ideas, expresadas con las palabras justas y necesarias, invierten muchas veces el sentido común, convocan a ver la realidad desde otra perspectiva. Una mirada indígena, que con una sabiduría que emana de la ancestralidad de la cosmovisión andina busca sacar el velo de tanta modernidad y tanta ciudadanía, para así poder ver lo que llama la “realidad profunda” de las cosas.


Visitar su territorio, su hogar y concretar

una entrevista filmada de 67 minutos

 como registro de memoria, ideas y propuestas.


Recordar y transmitir


Había una larga lista de preguntas, pensadas durante días, buscando la mejor forma de aprovechar la ocasión. Pero alcanzó con apretar el botón "grabar" y pedirle que se presente para que comience una alocución libre, sin apurar las palabras, pero sin detener el curso de su pensamiento. No importaron las preguntas, ya que aconteció algo más interesante: un testimonio extenso, donde Pastrana reflexiona a partir de años caminando los territorios en defensa de la vida.


Sus palabras transcurren entre sentires autobiográficos, análisis de un presente que le preocupa fuertemente, reflexiones sobre el cosmos y la estética natural, pero también sobre el robo de los recursos genéticos, el saqueo de las tierras raras a través de mineraloductos, de las guerras y de la historia de la humanidad y cómo nos la cuentan. Reivindica los derechos de los pueblos indígenas, que deben ser reconocidos por las instituciones, pero poniendo una alerta a cuando los Estados, gobiernos y demás entidades globales no lo hacen: el derecho natural fluye, no es algo que dependa de un acta.


Pastrana describe a la Pacha no como una “figura de adoración”, sino como el “espacio que debemos ocupar en el tiempo que nos toca vivir”. Y es esa, su Pacha, la que le ha dado la obligación, la responsabilidad histórica, de “recordar y transmitir” el concepto del "Buen Vivir" comunitario.


Foto: María Teresa Cañas


Los cuatro elementos


“No hay que temerle al caos, porque del caos venimos”, afirmó Pastrana en el

Congreso de Salud Socioambiental en 2023

, en un momento ciertamente caótico, a meses de las elecciones presidenciales donde finalmente ganaría Javier Milei.


¿A qué se refiere con caos?”. Para el pensamiento de Pastrana es fundamental la diversidad. Lo que el sistema extractivista llama “orden”, no es más que una homogeneización, una clausura de la diversidad, en pos de la estética artificial. Esto anula lo que realmente es el orden cósmico, al que el sistema llamaría “caos”, y que es energía, vida en expansión, y que es fundamental entenderla como el verdadero orden cósmico para así poder abrazar la estética natural.


“La estética precede a la ética”, define Pastrana. Y recuerda un debate con académicos y amautas (palabra quechua que refiere a las sabias indígenas), donde Leonardo Boff —filósofo y ecologista brasilero— describe a la ética como uno de los cuatro elementos para el Buen Vivir. Un amauta de Cusco (Perú) le responde que se está olvidando de la estética. Porque justamente el apego y respeto por la estética natural, por sobre la estética artificial, es la que luego no permite hacer daño “a nadie ni a nada”.


De este modo, el abuelo diaguita reivindica el entorno y los cuatro elementos de la cosmovisión andina que lo conforman: el agua, el aire, la tierra y el fuego (la energía). Son esos cuatro elementos, es decir la naturaleza, los que hay que defender, como base de toda lucha. “Quien no defiende ni valora los cuatro elementos, no defiende a nadie. Ni a las personas, ni al ambiente, ni a los pueblos, ni a la democracia”, arremete.


Y define que ésa es la esencia del ser indígena. Si se abandona la lucha y la defensa de los cuatro elementos, del entorno y la estética natural, la persona deja de ser indígena en toda su dimensión, y pasa a ser otra cosa, independientemente de su color de piel, origen étnico o nombre. Esa es, entonces, la base de una vida en armonía con el entorno y el resto de los seres humanos. Afirma que quienes buscan instaurar un “orden” a través de la estética artificial no hacen más que crear daño, por más que ello se “adorne con todas las leyes, convenios, constituciones”.


Pastrana advierte sobre la

patrimonialización de los territorio, las creaciones de reservas

 por y para las élites financieras del mundo, mientras el resto del planeta …

title: Transmisión en vivo, 18:00 horas y palabras del Subcomandante Insurgente Moisés en la reunión del 3 de octubre del 2026 a las 1100 hrs.
content:

Sesión Informativa sobre el Viaje-Abrazo a Buscador@s, diciembre 2026-Enero 2027 CIDECI de San Cristóbal de Las Casas, Chiapas, México
