Palabras del Subcomandante Insurgente Moisés en la reunión del 3 de octubre del 2026 a las 1100 hrs.

.- El principal objetivo: el encuentro-abrazo con buscadoras. Es importante que esto se entienda bien y quede bien claro. Porque no vamos a cancelar una reunión o actividad con Buscadoras por cualquier otra cosa.

Llevamos muchos años esperando el momento de encontrarnos con ellas.

Entonces, la prioridad o lo más importante en nuestra agenda o programación son las reuniones, encuentros y actividades con las Buscadoras, el día y la hora que ellas establezcan.

Cualquiera otra propuesta de actividad o reunión, deberá ser cuando no haya encuentro o actividad con buscadoras.

Incluso la celebración del aniversario del alzamiento será dependiendo de nuestro abrazo con las Buscadoras.

.- Ya está la paga para los buses de la delegación. Se consiguió gracias al apoyo de la Europa Insumisa, que donó lo que se había juntado para el Capítulo Europa de la Gira por la Vida, y que no se usó completamente. Estas compañeras, compañeros y compañeroas nos dijeron, desde hace tiempo, que esa paga es de los zapatistas, pero, hay que decirlo, es producto de su trabajo, su esfuerzo y su dedicación, y hay que reconocerles esa solidaridad incondicional. Esperamos que ese ejemplo sea luego replicado en capítulos siguientes de la Gira por la Vida, de modo que cada capítulo apoye la realización del siguiente.

Mientras tanto, aquí reconocemos el trabajo desinteresado de todas las personas, grupo, colectivos, organizaciones y movimientos de la Europa de abajo y a la izquierda.

También ha sido fundamental el trabajo de apoyo del colectivo de la Sexta México. “Mujeres y la Sexta”, para conseguir los autobuses.

Gracias compañeras, compañeros y compañeroas. A las Buscadoras les haremos saber de su apoyo.

.- Por lo tanto, toda la campaña económica será ahora para apoyar el traslado de todos los grupos, colectivas y organizaciones posibles a la Ciudad de México, en las fechas que les parezcan más adecuadas a ellas, dentro del mes de diciembre del 2026 y la primera semana de enero del 2027.

En el caso de amenazas y peligros, se tratará de que su traslado ida y vuelta sea por vía aérea, de modo que no corran riesgos al transportarse por tierra.

.- Les vamos a quedar mal porque no vamos a ir 1,111, sino que hasta ahora van 1,509. Más los que se suben de última hora. Pero hay lugar para el Frayba por si quieren acompañarnos.

.- el segundo objetivo es reunirnos con algunos grupos, colectivos, movimientos y organizaciones de la Sexta para planear juntos, en común, lo que sea posible para la segunda etapa de la Gira por la Vida-Capítulo México.

Esto es, cuando vamos a ir a escucharles de lo que son y están haciendo, y hablarles de lo que somos y estamos haciendo, o sea del común.

.- Si hay tiempo y modo, podemos movernos a lugares cercanos geográficamente a la Ciudad de México.

Pero sólo si hay condiciones y somos invitados. Hasta ahora hemos recibido invitación a Oaxaca, Oaxaca; a Querétaro, Querétaro, y se está viendo si a Puebla, Puebla. Si es posible en otros lugares, hay que organizarse y proponer.

Las compañeras de Oaxaca empezaron a organizarse desde que se anunció la salida a la Ciudad de México. Tienen ya resuelto el hospedaje y la alimentación para un parte de la delegación zapatista.

.- Estamos organizados por equipos y podemos cubrir bien lo que se haga en el Valle de México y hacer presencia en geografías cercanas. Así, dislocados, podríamos cubrir al mismo tiempo varios lugares, y varios temas.

Hemos elegido ese día, por si alguien de la Ciudad de México o de puntos …

author: La Zarzamora
title: Comunicado público ppm Caso Grollmus
content:
Frente a las exuberantes condenas y tras un viciado proceso declaramos:

Mari mari pu machi, pu lonko, pu werken, kom pu che. El día de hoy nos dirigimos a la sociedad en general, a todos y todas quienes nos han brindado su apoyo y respaldo en este proceso denominado “Caso Grollmus”.

Actualmente a nosotros como comuneros mapuche se nos ha condenado a penas que marcarán un precedente como obscenamente políticas, se nos condena por decisión política, por ser mapuche que vivimos y recuperamos nuestro territorio.

Tras el gigantesco despliegue comunicacional, y tras el espectáculo montado por el Ministerio Público y la PDI, la familia Grollmus demanda al estado en busca de indemnizaciones y reparaciones.

La fiscalía con el aval del tribunal logró su objetivo: condenar a una pena que ponderada resulta en 1055 años de prisión contra nosotros. La prensa vociferó la sentencia y el poder político respaldo, claridad absoluta.

Les decimos, su ocupación contra nuestro pueblo y su territorio apenas tiene 143 años. Nuestro pueblo resistió al imperio español casi 300 años.

Hoy Chile soberbio y republicano nos condena a más de 1000 años. Por el único motivo de luchar por nuestra soberanía, por nuestro buen vivir y dignidad. Lo anterior tendrá la más necesaria respuesta: continuar con el legado de nuestro pueblo, luchar por nuestra dignidad y libertad.

Los Grupos de Tarea y la BIPE de la PDI recorren los penales de forma morbosa buscando testigos a quienes poner corbata de protegido y sin rostro. Sólo por cuatro relatos de estos “testigos” se dictó sentencia y veredicto. Nuestro territorio se militariza y vuelven a saquear nuestros recursos naturales, vuelven las concesiones mineras, CMPC y Mininco cual mecenas entregan dinero y donaciones a Postas y Escuelas.

Queremos manifestar nuestro agradecimiento por todo el respaldo de nuestros hermanos y hermanas en otros territorios y ciudades. No renunciaremos jamás a la lucha por un debido y objetivo proceso.

Nos movilizaremos por nuestra libertad y juicio justo.

Finalmente los invitamos a sumarse a la próxima movilización articulada en distintos territorios para este 12 de octubre, Día de la resistencia de nuestros pueblos.

¡NULIDAD Y LIBERTAD! ¡NO MÁS TESTIGOS PROTEGIDOS! ¡UNIDAD EN EL WEYCHAN! ¡LIBERTAD A TODOS LOS PRESOS POLÍTICOS MAPUCHE!

Presos Políticos Mapuche del Caso Grollmus de la Franja Lavkenche, CP Biobio, CERECO Coronel, Cárcel Llancahue de Valdivia.

author: Riyad Insanally
title: La autonomía indígena en el sistema interamericano: a cinco años del informe de la CIDH sobre libre determinación
content:
El sistema interamericano reconoce la autonomía de los Pueblos Indígenas y Tribales como un derecho preexistente. De este modo, no debe ser entendido ni como una concesión ni como una cuestión otorgada. El fallo de la Corte Interamericana de Derechos Humanos a favor de la autonomía del pueblo U'wa de Colombia es la expresión más reciente del derecho de los Pueblos Indígenas a autogobernarse, a definir sus propias instituciones y a decidir sobre sus asuntos internos.

El 4 de julio de 2024, la Corte Interamericana de Derechos Humanos condenó al Estado colombiano en el caso del Pueblo Indígena U’wa y sus miembros, por no haber garantizado la consulta previa, libre e informada frente a decenas de proyectos extractivos superpuestos a su territorio ancestral. Dictada tres décadas después de que el pueblo U’wa hiciera pública su resistencia frente a la exploración petrolera en su territorio, la sentencia reafirmó estándares centrales sobre la libre determinación indígena: la relación indisoluble entre el territorio, la identidad cultural y la capacidad de un pueblo de decidir su propio destino.

Ese pronunciamiento no aparece de la nada. Confirma y aplica estándares que la Comisión Interamericana de Derechos Humanos (CIDH) había sistematizado cinco años antes, cuando el 28 de diciembre de 2021 aprobó su informe temático “Derecho a la libre determinación de los Pueblos Indígenas y Tribales”. Allí, la Comisión identificó a la autonomía, es decir, al derecho de los pueblos a autogobernarse, a definir sus propias instituciones y a decidir sobre sus asuntos internos, como uno de los elementos constitutivos de la libre determinación, junto con la autoidentificación, la identidad cultural, la propiedad colectiva, los derechos políticos y de participación, y la consulta y el consentimiento previo, libre e informado.

A cinco años de ese informe, y con un caso reciente que vuelve a poner el tema en la agenda regional, vale la pena revisar qué ha dicho específicamente el sistema interamericano sobre el derecho a la autonomía y al autogobierno de los Pueblos Indígenas y Tribales, en sus distintas dimensiones. Ese es el propósito de este artículo: recorrer los estándares desarrollados por la Comisión y por la Corte, mostrando que el caso U’wa no es un hecho aislado, sino la expresión más reciente de una línea de trabajo institucional sostenida durante más de dos décadas, a través de informes temáticos y de casos de la CIDH, y de una jurisprudencia interamericana en constante desarrollo.

La libre determinación de los Pueblos Indígenas y Tribales no se agota en el reconocimiento de la propiedad colectiva de sus tierras. Según ha señalado la CIDH, ese derecho conlleva también la facultad de autogobernar los territorios a través de las propias autoridades, en ejercicio del derecho a la autonomía o al autogobierno reconocido expresamente en el artículo XXI de la Declaración Americana sobre los Derechos de los Pueblos Indígenas (DADPI) y en el artículo 4 de la Declaración de las Naciones Unidas sobre los Derechos de los Pueblos Indígenas (UNDRIP). La Comisión advierte que el ejercicio de la gobernanza territorial es una de las expresiones más relevantes de la libre determinación indígena y tribal, porque supone el reconocimiento de sistemas de gobierno propio que asumen el control, el manejo y la administración del territorio ancestral.

Ese control no se limita a un título de propiedad. La CIDH subraya que un componente esencial de la autonomía indígena y tribal es el control efectivo de los territorios ancestrales y de los recursos naturales que allí se encuentran, en tanto son la base material de la existencia de estos pueblos como sujetos colectivos, y no una mercancía: son “la base de su subsistencia económica” y también “fuente de su identidad cultural y bienestar espiritual”. Sin embargo, la Comisión constata con preocupación que, a la fecha, muy escasos Estados de la región han establecido mecanismos legales o administrativos que garanticen la autonomía de los Pueblos Indígenas y Tribales sobre sus recursos naturales y medios de subsistencia. Por el contrario, señala que los ordenamientos internos, en general, impiden que estos pueblos sean titulares de derechos sobre los recursos naturales de su propio hábitat.

Ya en 2001, en el caso de la Comunidad Mayagna (Sumo) Awas Tingni Vs. Nicaragua, la Corte Interamericana había reconocido la estrecha relación entre el territorio y la subsistencia de los Pueblos Indígenas como colectivos …

author: Comunizar
title: Revista Crítica Anticapitalista 6 – La Comuna, la clase y la lucha de clases
content:
PRESENTACION


¿Qué relación existe entre la Comuna como forma política de la emancipación social y la clase, entendida ésta no como categoría positivizada y sociológica, sino en su carácter dual y contradictorio? ¿Es la Comuna una manera de entender la clase y la lucha de clases en clave no identitaria, no positivizada? ¿La oposición entre Comuna y clase es algo derivado de una concepción anti-dialéctica de la lucha de clases? En ese campo ¿a qué dialéctica nos referimos? ¿A la dialéctica hegeliana orientada a la síntesis estatal como forma política de la identidad? ¿A la dialéctica negativa que la cuestiona? ¿La lucha de clases, entendida en clave dialéctica no-identitaria, permite entender la Comuna como proceso contradictorio de disolución de la clase? ¿Implica esto un desafío a nuestro concepto de proletariado y a la idea de revolución calcada en el canon leninista?

author: Andrea DiP
title: Há três anos os palestinos pagam pelo 7 de outubro
content:
Quis o destino que eu estivesse na Cisjordânia neste 07 de outubro, e que essa coluna fosse publicada no exato dia em que,

3 anos atrás, o ataque terrorista do Hamas que resultou na morte de cerca 1000 pessoas entre civis e militares, deu início a um massacre cometido pelo

Estado de Israel

 que, até agora, somente na

Faixa de Gaza, já matou mais de 75 mil e feriu mais de 170 mil palestinos. 


Eu sei que o Brasil pega fogo neste momento e é difícil falar em outra coisa ou pensar em um povo que está tão longe geograficamente. Mas talvez nós possamos aprender uma coisa ou duas sobre resistência e resiliência

 com um povo que vem sendo oprimido, colonizado e sofre tentativas reiteradas de apagamento há mais de 100 anos. 


Meus avós são sobreviventes do Holocausto. Minha avó polonesa e meu avô romeno passaram por campos de concentração e tinham números tatuados neles. Ainda jovens migraram para o Brasil, onde se conheceram e formaram família. E é também por respeito a essa história que não posso me calar diante de um genocídio étnico que acontece

live stream

 nos celulares na palma de nossas mãos. 


Nos últimos dias estive rodando pela Cisjordânia, visitando comunidades palestinas que estão sendo despejadas, torturad

as, roubadas e dizimadas por milícias israelenses formadas por colonos e por militares.

 A Cisjordânia é um território palestino que fica no Oriente Médio, situado na margem ocidental do rio Jordão, entre Israel e a Jordânia. É dividida em três zonas administrativas – zonas A, B e C –  segundo os Acordos de Oslo, assinados na década de 1990, que previam transferir gradualmente o controle do território para a Autoridade Palestina. A área teoricamente estaria sob controle total da Palestina. A área B teria um controle misto entre Israel e Palestina e a área C, cerca de 60% da Cisjordânia, está sob controle israelense total, tanto para administração civil quanto para segurança. 


Mas atualmente esses contornos estão cada vez mais borrados, com colonos israelenses tomando cada vez mais áreas.


Tudo isso ainda vai virar reportagem e indico o Pauta Pública desta sexta-feira (09/10) com o diretor geral do Centro de Assistência Jurídica e Direitos Humanos de Jerusalém (JLAC) e membro do Conselho de Comissários da Comissão Independente de Direitos Humanos da Palestina (ICHR), Issam Aruri, que traz uma verdadeira aula sobre o conflito na região. 


Mas queria contar aqui na coluna uma


das histórias que mais me marcou até agora: A de uma mulher de 67 anos, moradora de um vilarejo em Masafer Yatta

, que fica nas colinas ao sul da cidade de Hebrom, cerca de 70km ao sul de Ramallah – capital administrativa da Cisjordânia. Não vou revelar seu nome por motivos óbvios. Mas

sua vila está totalmente cercada por


assentamentos israelenses, que tentam a custo de barbárie expulsar os palestinos que estão ali há dezenas de gerações, vivendo da colheita de azeitonas e do pastoreio de ovelhas e cabras. 


Sua vila não tem água encanada nem luz. Se vê apenas pedras, areia, pequenas casas e barracões. Os cabos de energia passam por cima da comunidade, de um lado a outro, para os assentamentos israelenses, mas os palestinos não podem usar. Foi instalado um portão na estrada, que pode ser fechado pelos soldados a qualquer momento e por tempo indeterminado, impedindo os moradores de entrar ou sair, mesmo que em emergência médica.

 Essa é uma prática bastante comum na região. Até mesmo ruas dentro de comunidades são fechadas indiscriminadamente pelas forças israelenses. 


“Foi aqui que um colono israelense matou meu filho”. A senhora aponta para um ponto do centro de convivência, que já foi destruído e reconstruído várias vezes e que abriga o único banheiro disponível para a comunidade.

 As casas tinham banheiro. Mas eles foram destruídos ou absurdamente declarados como zonas militares, tornando-se inacessíveis aos moradores. Sua filha mora em uma casa há poucos metros dali e não pode usar o próprio banheiro nem construir outro sem permissão. Mais: o celeiro, que fica no quintal da casa, foi declarado “zona militar” e trancado, então a família não pode levar os animais para o pasto ou mesmo chegar perto do pequeno barracão. O exército israelense passa por lá uma vez na semana (quando muito) para alimentar as ovelhas e cabras, que estão obviamente morrendo paulatinamente. 


“Um colono entrou na comunidade e atirou na cabeça do meu filho. Meu neto, aquele ali  – aponta para um gurizinho de uns 3 anos – estava no colo …

author: anred
title: «Construir colectivamente donde dicen que no se puede»: presentan experiencia de los barrios comunitarios Crisol Popular y Norita Cortiñas
content:
¿Cómo se construye un barrio cuando todo parece indicar que no se puede? Este jueves 8 de octubre, a las 17, se presentará en la Facultad de Ciencias Exactas y Naturales de la UBA el cuadernillo “Barrios comunitarios: construir colectivamente donde dicen que no se puede”, que sistematiza la experiencia de los barrios comunitarios Crisol Popular, en Cuartel V, Moreno, y Norita Cortiñas, en Guernica. La actividad se desarrollará en el Aula 1115 del Edificio Cero + Infinito y contará con un conversatorio sobre el rol de la universidad y la academia en los procesos de organización territorial.


La publicación reconstruye una experiencia nacida después de la recuperación de tierras de Guernica en 2020 y desarrollada a partir de la organización comunitaria, el acceso a la vivienda, el trabajo autogestionado y la articulación con equipos técnicos, universidades y organismos públicos. Ambos proyectos comparten “acceso a la vivienda con perspectiva comunitaria”, “asamblea como método de organización”, “defensa de los derechos humanos” y “generación de trabajo autogestionado comunitario”.

Por ANRed.


Este

jueves 8 de octubre

, a las

17

, se presentará en la

Facultad de Ciencias Exactas y Naturales de la UBA

 el cuadernillo

“Barrios comunitarios: construir colectivamente donde dicen que no se puede”

, una sistematización de la

experiencia de los barrios Crisol Popular

, ubicado en

Cuartel V, Moreno

, y

Norita Cortiñas

, en

Guernica.

 La actividad será en el

Aula 1115 del Edificio Cero + Infinito

 y estará acompañada por un conversatorio sobre el

rol de la universidad y la academia en los procesos territoriales

.


La experiencia tiene su origen en la

recuperación de tierras de Guernica de 2020

. El documento que convoca al conversatorio señala que en aquel momento “

2.000 familias resistieron tres meses hasta ser violentamente desalojadas el 29 de octubre de ese año

” y que, posteriormente,

las familias continuaron organizadas en asambleas para reclamar tierras destinadas a vivir y producir alimentos

. A partir de esa organización surgieron

los proyectos que luego dieron lugar a ambos barrios comunitarios

.


El cuadernillo reconstruye una experiencia que busca enfrentar una problemática estructural.

Según los datos del ReNaBaP citados en la publicación, existen “6.467 barrios con graves problemas de infraestructura y de habitabilidad” donde viven “1.287.942 familias en situación de pobreza e indigencia”

; la mitad de esas familias se encuentra en la provincia de Buenos Aires. El documento ubica allí el contexto de la recuperación de tierras y de la posterior construcción comunitaria.


El barrio comunitario

Crisol Popular

 se constituyó en 2022 sobre un terreno de cinco hectáreas en

Cuartel V

, adquirido luego de que uno de los proyectos impulsados por las asambleas fuera aprobado por la Secretaría de Integración Socio Urbana. En el caso del barrio

Norita Cortiñas

, la propia organización logró concretar la compra comunitaria de un terreno de dos hectáreas en Guernica, después de que el segundo proyecto no obtuviera financiamiento estatal.


 


Ver esta publicación en Instagram


 


Una publicación compartida por Barrio Comunitario CRISOL POPULAR (@barriocomunitariocrisolpopular)


 


Ver esta publicación en Instagram


 


Una publicación compartida por Taller Libre Proyecto Social (@tlpsfadu)


Los dos barrios comparten una serie de acuerdos que colocan a

la organización comunitaria en el centro

. Entre ellos aparecen el “

acceso a la vivienda con perspectiva comunitaria

”, la “

asamblea como método de organización

”, la “

defensa de los derechos humanos

”, la “

perspectiva de género, rechazo a la violencia hacia mujeres, niñeces y disidencias

”, la “

preocupación sobre el impacto ambiental y energético

” y la “

generación de trabajo autogestionado comunitario

”.


La publicación también sistematiza el trabajo realizado para resolver necesidades básicas que el acceso formal a una vivienda no garantiza por sí solo. Entre los objetivos aparecen “lograr condiciones dignas de habitabilidad para las familias de ambos barrios”, garantizar agua potable, mejorar el acceso a la energía y desarrollar sistemas de drenaje y tratamiento de efluentes. En los dos barrios, los estudios realizados determinaron que el agua disponible no era apta para el consumo.

title: Karasu: Once Öcalan’s freedom is secured, the conspiracy will be completely defeated
content:
In the second part of this interview with

Medya Haber

, KCK Executive Council member Mustafa Karasu said that the aim of the conspiracy against Abdullah Öcalan on 9 October 1998, was to completely dismantle the Freedom Movement. He said that the political approach pursued by Leader Apo, and the prospect of resolving the Kurdish question on a democratic basis, would weaken the collaborative foundations on which the United States and other external powers relied, and that the International Conspiracy was therefore carried out by the United States and Israel.


The first part of this in-depth interview can be read

here

.


We are approaching the 28th anniversary of the international conspiracy against Kurdish people’s leader Abdullah Öcalan, which started on 9 October 1998, and concluded on 15 February 1999. What kind of approach and stance towards the international conspiracy, given the current political juncture, do you see as appropriate?


Before answering these questions, I must mention our very dear comrades who were martyred in October. They were pioneered by the comrades Gurbetelli Ersöz (8 October 1997), Nagihan Akarsel (4 October 2022), and Bêrîtan (25 October 1992), who fell as martyrs in the month of October. I knew comrade Gurbetelli Ersöz personally. While we were in prison, she would regularly attend our meetings. Later, she was assigned to work in the press, and we maintained contact during her time in Europe. She was a good friend, and I knew her well. Truly a conscious comrade. She had strong patriotic feelings and was a person who had a good understanding of Rêber Apo [Kurdish people’s leader Abdullah Öcalan] and the movement. When she first came to prison, she hadn’t yet fully joined the movement as a cadre. At that time, she was still in college, but she was already actively involved. She had actually decided to join but still had academic work to complete at the university. Later, she took on responsibilities in the press and truly shaped the press work.


During the 1990s, when our movement was developing, the role of the press was extremely important. The press’s coverage of our struggle truly made significant contributions to the development of the struggle. Particularly in this regard, our comrade Gurbetelli played a very important role. She laid the foundation for our press, shaped its spirit, and defined its perspective. Gurbetelli Ersöz is a pioneer of the press within the freedom movement. It is therefore that our press academy today is named the ‘Gurbetelli Ersöz Academy.’ Press activities, the academy, and the training programs are all conducted in the name of our comrade Gurbetelli. She holds a truly vital place in our struggle, and still today her stance is of great importance to us. After her work for the press in Europe, she came to the guerrillas. Her participation in the struggle in the mountains was truly enthusiastic and meaningful. Her transition from the press to the guerrilla ranks – joining the guerrillas with such a level of consciousness – naturally represented an important stance from the guerrillas’ perspective in terms of guerrilla training, organization, and the struggle. I commemorate her with respect and gratitude.


Nagihan Akarsel was also an important journalist. She was a force of thought. As is known, she was assassinated in Sulaymaniyah. The Turkish state bears great guilt in this murder. The Turkish state has murdered many of our comrades, particularly our journalists, with their UCAVs. Many of our comrades working in the media in Sulaymaniyah, the Medya Defense Zones, and in Southern Kurdistan in general have been murdered by the Turkish state’s airstrikes and UCAV attacks. I commemorate all of them with gratitude and respect.


Comrade Nagihan Akarsel was not only a journalist but also made very important contributions to Jineolojî, the science of women’s liberation. She is one of the pioneers of the science of women’s liberation. And Jineolojî is the mother of all sciences. It is the mother of the social sciences. Without understanding the science of women’s liberation, the social sciences cannot be properly understood. The social sciences cannot be properly addressed. And the contributions of Nagihan Akarsel to Jineolojî have truly been immense. I also remember her with gratitude and respect.

author: Kodao Productions
title: Leandro Leviste’s arrest order explained
content:
A local court ordered the arrest of one of the country’s youngest and richest legislators over alleged alleged failures to put up solar energy farms in accordance with a congressional franchise awarded in 2019.


Makati City Regional Trial Court Branch 235 issued a warrant of arrest against Batangas Rep. Leandro Leviste on Monday, October 5, for allegedly violating the country’s Public Service Act (PSA). The warrant set Leviste’s bail at P72,000.


Leviste, however, is in Europe in an extended and unexplained absence from his duties as a member of the House of Representatives .


What is Leviste accused of?


Leviste is the founder of the Solar Para sa Bayan (Solar for the People) Corporation, granted a 25-year franchise to construct, install, establish, operate, and maintain solar-powered generation facilities and mini-grid systems in the Philippines. His company promised to supply affordable, reliable, and sustainable electricity to underserved areas in the Philippines.


The company, however, failed to deliver, resulting in cancelled service contracts and billions of pesos in government penalties, the Department of Energy (DOE) reported.


Leviste however succeeded in raising more capital by going public with a derivative company, the Solar Philippines Nueva Ecija Corp. that was valued at P60.9 billion (Dh3.57 billion) at the time of its initial public offering in December 2021.


He subsequently divested large blocks of shares to Meralco PowerGen Corporation (MGen) and other investors, earning over P34 billion in the process.


Government regulators said Leviste violated his congressional franchise by not seeking permission before selling parts of his operations to other entities. Leviste’s firm was subsequently slapped with a P24 billion fine.


Who is Leviste?


The 33-year old first-term legislator is a son of incumbent senator Loren Legarda and former Batangas provincial governor Antonio Leviste.


The younger Leviste came into national political consciousness when he publicly criticized former allies of past Philippine President Rodrigo Duterte who jumped ship and allied themselves with the ruling Ferdinand Marcos Jr. clique after the Marcos-Duterte fallout in 2024.


His troubles escalated when Marcos’ Executive Secretary Ralph Recto publicly accused him of attempting to offer large-scale payoffs (allegedly ranging from P400 million to P1 billion) to influence political outcomes in Batangas. Recto, himself from Batangas Province, is a political rival of the Levistes.


Leviste left the Philippines in August, purportedly to accompany his mother Legarda in seeking medical treatment abroad. Legarda’s medical leave with the Philippine Senate had been extended six times.


Does Leviste deserve arrest?


Leviste’s lawyer Antonio La Viña said Leviste’s arrest warrant was based on “a complaint looking for a crime.”


La Viña said Leviste did not implement the franchise because the DOE did not issue the necessary rules and regulations. The agency did not identify the places where the franchise could be implemented.


“[Y]ou cannot invoke a general penal clause of a law without identifying specific provisions in the law which an accused has committed. In other words, ‘no harm, no foul,’ the lawyer added.


Leviste belittled the arrest order, saying it is “a small matter compared to the other things happening.”


“I am more concerned about you,” he added.


Center of the crisis


As two of the rapidly dwindling Duterte allies in the Philippine legislature, the mother-son’s legal troubles are only expected to worsen.


Last Sunday, Philippine Ombudsman Jesus Crispin Remulla announced the impending filing of about 20 graft and corruption charges against Leviste and Legarda.


Legarda is a member of the Senate minority allied with Vice President Sara Duterte who is undergoing an impeachment trial. Two of her colleagues are in jail for plunder while another is in hiding from an International Criminal Court arrest order.


In a heated debate two weeks ago, the Senate decided that only those who are physically present during the trial promulgation may vote whether to absolve or to oust the Philippine vice president from office.


Duterte’s public threats to have Marcos assassinated and the ongoing trial to oust the vice president are described as one of the worst political crises in the Philippines in the century. #

(Raymund B. Villanueva)

title: Why do we Protest? A Moral and Philosophical Basis
content:
The protests that have sparked in most South Asian countries in the last few years have sparked hope for socio-political, economic, and cultural change. Bangladesh’s protest over the job crisis in 2024, Nepal’s Gen Z protest (2025), and Sri Lanka’s protest of 2022 shocked the nations and their corrupt political systems. The Gen Z protest forced ruling BJP minister Dharmendra Pradhan in India to resign and raised demands for educational reform and accountability in 2026. The growing unrest of youths and their protests demand an objective analysis. This article asks some fundamental questions on the moral, philosophical, existential, and political basis of protest. More than answering the question of why we protest, this article is about why we should protest. While the outward manifestation and result of protest are obvious, the inward changes that protest brings are pertinent in shaping the morale of individuals in particular and society in general.

Let us ask, therefore, why shall we protest? Do we protest because we are bad? Bad as citizens, bad as human beings, bad daughters, and sons? Why do our youth protest? Why does this act of protest arouse so much fear? Fear from society and the state. Aristotle writes that “young men (and women) have strong passions and tend to gratify them indiscriminately” (Aristotle 2012). The younger generation possesses tremendous energy, creative force, and potential. More importantly, they are full of life, and life, to thrive, needs proper conditions that the current regime has failed to provide. However, it is the nature of life to expand itself. Hence, the protest of the youths. The old society, religion, and state use force to serve their purpose, and they try to control the boundless possibilities of youths. When any social and political structure downplays human nature and the necessities of life, we can no longer contain ourselves and remain silent. There is a limit to the control of the inner nature of humanity. Family, society, religion, and political power have always been terrified of human nature. They are forever trying to control, subjugate, and overpower the true potential of humanity.

Gods came, religion came, and then came the state! But is it possible to contain our boundless humanity that runs in our veins? History has proven again and again that it has never been, and never will be, able to suppress the beauty of humanity. The way religion, society, and the state forever wish to control individuals, individuals, in return, have forever rebelled and protested in every way possible. No god, no religion, no society, or no state can contain our boundless humanity. Is it possible to contain a forever-flowing river? We might try to control and put a brake on its flow for a temporary period of time, or it may dry out in a particular season. But for how many days? For how many seasons and years? It will return in the next season; it will return next time; eventually, with more vigorous force, it will make its own course. Nothing can stop it from reaching its destination.

In the same way, human beings possess immense potentiality. Hence, their free actions, thinking, and will cannot be stopped. Protest and rebellion can manifest in different ways. It may not always be political in nature. Sometimes it is chaotic, enigmatic, mysterious, decadent, and even in the form of telling the truth. When politics reduces to a level of tyranny, we rebel not only in the political domain but also in art, literature, science, and even in philosophy. Rebellion is a part of human life and its very existence. Reducing everyone who reads, thinks, and creates to the level of ‘Dimagi Naxal’ by none other than Narendra Modi, PM of India, is absurd and brands basic human nature and constitutional rights as criminality. His comments came in the wake of the Gen Z protest that was led by highly educated minds of India. Hence, delegitimising them while branding them with various tags is an act unbecoming of a leader of the nation. It must have been an act of rebellion that attracted people in power. All of these are various forms of negotiation with the existing socio-political structure. When we refuse the dictates of family, society, religion, or the state, that act of refusal becomes a site of protest. The protest must be understood as an act of negation. Camus rightly asked, “What is a rebel? A man who says no” (Camus 2013). While saying ‘no’ to negative politics, organisations, and beliefs …

author: Brian Hioe
title: What Did China Intend to Accomplish Through Surveilling Lai Ching-te’s Son?
content:
THE FBI HAS arrested a woman, Wanying “Heather” Zhang, for acting as an unregistered foreign agent of China. In particular, Zhang’s arrest occurred because she was apparently conducting surveillance on Lai Ting-yu, the son of President Lai Ching-te.

Lai’s family generally keeps a low public profile. Lai, who is in his 30s, is thought to work for electronics manufacturer Philips and to have a young child. Zhang is accused of traveling to Seattle from Los Angeles and renting a vehicle to surveil Lai’s home along with an accomplice.

Zhang is accused of being in contact with a Chinese handler through WeChat, as well as other individuals she knew were Chinese government officials. Zhang worked as a real estate agent and was detained as she was about to board a flight for Shanghai. It is possible, then, that Zhang could be a civilian recruited by China, or that the Chinese government has continued with its practice of employing “disposable” agents.

It is unclear what China hoped to gain from surveilling Lai, who was not likely to have any sensitive government information. Nevertheless, one aim could be to threaten, by putting Lai and his family members living abroad on edge, and to warn of the potential repercussions of going against China. If China wished to broadcast that it was aware of Lai Ting-yu’s whereabouts and could potentially threaten him, this could be used for leverage over Lai, or to blackmail him. China might also seek to project power, in suggesting that it is omnipresent and all-reaching, such that it can surveil and threaten relatives of Taiwanese politicians abroad.

Otherwise, it is possible that China aimed to obtain political ammo from surveilling Lai’s son. The presence of Lai’s son in the US, for example, could be used to suggest that Lai himself may push for strengthening defense against China, but that his own children live in the US, and that Lai would potentially abandon Taiwan in wartime.

Indeed, even if the daughter of Chinese President Xi Jinping is also thought to live in the US, the presence of Lai’s children in the US has been used as a political attack for some time by the KMT. More generally, Taiwanese politicians who have children in the US, or who may have potentially held Green Cards or US passports in the past, have been used to attack them with the allegation that they plan to abandon Taiwan in wartime.

More generally, one notes that the Chinese government has been increasingly willing to target relatives of Taiwanese politicians. DPP legislator Puma Shen’s father has been sanctioned, for example, due to owning a car parts company in China. It is possible that there are other cases in which relatives of Taiwanese politicians have already been threatened, but which have not necessarily come to light.

title: Fuel hikes squeeze jeepney drivers, commuters dry
content:
Jeepney with signage: "No to Oil Price Hike" (Photo by Roselle Ochobillo/Bulatlat)

By Wendyl Geronimo and Roselle Ochobillo

For commuters, the recent P1 increase in jeepney fares may seem small. But for workers who rely on public transportation every day, the additional peso can add to an already tightening budget.

For jeepney drivers, meanwhile, the bigger burden is not the fare increase itself but the fuel prices behind it.

After several rounds of oil price increases, diesel prices have continued to eat into drivers’ daily earnings, leaving some struggling to provide food, pay rent and keep their children in school.

The pressure was among the reasons transport groups, including the Pagkakaisa ng mga Samahang Tsuper at Opereytor Nationwide (PISTON), held a nationwide strike on Sept. 29 and 30, calling for lower petroleum prices and relief from fuel taxes.

For 52-year-old jeepney driver Teody Bermejo, National Capital Region and Alabang Pasay President said that the additional peso in fare does little to address what drivers actually spend to keep their vehicles running.

Bermejo, who has been driving for around 30 years, said he now spends much of his working day trying to recover the cost of diesel.

He drives from around 4:00 a.m. until 9:00 p.m., or as long as 16 hours a day. When diesel was around P50 to P55 ($0.80 to $0.88) per liter, he said he could take home around P1,000 ($15.98), sometimes reaching P1,500 ($23.97).

Now, he said, his take-home income has fallen to around P500 to P600 ($7.99 to $9.59), despite the long hours on the road.

“That is really not acceptable to us because diesel prices have increased by around P52 to P55 ($0.83 to 0.88), while they only added P1 to the fare. There is a huge difference. It really won’t be enough for us.”

For Bermejo, the impact of rising fuel prices has reached his household. He has four children in school, but his income can no longer cover their needs at the same time.

One of his children who was in college had to temporarily stop studying and find work to help the family.

“My child in college had to stop studying for now. In a way, they also had to find a job to help me because my income now is not enough to support all of them in school at the same time.”

He said the family is now trying to continue the education of his other children while making ends meet with his reduced income.

The same struggle is felt by 50-year-old Janet “Arja” Tumbaga Pocsidio, a member of Piston Women who helps operate a Cubao-Divisoria route.

Pocsidio is a mother of five and helps provide for her children and grandchildren. When diesel prices reached around P140 to P145 ($2.24 to $2.32) per liter, she said their earnings from driving became too small to sustain the family.

On some days, her husband would earn only P70 to P80 ($1.12 to $1.28).

The family eventually stopped operating their jeepney for periods because the cost of fuel outweighed what they could earn from passengers.

Pocsidio then worked as a barker, earning around P250 to P400 ($3.99 to $6.39) a day, which she used for food and her children’s school expenses.

The rising cost of basic necessities also changed what the family could afford to eat.

She said they often relied on dried fish and eggs, while even small increases in food prices became noticeable in their daily budget.

Housing became another burden. Pocsidio said their family was paying P6,000 ($95.88) in monthly rent, aside from electricity and water.

Eventually, they were forced to leave their rented home because they could no longer keep up with the payments.

“We were evicted, and we ended up sleeping in our jeep. Yes, we were evicted because we couldn’t afford to pay,” Pocsidio told Bulatlat.

The family later stayed at the Piston San Juan office for about four months, where they paid for electricity.

For her, depending on the organization for shelter was difficult.

“I feel ashamed. I’m extremely ashamed. I’m quite self-conscious, but I have no other choice. I just told myself that I would leave it in the Lord’s hands.”

While drivers struggle with operating costs, commuters are also adjusting their budgets.

Bench Cuabo, a government worker, said that the P1 ($0.02) fare increase may appear minimal but still affects his daily transportation expenses.

He said his usual P15 ($0.24) fare has increased to P17 (0.27), and when drivers cannot provide change, he sometimes ends up paying P20 ($0.32).

title: ‘We can’t report anything against AP govt’: National media silent on Tirumala Tirupati controversy after ED and CBI probes debunk false claims of ‘beef tallow’ use
content:
In a press release on 17 September 2026, eight months after the Supreme Court-appointed CBI Special Investigation Team (SIT) explicitly ruled out the presence of animal fats in the ghee used for manufacturing the Tirumala Tirupati temple’s prasadam, the Enforcement Directorate has arrested a promoter of a private food company allegedly involved in contamination after lab forensic analysis revealed the presence of seven adulterants. Notably, none of them are animal fats, specifically ‘beef tallow’, the allegation of whose presence triggered outrage and investigation in the first place, and cemented a political upset in the state by amplifying communal tensions.


 


by

 Mouli Sharma


 


On 19 September 2024, Andhra Pradesh’s Tirumala Tirupati temple had taken over national and regional news by storm for an unsavoury reason: an allegation of the presence of animal fats in the temple’s

prasadam

 (consumable offerings to Hindu deities given as blessed alms to devotees), specifically the accusation that ‘beef tallow’ was used in the rendering of adulterated ghee used to make the temple’s laddus. Unverified accounts of ‘lab reports confirming the allegations’, which were amplified by TDP’s CM Chandrababu Naidu himself, eventually led to an FIR about the same being registered on 25 September 2024, followed by a PIL being filed in the Supreme Court by one Dr. Subramanian Swamy.


Over a year later, the allegations were debunked by a Special Investigative Team constituted by the CBI to investigate the case, whose forensic examination categorically ruled out the use of animal fats, though the presence of synthetic adulterants was confirmed.


On 17 September 2026, almost exactly two years later, the enforcement directorate reproduced the same findings. Seven adulterants were listed in an ED press release announcing the arrest of a food promoter allegedly involved in multi-crore transactions behind the procurement of the adulterated ghee—Refined Palm Oil, Palm Kernel Oil, Palmolein, MG-90, Monoglycerides, Myvacet Soft 400 and Acetic Acid Ester—none of which are animal fats of any kind, let alone fats of particularly polarising animals, like cows.


 


On 17 September 2026, almost exactly two years later, the enforcement directorate reproduced the same findings. Seven adulterants were listed in an ED press release announcing the arrest of a food promoter allegedly involved in multi-crore transactions behind the procurement of the adulterated ghee—Refined Palm Oil, Palm Kernel Oil, Palmolein, MG-90, Monoglycerides, Myvacet Soft 400 and Acetic Acid Ester—none of which are animal fats of any kind, let alone fats of particularly polarising animals, like cows.


In the light of both revelations, the dozens of mainstream media outlets across the country who expounded the now debunked claims without any evidence of their legitimacy back when the controversy had first surfaced, fanning communal sentiments within the country’s dominant caste-Hindu population, triggering a rise in hate speech, and cementing the popularity of the then newly elected NDA government in the state, have remained conspicuously silent.


“Unfortunately, we cannot use any news content against the AP government. I cannot say more than that,” he said.


Major newspaper outlets with the largest circulation rates in India; channels with the highest viewership statistics, and websites at the top of Search Engine Optimisation and provenance score rankings—The Times Group, The Express Group, Firstpost, The Hindu, Dainik Bhaskar, NDTV, and many more—all solicit their newsdesk items from this agency. This is possibly why the only visible headlines currently in the public domain that acknowledge this debunking, are the opposition party’s own social media posts, and an article by The News Minute, an independent alternate online news portal focusing on the South.


 


A noteworthy aspect of the entire controversy was that the allegations, from the outset, were being made in retrospect. Though the Telugu Desam Party had already come to power by the time the FIR was registered, with Naidu having replaced YSRCP’s Jagan Mohan Reddy (who was then targeted for his Christian identity) during the Legislative Assembly elections in May 2024, the complainant made it clear that his accusations were about procurements made during the preceding government’s tenure.

title: Announcing Asian Labour School Oct-Nov 2026 Semester
content:
Dear friends,


We are back with an amazing list of new and returning courses for the Asian Labour School. If you are interested in

acquiring democratic facilitation skills, navigating conflicts and taking collective care, working cooperatively, strengthening a union core or leading your own radical walking tours

, please check out the course information below and study with Asian Labour School.


Building Movement Democracy through Democratic Facilitation (Course Starts on Oct 15, 2026)


Facilitator: Chie Matsumoto


We all have attended meetings where decisions were made by only a few members, most outspoken ones or someone at the top. We may have once thought, “Why am I even here?” and left without saying a word. Democracy starts in the smallest conversations, dialogues and meetings by raking in most diverse opinions and ideas, piecing them together to create something new and meaningful to all participants.


Building Movement Democracy through Democratic Facilitation (Course Starts on Oct 15, 2026)


Worker Cooperatives: Can Cooperating Transform How We Work Together? (Course Starts on Oct 10, 2026)


Facilitators: Emi Do and Matt Noyes


Worker cooperatives are enterprises that are owned and governed by workers. When all of our working experiences have been in profit-maximizing enterprises, or in workplaces that are structured hierarchically, it is no wonder that we can encounter challenges when attempting to work together cooperatively. In this course we will explore the challenges and tensions when there are no bosses to hate!


Worker Cooperatives: Can Cooperating Transform How We Work Together? (Course Starts on Oct 10, 2026)


Careful, We’re Organizing aka How to Fight without Falling Apart (Course Starts on Oct 21, 2026)


Facilitator: Nash Tysmans


Movements are built through relationships. Yet the pressures of organizing (urgency, conflict, exhaustion, political disagreement, and unequal power) can strain those relationships and undermine our collective capacity. How can we build movements that are both effective in challenging injustice and caring in how we work together?


Careful, We’re Organizing aka How to Fight without Falling Apart (Course Starts on Oct 21, 2026)


Building Strong Union Committee at Workplace (Course starts on Oct 15, 2026)


Facilitator: Sithar Chhim


In order to win any campaign at workplace, unions need to be strong enough to pressure the company. Building a strong and representative committee is the only way to win over the bosses who have well organized structure at workplace compare to workers.


Building Strong Union Committee at Workplace (Course starts on Oct 15, 2026)


Designing Radical Walking Tours (Course Starts on Oct 12, 2026)


Facilitator: Kevin Lin


Have you ever thought about leading your own radical walking tour to share with friends the significance of places and histories in your city? Leading and participating in a radical walking tour is not only educational but fun and always memorable. A walking tour provides a concrete sense of places, people, and histories. This course will walk you through the conceptualisation, research and logistics of a radical walking tour, and hear ideas and experiences from other participants across Asia.


Designing Radical Walking Tours (Course Starts on Oct 12, 2026)

title: Sleeper-Cell Report July 2026 – Global Coalition reports 0 confirmed ISIS attacks
content:
An ISIS flag was raised on a school building in al-Zubari, eastern Deir ez-Zor countryside


 


Key Points


– Six sleeper-cell attacks recorded by RIC, but the Global Coalition claims 0 attacks were officially claimed by ISIS


– One military personnel was killed, and a further five injured


– A minimum of seven alleged ISIS members were arrested


– A total of 36 civilians were injured, two killed


– An ISIS flag was raised on a school building in Deir ez-Zor


–

Two Tunisian families linked to ISIS mercenaries repatriated from Roj camp


 


In-Depth


In July of 2026, RIC

recorded six sleeper-cell attacks which some publications have attributed to ISIS, according to


North Press Agency

 one of these attacks was claimed by ISIS whereas the


Global Coalition


reported that July was the first month since the territorial defeat of ISIS in 2019, where they claimed 0 attacks. Also this month at least 7 members of ISIS cells were arrested.


On July 7, Bombings struck central Damascus near the Ministry of Tourism and the Four Seasons Hotel, during the visit of Macron the president of France to Syria. Ministry of Interior has attributed the attack to ISIS, the bombing resulted in the killing of one civilian and injury of 36.


On July 8, three attacks happened during the same day and the are believed to have been carried out by ISIS members.

Unidentified gunmen on a motorcycle used machine guns to target an oil truck in Abrahyah town in eastern Deir ez-Zor countryside, killing the driver.


Similarly, unidentified gunmen on a motorcycle, attacked a checkpoint of the Internal Security Forces near al-Baserah city bridge.


According to North Press Agency, also on July 8 ISIS

claimed responsibility for the killing of Rashad Khalaf al-Ghurair in the northern countryside of Deir ez-Zor.


On July 15,

unknown gunmen on a motorcycle opened fire on a member of the 72nd Division on the road linking al-Arimah and Manbij in eastern Aleppo countryside, injuring the him.


On July 18,

two unidentified gunmen on a motorcycle opened fire directly on member of the Defence Ministry


near al-Awsajli junction in eastern Manbij city.


On July 9,

Syria’s Interior Ministry announced its security forces had dismantled several ISIS cells in southern Syria, arresting a senior leader and several members accused of involvement in assassinations and financing terror.


On July 28,

Syrian Internal Security Forces and the General Intelligence Service in Aleppo announced the arrest of individuals allegedly affiliated with the ISIS, during a security operation in Aleppo and its surrounding countryside.


An ISIS flag was raised on a school building in al-Zubari, eastern Deir ez-Zor countryside, in an incident that sparked widespread concern among residents.


During July, Two Tunisian families linked to ISIS were repatriated from


Roj Camp, which houses families of ISIS members, and returned to Tunisia. Additionally, Tunisian citizen Bilal Chawachi was sentenced to 55 years in prison after being convicted on terrorism-related charges, specifically traveling to Syria and fighting alongside the extremist organization.


Germany sentenced an Iraqi man to life imprisonment and his former wife to nine years and six months in prison after convicting them of enslaving and torturing two Yazidi girls while they were members of ISIS in Syria and Iraq between 2015 and 2017.


Three U.S. citizens pleaded guilty to terror charges, prosecutors said the defendants communicated through encrypted messaging applications between July and November 2025 and planned to travel to Turkey before crossing into Syria to join ISIS. 


* Due to the low rate of confirmed ISIS attacks RIC has decided to stop publishing monthly sleeper-cell reports and instead share a bi-annual summary of ISIS activity throughout Syria.

title: Once again on Kurdish democratic unity
content:
The creation of Kurdish democratic unity continues to be a matter of urgent importance. The stage reached by the Third World War, which is spreading and deepening across the Middle East, makes this an immediate necessity. The process initiated by Abdullah Öcalan’s Call for Peace and Democratic Society on 27 February 2025 has made Kurdish democratic unity an urgent task.


Although some collaborationist-nationalist circles continue to create obstacles, the forces supporting national democratic unity are growing by the day. Kurdish intellectuals and politicians are placing greater emphasis on democratic unity than ever before. Politicians are speaking about democratic unity, while intellectuals are writing about it. There is a demand both for unity and for that unity to be democratic, because the Kurds need both unity and democracy. At present, there is neither sufficient national unity nor sufficient democracy. Yet developments in the region and the struggle in Kurdistan need democratic unity more than bread and water.


The stage reached by the Third World War in the region is creating both significant opportunities for the Kurds and very serious dangers. To seize these opportunities and avert these dangers, the Kurds need to unite and develop their democracy. With Kurdish politics fragmented, lacking unity and democracy, it does not appear possible to seize these opportunities or avert the dangers. Almost everyone now sees and expresses this. More importantly, all of us have a responsibility to fulfil such a task for the success of the Peace and Democratic Society Process initiated and led by Abdullah Öcalan.


The process initiated by the Call for Peace and Democratic Society on 27 February 2025 is clearly pushing both the Kurds and Turkey as a whole, including the state and society, towards change and democratization. The steps taken by the Kurdish Freedom Movement in this direction are prompting everyone to reassess their current position and move towards democratic change and transformation. This is undoubtedly not easy in one respect; it requires greater courage and sacrifice, as well as more courageous criticism and self-criticism. In another respect, it places new and greater responsibilities before everyone, requiring a more organized and creative struggle. The tasks of the new process cannot be accomplished through the fragmented, excessively centralized approaches and structures of the past that placed only one’s own party at the centre. In short, the Peace and Democratic Society Process is compelling all Kurds to create democratic unity.


The approach of the Turkish side, namely the state and the government, to the Peace and Democratic Society Process makes Kurdish democratic unity even more important and urgent. For example, the final statement issued after the National Security Council meeting on 30 September clearly shows that there is nothing new on the Turkish side. In both content and tone, the statement is identical to National Security Council statements from two years ago. Despite a new process having been underway in Turkey for two years, it still refers to the “Kurdistan Workers’ Party (PKK)-Kurdistan Communities Union (KCK) terrorist organization” and places it in the same category as ISIS. Naturally, when the National Security Council uses such language, the special warfare media uses the same language and content. But what will happen if the Kurdish side and Kurdish media also continue to speak of the “fascist Turkish Republic”? The National Security Council statement is entirely anti-Kurdish and makes the elimination of Kurdish gains and Kurdish existence a central political objective. What, then, remains of the discourse of Turkish-Kurdish brotherhood?


The final statement of the National Security Council meeting on 30 September makes it very clear that there has been no change in the anti-Kurdish mentality and policies of the Republic of Turkey. With the state maintaining this position, the Justice and Development Party (AKP) government is also implementing the same mentality and policies on a daily basis. In this context, we should look at what the AKP government is doing. Has there been any democratic change compared with two years ago? Not only is it clear that there has been no such change, but it can even be said that repression and exploitation have increased. Most importantly, there has been no change in the conditions of Abdullah Öcalan. Even the Peoples’ Equality and Democracy …

author: Kodao Productions
title: How the Al-Aqsa Flood Shattered the Two-State Solution
content:
By

Prof.


Sarah Raymundo


Marking three years since Operation Al-Aqsa Flood requires confronting how October 7 shattered the foundational ideological facade of modern imperialist diplomacy: the two-state solution.


Far from being a mere military escalation, the Flood operated as a decisive historical rupture that definitively broke the illusion that occupation could be perpetually managed through endless diplomatic process. It shattered the false premise that a people under genocidal  foreign domination could be pacified by paper accords built on the systematic erasure of history.


Where imperial diplomacy attempts to reduce occupation to a manageable border dispute, the underlying reality has been laid bare: the Palestinian question is fundamentally a struggle for national liberation against settler-colonialism, driven by the historic necessity of an oppressed nation to achieve emancipation by all means necessary, including armed resistance.


Even comprador regimes thoroughly integrated into the US-Israeli orbit are occasionally forced to acknowledge the weight of global outrage. The Philippine state—despite its active complicity in Israeli settler-colonialism through agricultural, economic, and military-cultural exchanges—joined the historic walkout at the UN General Assembly during Netanyahu’s address.


This integration runs deep: under Washington’s direction, the Philippines is being incorporated into Pax Silica, a US-led technology and critical minerals framework that serves as direct war infrastructure. The semiconductors and supply corridors produced under this arrangement function to power the Zionist military apparatus and its broader campaign across the Arab-Iran region.


Yet, while the UN walkout presented a momentary divergence, the Philippine diplomatic apparatus swiftly reverted to form, clarifying its position by reaffirming adherence to the very two-state dogma that October 7 shattered.


Far from offering a pathway to liberation, the two-state doctrine represents one of the most persistent, insidious ideological constructs of modern imperialism. It operates precisely to allow international actors to project a humanitarian stance while ensuring the structural preservation of settler-colonial dominance. Dialectically, this framework functions not as a resolution to national oppression, but as a management technology designed to institutionalize it across three critical dimensions:


First, an examination of the primary diplomatic texts reveals a foundational deception. The phrase “Palestinian state” is entirely absent from the Oslo Accords; from its inception, the framework was engineered to reduce national liberation to a series of fragmented, demilitarized bantustans under administrative proxy control.


Second, rather than reflecting an indigenous aspiration of the Palestinian national liberation movement, the two-state model emerged as a liberal Zionist construct later adopted and weaponized globally by US imperialism—particularly under the Bush administration—to neutralize regional resistance and manage imperial stability.


Third, the material reality of the occupation exposes the structural utility of the framework: while Washington maintained the diplomatic illusion of negotiations, the Israeli ruling class proceeded with complete clarity that no sovereign Palestinian state would ever be permitted.


Imperialism utilized the rhetoric of the “peace process” as an ideological shield, securing the necessary time and political cover to expand illegal settlements, fragment territory, and entrench apartheid.


The Al-Aqsa Flood permanently shattered this paradigm. Historically, Palestinian revolutionaries and regional anti-imperialists have understood that the Palestinian condition cannot be resolved through diplomatic management between unequal entities. It is an ongoing anti-colonial war against foreign occupation and imperialist hegemony.


A framework engineered by imperial powers to preserve a colonial garrison state can never produce genuine self-determination. True liberation requires the complete dismantling of the apartheid state of Israel, an end to foreign occupation, and the realization of Palestinian national sovereignty from the river to the sea. #

author: Yuanyi Tham
title: Mega Anthropic data centre to blight Queensland
content:
Queensland is set to become home to Australia’s largest AI data centre. Last month, Liberal National Party Premier David Crisafulli announced a landmark deal with Anthropic to develop the Western Downs Digital Park, near the town of Dalby, about 250 kilometres northwest of Brisbane. Led by Singaporean developer Zerra DC, the site will be constructed in four phases, with the first building expected to be operational next year.

The data centre will occupy 725.5 hectares, an area twice the size of New York’s Central Park. Its estimated value is $32 billion, nearly five times the 2032 Brisbane Olympics infrastructure budget.

Data centres suck up huge amounts of power, driving up energy prices and accelerating climate change. When fully constructed, electro-mechanical engineer Dr Andreas Helwig told the ABC it would use the equivalent of 25 to 30 percent of Queensland’s total energy consumption.

The data centre will run primarily on electricity generated by coal and gas, drawn from the state’s electricity grid. Greenpeace estimates that the data centre would raise the grid’s emissions by 6.6 million tonnes, the equivalent of two million extra cars on the road.

Last month, Crisafulli wrestled with the federal government and eventually won a state exemption from the requirement that data centres run on renewable energy. The exemption, Crisafulli argued, was simply “common sense”; according to him (and now the Labor cabinet), environmental protections shouldn’t get in the way of AI investment opportunities.

While workers worry about AI’s impact on their jobs, power bills and the environment, Crisafulli has never been happier. He celebrated the data centre deal as the fruits of his five-day trip to the US in early September, where he met with the CEOs of OpenAI and Anthropic. On the same trip, he met with US Vice President J.D. Vance and discussed Queensland’s potential to become the next link in the American critical minerals supply chain.

Crisafulli’s MAGA meetings highlight that this data centre is a story of more than just environmental degradation and corporate greed. Attracting investment in areas like AI and critical minerals is a part of a broader mission to strengthen Australia’s alliance with the US. The data centre boom is driven in part by the AI arms race between the US and China. In this context, striking a deal with the US’s largest AI corporation is not just a step towards turning Queensland as an AI investment hub. It also further integrates the Australian and US economies, so both countries are better placed to outpace competitors in the global tech arena.

Anthropic’s new project adds to the 225 other data centres currently in development in Australia and supported by both major parties. Politicians and tech billionaires have no compunction about the impact of their actions on people or the environment, so long as they are making money and moving up the imperialist pecking order. We need a political alternative that will fight for an immediate moratorium on data centres and a socialist society where we can all have a say in the future of our lives and the planet.

author: Önder Algedik
title: COP31: A fair, not a climate summit
content:
The Pacific finally got its pre-COP meeting this week and only around 30 leaders gathered in Fiji and Tuvalu, with only five countries from outside the Pacific.

Vanuatu’s climate minister said he was hoping for more, adding that it “reflects the lack of attention and priority given to what Pacific nations consider the greatest threat to their future”.

The co-host, who did turn up, made the contradiction clear.

Australia’s energy minister Chris Bowen said in Nadi, Fiji, that “as a fossil fuel exporting nation, we can bring something different to the table”. He certainly can. Labor has approved 37 new or expanded fossil fuel projects since 2022.

The other COP31 host is preparing for Antalya in its own way. In September alone, Türkiye blocked at least 1270 X accounts, journalists and Amnesty Türkiye among them, more than in the whole of last year. Green Left itself is blocked in Türkiye: I can only read it through a virtual private network.

The COP31 host agreement, made public only last month, tells accredited participants they have a “duty” not to interfere in Türkiye’s “internal affairs”, a clause Brazil dropped for COP30.

Put the two together and the division of labour is clear. One host keeps approving the fuel. The other prepares to silence those who might object to it. This is climate politics as it actually works.

The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change’s first report in 1990 called for emissions to be cut “immediately” by more than 60%. By 2019, its sixth report found, they were 54% higher.

Last year global energy demand grew 2.7%, with oil, gas and coal all growing.

The problem, then, is not “climate change”, a phrase that turns policy into weather. The problem is a climate-changing policy — the deliberate fueling of climate change, through more and expanded coal mines, liquified natural gas terminals and 20-year gas contracts.

The system behind the deals and who pays the bill has a name — the fossil order.

COP31 is no longer a climate summit. It is a climate-changing summit and, increasingly, a climate fair. Its Action Agenda lists 10 themes, from zero waste to electrification. None names coal, oil or gas.

Its “global business partner”, Koç Holding, owns Türkiye’s oil refineries. Its “electrification partner”, Sabancı, co-owns a lignite power plant. Its “global banking partner” will run a 400-square-metre pavilion. In Antalya, the stands will be busy and the products on display will be green. An end to fossil fuels will not be up for discussion.

Asking for a “better COP” means asking for a “better fair”.

Stopping new fossil fuel projects is no longer enough; we need to start shutting down the coal, oil and gas which is being mined now.

Free public transport, the public ownership of energy and climate-friendly cities are revolutionary demands today. They do not just make new oil wells unnecessary, they empty the ones already pumping and let us begin to close mines, wells and gas lines.

The freedom to say all this out loud, in Antalya, is a challenge to the status quo.

Movements can win these demands. Australia’s High Court ruled on October 7 that the states planning bodies must consider how the burning of fossil fuels, exported from Australia, contribute to climate damage.

“We cannot dig up coal, ship it overseas, watch it drive climate change, and pretend the consequences have nothing to do with us,” said Wendy Wales, one of the retired teachers behind the campaign to get Australia to minimise all greenhouse gas emissions, including emissions produced from burning the exported coal emissions.

Wales said the court decision “has finally made a change in direction in our laws. The [planning rules] will now have to reflect the need to consider climate impacts of our scope three emissions from the coal that we export.”

The real climate summit has to be taken to the streets and wherever people dare to name the fossil order creating the climate emergency, which is devastating communities, who have had the least to do with creating problem.

[Önder Algedik is a climate researcher and activist with 350Ankara. His new book, Ya Fosil Düzen Ya Devrim (Fossil Order or Revolution), is published by İletişim this month.]

This week on Yeah Nah Pasaran! we talk to Emma Hagberg. According to Hagberg, RF had ‘a strong collective identity, the view of fascists as class traitors, and the critique of an autonomous left that often had no place for working-class people’; Comrades was originally published in Swedish as 18.6 – Kamrater, Inte Vänner (B.E.L Publishing, 2024) and is also available in a German translation.

The Revolutionary Front (RF), 2001–2015, was the most militant organization on the left in recent Swedish history. Staunchly working class, the first generation of RF members engaged in numerous street battles with Swedish fascists. When the fascists retreated from the streets, RF attacked them in their homes. The police cracked down on the organization in 2013, raiding the apartments of several alleged members at the crack of dawn. The courts handed out prison sentences of up to six and a half years. author: AWSM
title: Why I Won’t Vote ~ A SYMPOSIUM #1
content:
Anarchy 37, March 1964, Why I Won’t Vote

Voting : “The instrument and symbol of a freeman’s power to make a fool of himself and a wreck of his country”

The saying that ” only a fool would put a loaded gun into the hands of an idiot ” is an especially apt analogy of government. An idiot (usually well-meaning) considers himself clever enough to run the affairs of a large number of people by taking a seat in parliament. A large number of people, acting like fools, vote for his party’s policy then spend the next few years grumbling about the results. The error in approach is that the voter thinks that he will get what he voted for. If he could vote for those who in fact control the country, say the Governors of the Bank of England, the directors of the industrial corporations and those behind the ministries, the illusion of democracy would be more understandable.

The real centres of power lie far beyond the people’s influence at elections. These remain constant whatever Party is ” in power “. In the terms of centralised ” democracy ” the only possible argument to justify voting is that marginal benefits may be gained. The state only incidentally attends to the well-being of its subjects. Its main concern is its power relation to other states, of which the most perfect expression is in war.

I am on the side of people anywhere who are prepared neither to live nor die for something that in the long run can only militate against survival and the conditions that make life worth living. Our immediate action must, by its nature, be to oppose that pathetic gesture, voting. It must be direct and direction. We can learn to live as free men and women only by organising against the condition we are in.

The Tenants Association, Consumers Association, and Direct Action in industry all provide opportunities for people to experience directing their own lives in positive ways towards positive ends.

Only by direct involvement in society can the individual hope to transform himself and his world. Freedom cannot be given, it must be taken; and the free society can only grow from experiments in the problems (ethical and organisational) of community.

Voting does not, and cannot, mean government by consent. By voting, one acts on the assumptions that certain men are fit to govern, and that a majority is necessarily right. Also should the state, acting in the name of a (frequently fictitious) majority, declare war, the individual loses the right to live, if he ever had it.

To me, voting is complicity with the State and a negative action, therefore I do not vote.

author: Mary Ellen Murphy
title: Hospital doctors strike for wages, safe hours and public health
content:
In July, Victorian public hospital doctors voted 97 percent in favour of taking industrial action for the first time in 20 years. The reason is simple: the healthcare system is unsafe for patients and staff.

The Victorian healthcare system is in crisis. Systemic failures at every level compound one another. Limited access to primary care and community services leaves people more unwell and reliant on emergency departments for care. This results in long wait times, overcrowding and unsafe workloads.

Bed shortages, often caused by delays in discharging patients due to the lack of support services, are also an issue. For example, recent data from the Victorian Health Department shows that nineteen of 21 mental health units fail to admit acutely unwell patients from the emergency department within eight hours. This results in staff attempting to care for patients in under-resourced and unsuitable environments in which they are at greater risk of violence. The lack of suitable facilities for mental health patients and adequate staffing also contributes to the ongoing failures to meet goals for the reduction in use of restrictive interventions such as seclusion and restraint.

It is no wonder then that burnout is endemic among public hospital doctors like me working in this broken system. We are expected to be machines and cope with unsafe workloads, under-resourcing and excessive hours without complaint. The system relies on unpaid overtime, guilt and obligation to keep going.

Our industrial claims highlight the punishing hours and minimal protections Victorian doctors currently face. They include a pay rise in line with what the nurses won in 2024, better guarantees of overtime for all non-rostered hours worked, permanent employment as a default model (instead of many thousands of “junior” hospital doctors, many with over a decade of experience, being given only yearly contracts), maximum shift lengths of 12.5 hours (rather than the 14 hours commonly worked at the moment), at least four rostered days off per fortnight including two consecutive days, a maximum of four consecutive night shifts, minimum doctor-to-patient ratios for safe care and mandatory 30-minute paid rest breaks every five hours.

During the fourteen months of unsuccessful bargaining discussions, the Victorian Hospitals Industrial Association (the association of employers in the public health industry) backpedalled on its previous agreement to simplify overtime payments, arguing it would cost too much to pay doctors the hours they actually work.

It is not only at work that public hospital employees are coming under attack. Over the last few months, we have seen our regulator, AHPRA, conflate antisemitism with anti-Zionism to silence healthcare workers speaking up about Palestine, including outside of work and on social media. This violates democratic rights and sets a terrible precedent for other professions. Many healthcare workers feel particularly obliged to advocate for Palestinians based on our roles as health workers. We suffer moral injury when we are prevented from speaking out about the atrocities committed against our colleagues in Gaza and against the Palestinian people as a whole.

When confronted about the lack of a public response to this attack on our freedom of speech, the Victorian branch of the Australian Medical Association admitted it was scared to address it publicly for fear of backlash, and that the federal organisation was engaged in back-room discussions with AHPRA. This approach aligns more with a lobby organisation than a trade union.

A union’s strength comes from its members’ involvement and activity. This also protects unions when they want to speak out about political issues important to their members. There is a reason that the Australian Salaried Medical Officers Federation (the part of the Australian Medical Association that is engaged in bargaining) in New South Wales—the branch involved most recently in prolonged industrial action with an active rank and file—was the only branch of our union that put out a statement condemning the AHPRA adoption of the pro-Israel International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance definition of antisemitism.
