author: Aaron Hemens, Local Journalism Initiative Reporter
title: In Tk̓emlúps, community gathers to ‘reclaim our space’ and denounce white nationalism
content:
At the same site where a white nationalist demonstration occurred in Tk̓emlúps te Secwépemc on Sunday, more than 100 Secwépemc people and their allies returned to the area two days later to reclaim the space. They drummed, sang and prayed to cleanse the spot, which is located a few hundred metres away from the former Kamloops Indian Residential School.

Photo by Aaron Hemens


Content warning: This article contains details about residential “schools.” Please read with care for your spirit.


On the eve of Orange Shirt Day, more than 100 people gathered in Tk̓emlúps te Secwépemc to cleanse and reclaim a site where a white nationalist demonstration occurred earlier this week.


For nearly three hours on Tuesday night, Secwépemc people and their allies drummed, sang and prayed — for the land and the people, and for all the families impacted by residential “schools.”


Secwépemc people and their allies drum, sing and pray on Tuesday, near the site where a white nationalist demonstration took place in Tk̓emlúps te Secwépemc two days prior.

Photo by Aaron Hemens


Ashley Michel from Tk̓emlúps te Secwépemc organized Tuesday’s gathering with four other Secwépemc (Shuswap) mothers.


After seeing images of a group of masked white nationalists circulating on social media early this week, she told IndigiNews that they felt they had to come together to create a safer place for their children, and to help ground the community ahead of the National Day for Truth and Reconciliation — also known as Orange Shirt Day — on Sept. 30.


“We’re all mothers. We don’t want our children growing up in a world like this. We brainstormed, and we just wanted to come together and cleanse the area,” said Michel, who is the owner of Four Generations Creations.


The organizers of Tuesday’s gathering in Tk̓emlúps te Secwépemc. From left to right: Ashley Michel, Cam Gottfriedson, Morning-Star Peters, Stephanie Lindley and Willow Peters.

Photo by Aaron Hemens


“We wanted to start things off in a good way and reclaim our space – take back our area and make it safe again. Especially for our children and our survivors.”


The group of about two dozen white nationalists were seen at Tk̓emlúps te Secwépemc reserve lands early Sunday morning. They hid their faces behind white masks and held a flag with the message “got bones?” — with images that quickly gathered outrage online.


The space where the group had gathered is a few hundred metres away from the former Kamloops Indian Residential School (KIRS) site and is located on the institution’s former grounds, which originally spanned 360 acres. 


At the same site where a white nationalist demonstration occurred in Tk̓emlúps te Secwépemc on Sunday, more than 100 Secwépemc people and their allies returned to the area two days later to reclaim the space.

Photo by Aaron Hemens


In 2021

, leadership at Tk̓emlúps te Secwépemc revealed that they had identified evidence of 215 unmarked graves on the site, which unleashed a national reckoning about children’s deaths at the institutions.


“Sunday was just an example of what we at Tk’emlúps te Secwépemc are facing on a daily basis; on a weekly basis; on a monthly basis,” said Jeanette Jules, a Secwépemc knowledge keeper who helps manage the First Nation’s Le Estcwicwéy̓ (the missing children from KIRS) case. 


“Since 2021, we’ve kept emails, texts, phone messages. Some of them are really disturbing and disgusting.”


Secwépemc people and their allies drum, sing and pray on Tuesday, near the site where a white nationalist demonstration took place in Tk̓emlúps te Secwépemc two days prior.

Photo by Aaron Hemens


Tk̓emlúps te Secwépemc Kúkwpi7 (Chief) Rosanne Casimir

said on Sunday

 that the group have ties to a group called Second Sons Canada, who are “linked to white supremacist and white nationalist ideology.”


“That blackness that they brought — that heaviness that they brought — is being lifted,” said Jules.


On Monday

, Tk̓emlúps RCMP said in a press release that they are investigating the incident. They described the masked men and their activities as “a cowardly attempt to avoid accountability for their actions and messages that are clearly intended to intimidate, provoke fear and division.”


Secwépemc people and their allies drum, sing and pray on Tuesday, near the site where a white nationalist demonstration took place in Tk̓emlúps te Secwépemc two days prior.

Photo by Aaron Hemens

author: Progressive International
title: From Law to Justice
content:
As Trump attacked the ICC and Netanyahu faced a walkout at the UN, forty states gathered to put an arms embargo, protections for the Court and a new UN mechanism modelled on the Special Committee against Apartheid.

Last week, the United Nations Conference on Trade and Development (UNCTAD) counted what remained of Gaza’s economy after almost three years of genocide and almost two decades of siege. Ninety-two per cent of its economic establishments have been damaged or destroyed. Unemployment has reached 78 per cent. GDP per person fell to $212 last year — barely 17 per cent of its pre-genocide level — while less than 1.5 per cent of Gaza’s cropland remains accessible and undamaged. Recovery and reconstruction will cost at least $71.5 billion. Pedro Manuel Moreno, acting head of UNCTAD, called it “the world’s most severe economic crisis on record”.

These were the conditions in which the governments of the world assembled in New York for the 81st United Nations General Assembly. On Monday 21 September, a thousand gathered at Riverside Church to celebrate the Charter on which the institution was founded, hosted by South Africa. Martin Luther King Jr stood in the same church in 1967 to deliver Beyond Vietnam. Nelson Mandela came there four months after his release from prison and thanked the movements that had sustained sanctions against apartheid — before urging them to keep up the pressure until victory was secured. “We acted because we know what global solidarity can do,” South African Foreign Minister Ronald Lamola told the gathering. The Hague Group, he said, embodies a “shared conviction that concrete action is needed.”

A day later, Donald Trump used the General Assembly podium to attack the International Criminal Court. He called it an “evil” and “rogue institution” and urged its 125 member states to withdraw. His administration has already imposed financial sanctions and visa restrictions on ICC officials and threatened further measures that could stifle the Court’s ability to operate. Trump has said the campaign is aimed at protecting Benjamin Netanyahu, for whom the Court issued an arrest warrant in 2024 over alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity in Gaza.

On Thursday, Netanyahu himself took the same podium. Dozens of delegates walked out as he began speaking. He held aloft a pager, invoking Israel’s 2024 terror attack in Lebanon: “Remember the beepers? Hezbollah certainly remembers them.”

Netanyahu denied that Israel had committed genocide in Gaza, denounced his critics as “moral cowards” and praised Trump as Israel’s greatest partner. Outside the UN, protesters blocked streets demanding an end to US arms supplies to Israel; at least 30 were arrested.

By Friday morning, another gathering was underway inside UN headquarters. In the Trusteeship Council Chamber, once at the centre of the UN’s work of decolonisation, forty states — represented by foreign ministers and senior diplomats — joined The Hague Group’s largest meeting yet, co-sponsored by South Africa and Malaysia in defence of international law.

Minister Lamola opened by recalling the machinery built against apartheid: the UN Special Committee established in 1962 to monitor and organise international action, followed by the campaign that turned a voluntary arms embargo into a mandatory Security Council measure in 1977. The Hague Group itself had begun with nine states in January 2025. “Our task today,” Lamola told the room, “is to turn concern into compliance, and law into protection.”

The states gathered in New York discussed a series of concrete proposals. One would create a new UN mechanism drawing on the Special Committee against Apartheid to monitor compliance with international law and coordinate action between states. Another would continue efforts for a Security Council arms embargo on Israel. For the ICC, states discussed blocking statutes against sanctions on the Court, measures to keep it operating under pressure, and coordinated action to protect judges and prosecutors from retaliation. Norway pledged to work on the Court’s “business continuity”, while other interventions stressed cooperation to ensure that its decisions can still be carried out. South Africa and Malaysia committed to continue consultations with participating governments on how to put the proposals into practice.

“The law is clear,” Indonesia’s representative told the room. “Our challenge now is to give it practical consequence.” That same week, UNCTAD had …

author: Ishita Chakrabarty
title: Hindus for Human Rights: ‘Racism is not just about violence, it manifests through misinformation’
content:
To all those who have come from far off-lands and continents; who have made it here despite the monumental barriers that passport privilege poses for some over others — the intense questioning as to motivation; the demand for return tickets; the visa costs that keep escalating year on year; the bank statements and medical reports to prove you will not become a burden onto the system, I am one among you.

To those who have lived here for generations and are yet still told to “Go back where you came from”.

To those who hold a sacred relationship to this land — whose belonging to this land can never be severed by the operation of an unjust, extractive and foreign imposed law.

And to all those who join us here in solidarity, who believe in the idea of an inclusive, egalitarian and multicultural Australia.

I come from Bengal in India. I am representing Hindus for Human Rights, a voice for progressive Hindus and Indians working for inter-faith and inter-community respect and understanding and advocating against all kinds of discrimination and bigotry.

Coming from India, I know all too well what hate, bigotry and the belief of the superiority of some over the other looks like, and how the destruction of the very fabric of society is tantamount to the destruction of the human within us.

It is because of the love I hold towards my home country and the appreciation for being here that I believe we must join hands in the fight against racism and bigotry, whether it comes from the far right politics of One Nation, or from the Hindutva ideology that considers Dalits, Muslims, Christians and other minorities inferior and less than human.

As I speak, Muslims are being lynched, evicted, legally stripped of their citizenship through complicit state institutions. Christians are being hounded, their prayer services are being stopped mid-worship on allegations of forced conversions. Dalits and other caste minorities remain trapped in a system where the so-called upper castes get offended by someone for sporting a moustache, or a Dalit man “daring” to attend their own wedding on horseback.

As a person bearing a majoritarian identity, I feel even more compelled to not only speak of racism emanating from a certain and distant political entity, but also the hatred, transpiring within our own South Asian community, including in Australia.

Identities, beliefs and practices travel alongside communities and are often seen through acts such as questioning one’s food preferences, tasking that one Indian student whose identity is given away by their surname to undertake the menial tasks in the house, through casual bullying. They perpetrate through closed social groups and in marriage alliances.

Hindus for Human Rights along with allies have worked hard and successfully to have caste discrimination included as a form of racism in city councils and universities.

When we speak of racism and bigotry it is also important to speak about these internal exclusions that we have created. For the same hatred that I mentioned earlier is then taken and twisted to justify that the far right is not against all immigrants — only the “bad ones” who refuse to “assimilate”, for example, the hijab- or turban-wearing student of Indian origin.

It is used to legitimise the exclusion of our fellow community members, as when One Nation leader Pauline Hanson keeps speaking of how Indians are the “good, hardworking migrants”.

It is seen when platforms show her attending Diwali festivals and being warmly received by diasporic Indians, represented through associations like the Hindu Council of Australia, or when she visits that one Indian migrant-run shop in Townsville, posing with the owner while eating fish and chips.

When I speak of racism, I speak of the overt acts: The people who called 22-year-old Harmanpreet Singh “a dog”, and physically assaulted him, leaving him with a broken nose in February in Corio. Or when they called 26-year-old Nayonika a “curry muncher”, “smelly Indian”, and a “Mrs. 7/11 driver” in Sydney’s CBD.

But racism also manifests through misinformation such as caricatures portraying Indians, and other immigrants, as being responsible for the housing crisis.

It co-exists in the digital world where desk warriors feel confident to call Greens Senator Mehreen Faruqi “a filthy Australian hating racist pig”.

It does not stop at that. Racism and bigotry also acts through constant daily acts of micro-aggression; through people staring you …

author: Frenny Jowi
title: Congo in Kenya: Why Xenophobia is a Racist Ideal
content:
Thirty-three-year-old Emmanuel is a freelance hairdresser in Nairobi. He is a refugee from the Democratic Republic of Congo and has lived in Kenya for six years.


The young man is chic, dressed in designer brands, with a gentle demeanour that reflects his customer-care style in the city’s beauty industry. His calm, collected appearance belies a history of strife, struggle, and an ongoing effort to recover from the decades of armed conflict he witnessed as a child in North Kivu.


‘I will never forget the night when rebels attacked our village in North Kivu. I must have been seven years old at that time. Some people were killed, and there was fire burning everywhere around us.’


Emmanuel narrated his story as he swung around in his styling chair in front of a large mirror that is popularly called a ‘station’ in Nairobi’s hairdressing and beauty salons.


I had visited Emmanuel at the salon where he works. Renting business premises in Nairobi is a significant cost for many young business owners, whether citizen or foreigner. In the beauty industry, most professionals can only afford to rent a mirror and a styling chair as a workstation – hence the name ‘station’.


While occasionally glancing at his WhatsApp notifications for customer bookings, Emmanuel continued to share his story with me.


‘The attack happened many years ago. I still remember how my mother stopped to pack her pot of fish stew and cassava leaves and rice. My father asked her to hurry up, leave the food, and run for safety, but she insisted she would not leave her delicious food. As we all escaped in the dim light of the moon, I recall our neighbours’ comments about my mother’s weird sense of what to salvage. She insisted the food would also save us and she would not leave it behind despite the gunfire. Now I find that funny.’


Emmanuel laughed, trying to find humour in a devastating story.


I knew that talking about traumatic childhood experiences from war would be difficult, so I did not press Emmanuel further about the night armed fighters attacked their village, killing many people and setting houses on fire.


The events Emmanuel witnessed as a child in 2000 were part of the Second Congo War, dubbed Africa’s World War. According to

Amnesty International

, the DRC’s current conflict has been ongoing since the 1990s, particularly in the eastern part of the country, which borders South Sudan, Uganda, Rwanda, Burundi, and Tanzania.


This armed conflict escalated in August 1998 when President Laurent Kabila fell out with the Ugandan and Rwandan allies who had helped him seize power.


Emmanuel narrated how the fighting between the Lendu-Ngiti and the opposing Hema began as communal land disputes involving farmers and pastoralists. Locals believe politicians and those with mining interests took advantage of these seemingly solvable disputes to fuel the ongoing war. He added that their radio broadcasts often mentioned various fighting groups such as the UPDF (Uganda People’s Defence Forces) and the UPC (United Congolese Patriots).


‘In the news, when we heard that Bosco Ntaganda was in court and wanted to defend himself in Kinyarwanda, we were all shocked, because locally, we knew him as one of us. We never thought he was from Rwanda. He lived here for so long, spoke our language, looked like one of us, and was always involved in Congolese affairs,’ Emmanuel said.


Decades of conflict have been fuelled by ethnic tensions, political rivalries, corruption, and fighting for control of valuable natural resources.


Over time, the war drew in nine African nations, making it one of the largest wars in African history. The 2017 Kivu Security Tracker Report by Jason Stearns and Christoph Vogel listed 132 armed fighter groups operating in North and South Kivu alone.


Today, Emmanuel is one of the over 100 million citizens of the DRC affected by incessant wars. The DRC is the fourth most populous country in Africa and the 14th in the world. Despite decades of war and pandemics such as Ebola, its population has continued to grow steadily. 


In 2025,

Human Rights Watch

 reported that the Congolese military and a coalition of armed fighters have continued to attack civilians. The report adds that throughout 2024, the

Rwandan

 army and the M23 armed group indiscriminately shelled displacement camps and other densely populated areas near Goma in eastern Congo.


Emmanuel arrived in Kenya in 2019, just before the COVID-19 pandemic. Earlier, in 2017 …

Δικαστήρια Οκτωβρίου: Συνεχίζουμε το monitoring


Δυστυχώς και αυτός ο μήνας ξεκινάει με τις ίδιες διαδικασίες να πραγματοποιούνται και να συνεχίζεται η πολιτική της ποινικοποίησης των μετακινούμενων πληθυσμών.

Εμείς όσο μπορούμε θα ενημερώνουμε, ενισχύουμε και στηρίζουμε τις υποθέσεις τους, αλλά και την συνέχιση των ζωών τους.

title: Migrantinnen in der (24h)Pflege: „Niemand überwacht die Arbeitsbedingungen“ in Privathaushalten
content:
Dossier


„

Dort, wo kranke oder alte Menschen gepflegt werden müssen, sind die Verwandten oft mit der Aufgabe überfordert. Neben der Lohnarbeit noch den Mann oder die Mutter waschen, für sie kochen und vielleicht sogar Medikamente verabreichen zu müssen, ist anstrengend und braucht viel Zeit. Deshalb beschäftigen viele Familien private Pflegerinnen. In Deutschland kommen die Frauen zum größten Teil aus Mittel- und Osteuropa. Helma Lutz forscht in Frankfurt zur Situation der Pflegerinnen in Privathaushalten. Die Soziologin fordert vor allem eine bessere Bezahlung der Pflegerinnen, ein Ende der 24-Stunden-Arbeit und mehr Unabhängigkeit vom Haushalt der Pflegeperson

.“

Interview vom 6. Mai 2019 bei Radio Dreyeckland


, siehe dazu auch unser Dossier:

Pflegenotstand ohne Lohnerhöhung: „(Wieder mal) Ausländer rein! Also in die Pflege.“

 und hier speziell zu den Arbeitsbedingungen:


»Ein Symptom der Lücken im Pflegesystem«: Verletzungen der Arbeitsrechte von migrantischen Pflegerinnen bei der Live-in-Betreuung sind Alltag


„…

Die Live-in-Betreuung ist für das deutsche Pflegesystem inzwischen von großer Bedeutung. Schätzungen gehen von 300.000 bis 600.000 überwiegend migrantischen Betreuer*innen aus, die Versorgungslücken in Privathaushalten schließen. Die Live-ins übernehmen Betreuung, Haushalt und häufig auch pflegerische Tätigkeiten und halten damit einen Teil des Pflegesystems am Laufen. Nötig wird dieses Modell, weil staatliche Angebote und familiäre Ressourcen vielfach nicht ausreichen. Zugleich ist es ein Modell, das stark auf dem Lohngefälle zwischen Deutschland sowie Mittel- und Osteuropa beruht.


[Wie steht es um die Arbeitsrechte der Beschäftigten?]


Unsere Interviews mit Berater*innen in arbeitsrechtlichen Beratungsstellen sowie Betreuer*innen selbst zeigen, dass Arbeitsrechtsverletzungen zum Alltag gehören. Besonders deutlich wird das bei der Arbeitszeit: Arbeit und Freizeit sind häufig kaum voneinander zu trennen. Betreuerinnen müssen nachts und am Wochenende verfügbar sein, ohne dass diese Zeiten entsprechend vergütet werden. (…)


Durch die Entsendung in Selbstständigkeit auf der Basis von Werk- statt Arbeitsverträgen werden sie von Schutzrechten ausgeschlossen, die Arbeitnehmer*innen zustehen. Denn Selbstständige haben keinen Anspruch auf Mindestlohn, die Begrenzung der Arbeitszeit oder Lohnfortzahlung im Krankheitsfall. Es ist allerdings häufig fraglich, ob überhaupt eine echte Selbstständigkeit vorliegt. Um ihre Arbeitnehmerinneneigenschaft durchzusetzen, müsste dies rechtlich festgestellt werden. Allerdings greift hier ein zweiter Mechanismus, den wir informelle Entrechtung nennen. Ihr Zugang zum Recht ist so erschwert, dass eine Mobilisierung von Recht fast unmöglich ist. (…)


Eine strukturelle Einbindung der Live-ins in die gewerkschaftliche Arbeit existiert nicht. Das hat mit mangelndem Interesse der Gewerkschaften zu tun, aber auch damit, dass klassische gewerkschaftliche Mobilisierung durch die Arbeitsorganisation in Privathaushalten und in Pendelmigration enorm erschwert ist.


Allerdings leistet das Beratungsangebot von »Faire Mobilität« des Bundesministeriums für Arbeit und Soziales und dem DGB einen wichtigen positiven Beitrag. Es vermittelt Wissen über Arbeitsrechte, unterstützt Betroffene bei der Durchsetzung von Ansprüchen und stellt überhaupt erst Kontakte zu Unterstützungsstrukturen her. (…)


Wenn die Pflegeversicherung weiterhin nur einen Teil der Kosten übernimmt, bleibt der ökonomische Druck bestehen, Betreuung möglichst billig zu organisieren. Die Live-in-Betreuung ist nämlich auch ein Symptom dafür, dass die Versorgungslücken im deutschen Pflegesystem nicht geschlossen werden. Das Problem der bestehenden Sorgelücken wird damit ins Private geschoben – und Kosten werden auf migrantische Beschäftigte abgewälzt. (…)


Es braucht langfristig eine bedarfsdeckende staatliche Kostenübernahme für die Betreuung pflegebedürftiger Personen, damit Haushalte Sorgelücken nicht durch die Unterbezahlung von migrantischen Arbeiter*innen stopfen. Mittelfristig sehen wir einen wichtigen Schritt im Direktanstellungsgebot über deutsche Verbände. Modelle für eine solche rechtssichere Anstellung finden sich zum Beispiel beim Projekt »CariFair«, das deutsche Caritas-Verbände in Kooperation mit der Caritas Polen etabliert haben und das eine faire und legale Beschäftigung in der Betreuung ermöglicht

.“

Interview von Peter Nowak vom 06.10.2026 in ND online


 mit der Soziologin Francesca Barp …

author: Wildcat #116
title: 1976 – 1991: Das Albartus-Papier der Revolutionären Zellen
content:
Die Jahre 1976 und 1991 markieren zwei deutliche Abstürze in der Geschichte der radikalen Linken in der BRD. Bezeichnenderweise kam Ende 1991 das Albartus-Papier der Revolutionären Zellen auf 1976 zu sprechen: die Flugzeugentführung von Entebbe. Anlässlich des 50. Jahrestags haben wir in der aktuellen Wildcat einen langen Artikel, der diese Verbindungen aufzudröseln versucht: »Entebbe und die Folgen«. Hier eine Kürzestfassung plus update:


Im Juni und Juli 1976 herrschte in Europa eine Hitzewelle. Die Temperaturen in Deutschland stiegen wochenlang regelmäßig über 30 Grad auf Spitzenwerte bis 36 und 37 Grad.


Politisch endete vor 50 Jahren das »rote Jahrzehnt«: 24. März 1976 Militärputsch in Argentinien. Am 9. Mai 1976 starb Ulrike Meinhof. Anfang Juni brach auf dem »Pfingstkongress« ein breiter Teil der radikalen Linken mit der Militanz und machte sich auf in die Institutionen. Am 10. Juli begann die Chemiekatastrophe in Seveso. Im August das Massaker von Tel al-Zaatar. Am 6. Oktober der Militärputsch in Thailand.


Auch kulturell war 1976 schlimm: ABBA »Dancing Queen«, Jürgen Drews »Ein Bett im Kornfeld«, Boney M. »Daddy Cool«. Kurz danach kamen dann die BeeGees »Stayin’ Alive« – der Sound zum Deutschen Herbst!


Für die deutschen Maoisten der diversen K-Gruppen lag 1976 zwischen dem Besuch von Franz Josef Strauß bei Mao (Januar 1975) einerseits, dem Krieg Vietnams gegen Kambodscha und den »Reformen« von Deng Xiao Ping (beides im Dezember 1978) andererseits. Die meisten fielen vom Glauben ab, viele von ihnen gründeten die Grüne Partei, andere später die Antideutschen. Diese eroberten nach 1991 die Hegemonie in der radikalen Linken.


Die Flugzeugentführung nach Entebbe…


Seit Anfang 1976 eskalierte der libanesische Bürgerkrieg. Nach monatelanger Belagerung stürmten Falangisten am 12. August das Lager von Tel al-Zaatar und töteten Tausende palästinensische Flüchtlinge.


Im Zusammenhang damit entführte ein deutsch-palästinensisches Kommando aus RZ und PFLP-EO am 27. Juni 1976 ein Flugzeug nach Entebbe und forderte die Freilassung von politischen Gefangenen. In der Nacht zum 4. Juli befreiten israelische Spezialkräfte die meisten der Geiseln. Das wird von gewissen Kreisen bis heute als das beste Kommandounternehmen aller Zeiten bejubelt (etwa: »Mit der Geiselbefreiung von Entebbe zeigte Israel vor 50 Jahren, wie man den Terror bekämpft« Nius 2. Juli 2026). Benjamin Netanjahu, dessen älterer Bruder bei der Befreiungsaktion starb, hat seine gesamte politische Karriere auf »Entebbe« und den »Kampf gegen den Terrorismus« aufgebaut.


»Die Aktion von Entebbe wurde rasch zu einem Vorwand für verschiedene Akteure, die bislang mit dem Milieu der radikalen Linken verbunden waren, sich von Internationalismus und Antiimperialismus ganz zu lösen.« (Gerhard Hanloser: »Desaster mit Nachspiel«)


Wegweisend war der Anti-Repressionskongress des Sozialistischen Büros Anfang Juni (»Pfingstkongress«). Am Abschlusstag hatte der spätere Außenminister Joschka Fischer vor 20.000 Besuchern in der berühmten Römerberg-Rede mit seiner militanten Vergangenheit gebrochen. Später hat er – die Dinge chronologisch auf den Kopf stellend – auf seinem Weg ins Außenministerium immer mal wieder betont, »Entebbe« sei das Ereignis gewesen, das ihn vom Saulus zum Paulus gemacht habe. Dabei lieferte es nur nachträglich den Vorwand.


»Entebbe« ist bis heute wirkmächtig. Das sah man an den Dutzenden von Artikeln und mehreren Büchern, die zum 50. Jahrestag erschienen. Das sah man aber auch daran, dass im März 2023 Mitglieder der Entebbe-Spezialeinheit eine der schärfsten Kritiken an Benjamin Netanjahu in einem offenen Brief formulierten. Netanjahu opfere den Staat Israel und das israelische Volk für seine eigenen Interessen, diffamiere Demonstranten gegen die Justizreform als Anarchisten und alle, die ihn nicht unterstützen, als Terroristen; er hetze Israelis gegeneinander auf.


… und die beginnende Institutionalisierung der radikalen Linken


1976 hätte auch anders ausgehen können. Im Juli hatten Chemiearbeiter in Seveso gestreikt, um die Katastrophe überhaupt öffentlich zu machen – aber sie hatten nicht mehr die Macht wie Jahre zuvor, die Wirtschaftspolitik des Landes neu zu orientieren. Die massenhaften Schüler- und Studentenproteste in Soweto seit Juni waren größtenteils selbst organisiert und schienen politisch endlich eine Alternative zum ANC zu eröffnen. author: Sharon Zhang
title: Report: Trump Admin Is Deporting LGBTQ Asylum Seekers to Hostile Third Countries
content:
Officials have deported LGBTQ people to Sierra Leone, where they could face life in prison for same-sex activity.

Support justice-driven, accurate and transparent news — make a quick donation to Truthout today!

The Trump administration has reportedly deported dozens of LGBTQ immigrants who sought or were granted asylum for their sexuality and gender to third countries where they face danger of persecution and criminalization, a new report says.

In an investigation published this week, Reuters identified 40 cases where these LGBTQ individuals were sent to countries that either criminalize same-sex relations or have been designated by the State Department as dangerous for LGBTQ people.

All of these people were granted legal protection in the U.S. for fleeing persecution for their LGBTQ status in their countries of origin, per Reuters. However, more than half of them were ineligible for asylum because of a restrictive Biden-era transit ban on asylum seekers.

Individuals tracked in the report have been deported to countries including Sierra Leone, Cameroon and Eswatini, three countries where same-sex acts are criminalized. In Sierra Leone, same sex acts carry a punishment of up to life in prison. Other countries that have signed deportation agreements with the U.S. have seen abuses against LGBTQ people like conversion therapy and “corrective rape,” the report notes.

The Trump administration has signed third country deportation agreements with at least 35 countries, and has deported over 25,000 people this way, sending them to places that they have no affiliation with. Many governments in Africa and central and South America have signed agreements to receive such deportees, often in exchange for direct funding or other financial incentives.

Reuters noted the story of one man, identified as Abdou Latifou, who fled his home country of Togo after a mob assaulted him and threatened to kill him after he kissed a man. A U.S. immigration judge decided last year that it was too unsafe for him to return home; he recalled thinking, “From this day on, I’m entering a world where I’m free to live as myself.”

But amid its mass deportation campaign, and while knowing that Latifou was gay, the Trump administration deported him to Sierra Leone, where he was held for two weeks under police surveillance before being put on a flight to Togo. Fleeing danger yet again, he went to the Ivory Coast, where he lives in fear of being recognized.

“When an individual is no longer in ICE custody then ICE will no longer be responsible for them,” Department of Homeland Security spokesperson ​Chandler Rebel told Reuters.

The report is the latest documenting the Trump administration’s deportations of people to places where they may be endangered. Other reports this week found that the Trump administration deported a former political prisoner back to the place he was imprisoned and tortured last week. Jeffrey Jarquín, who led pro-democracy protests against the Nicaraguan government, was reportedly taken directly from the deportation flight to the capital of Managua to a notorious Nicaraguan prison.

The Trump administration is facing a lawsuit from Iranian asylum seekers who say that U.S. officials secretly shared sensitive information, including LGBTQ status, about them with the Iranian government — as it’s tried to deport them into a country where they may face persecution.

Meanwhile, the Trump administration has terminated Temporary Protected Status (TPS) for Haitians in the U.S., and has deported hundreds of immigrants back to Haiti, which has experienced a surge of violence and hunger.

We now have three full months of data since Google changed its search to feature AI results. The numbers are worse than we anticipated. Overall readership that comes to Truthout through Google is down 54 percent against last year. The number of new readers who discover Truthout via Google searches is down 49 percent, and returning users from Google are down 51 percent.

title: "Incredible Moment for the Borderlands": Judge Blocks Border Wall Expansion in Big Bend & West Texas
content:
In a victory for environmentalists and immigration rights’ advocates, a federal judge in El Paso, Texas, has blocked further border wall construction inside Big Bend National Park. “We slammed the brakes on $7 billion worth of corrupt construction contracts,” says Laiken Jordahl, a national public lands advocate with the Center for Biological Diversity, which sued to block the expansion. “We have effectively stopped construction across West Texas, and it’s incredible.”


Jordahl also responds to the Trump administration’s excavation of a 200-year-old cottonwood tree on the Arizona-Mexico border that had been protected by activists for months. “Watching those videos of them toppling this ancient tree that was very likely older than the border itself is symbolic of how

DHS

 has treated the border region. They see our communities, our wildlife, our nature as a sacrifice zone,” says Jordahl.

author: Andrés
title: Dos años bordando historias: memoria, identidad y comunidad
content:
Foto: Daniel Ávalos


«Bordando Historias – Construyendo Memoria» cumplió dos años y lo celebró con música, baile y encuentro entre distintas comunidades. Mujeres paraguayas y bolivianas compartieron sus danzas, la música del norte argentino acompañó la jornada y la memoria volvió a aparecer como un territorio común. A pocos días del 12 de octubre, la celebración puso en el centro la diversidad cultural y las historias de quienes construyen sus identidades lejos de los relatos oficiales.

Por Daniel Ávalos (ANRed).


Hay memorias que se escriben con palabras y otras que se construyen con las manos. Hay historias que sobreviven en fotografías, en relatos familiares, en canciones y también en una tela atravesada por hilos de colores. Hace dos años nació Bordando Historias – Construyendo Memoria, un espacio que encontró en el bordado una herramienta para recuperar historias, encontrarse y construir memoria colectiva. Ayer, sus integrantes celebraron ese recorrido con una jornada donde el arte, la música y las distintas identidades culturales ocuparon el centro de la escena.


La celebración tuvo música y baile. Mujeres compartieron sus danzas, mientras la música del norte argentino acompañó un encuentro que reafirmó los lazos entre distintas comunidades. Porque allí donde muchas veces se construyen fronteras, el encuentro puede convertirse en una forma de resistencia.


El aniversario estuvo atravesado también por la proximidad del 12 de octubre, Día del Respeto a la Diversidad Cultural. Una fecha que invita a revisar las miradas históricas sobre los pueblos originarios y, al mismo tiempo, a reconocer las múltiples culturas que forman parte del presente. En ese sentido, la celebración de Bordando Historias tuvo algo de declaración colectiva: las identidades no están congeladas en el pasado. Se encuentran, se mezclan, se transforman y se sostienen en comunidad.


Foto: Daniel Ávalos


El espacio está vinculado además a la memoria de los trabajadores textiles, con las historias de quienes padecieron condiciones de explotación y precarización, particularmente en torno a la Masacre de Luis Viale, ocurrida en 2006.


Recuperar ese pasado es también poner en discusión las condiciones de vida y trabajo de las comunidades migrantes y de los sectores populares. Pero la memoria no apareció ayer como una pieza de museo. Apareció viva. En las manos que bordan. En las mujeres que bailan. En las canciones compartidas. En las distintas maneras de hablar, de recordar y de celebrar. En una comunidad que se reconoce diversa y que hace de esa diversidad un punto de encuentro.


Dos años de Bordando Historias son dos años de construir memoria desde abajo, de recuperar voces y de transformar el recuerdo en encuentro. Puntada a puntada, historia a historia, las distintas comunidades siguen tejiendo una trama común. Quizá allí esté la potencia de este espacio: entender que la memoria no solamente se conserva; también se construye colectivamente, se baila, se canta y se vuelve presente.

From the 1880s through the 1940s tens of thousands of anarchists were active in the United States, the overwhelming majority of them first- and second-generation immigrants. But most were not yet devotees of the anarchist cause when they arrived on American shores. Instead, a clear link existed between migration and the embrace of anarchist ideology. This study asks how and why thousands of migrants became anarchists, and how their embrace of an anti-nationalist and cosmopolitan ideology shaped their identities, experiences and actions.

Utilizing anarchist publications, government surveillance files, and archival materials, it focuses on Eastern European Jews and Italians—the two largest segments of the anarchist movement by the turn of the century—and the development of anarchism among these groups in three important centers of American anarchism: New York’s Lower East Side, Paterson, New Jersey, and San Francisco. It then follows the changing fortunes of the movement in the face of war, the Russian Revolution, the First Red Scare, and the birth of communism and fascism, and ends with an examination of immigrant American anarchist participation in the Spanish Civil War of 1936–39, and that conflict’s dramatic impact on the movement in the United States.

author: Joshua W.J. Brown
title: What replaced the slave trade?
content:
The first thought came out ugly because the event itself was ugly: tens of thousands of people moving at once toward Ceuta, a Spanish city in North Africa, beaches and roads filling, people dying, police lines folding, rumors moving faster than governments. I looked at Morocco on one side, Spain and the European Union on the other, and thought: What exactly is being traded here?

I don’t mean that migrants are slaves. They aren’t. That isn’t the argument, and collapsing the two would make the argument stupid. Slavery means ownership: a human being captured, bought, sold, inherited, coerced, and legally treated as property. A migrant is not somebody else’s property simply because a state wants to stop him, move her, return them, admit them, or keep them out.

What I’m asking is what came after. What happens to economies and states that once participated in systems where human movement itself generated external value? Does abolition erase that logic, or does value move somewhere else?

Ceuta is where the question became impossible for me to ignore.

On July 30, more than 70,000 people crossed or attempted to cross

 from Morocco into the Spanish enclave in the largest such surge the border has seen.

Current reporting doesn’t support the easy conspiracy version

. Economic frustration mattered. False claims spread online that the border was open. Smugglers and informal networks mattered. Moroccan security forces were overwhelmed, and Morocco later reinforced the frontier and prosecuted people accused of facilitating the crossing. If I have to invent a secret order from Rabat to make my argument work, then I don’t have an argument.

But I don’t need one. Europe already pays for migration control in public.

In 2023, the European Union announced a

€152 million migration program for Morocco

 covering border management, anti-smuggling work, migration and asylum policy, voluntary returns, and reintegration. The EU describes cooperation with countries of origin and transit as a core part of its migration system. In July 2026, on the very day the Ceuta crisis exploded, the

European Commission announced new funding calls

 for migration partnerships, border management, and internal security with partner countries.

That isn’t a scandal by itself. Borders cost money. Refugees need housing. Smuggling networks need to be investigated. Returns require cooperation between governments. A state beside a major migration route will obviously spend resources managing it, and there is nothing inherently corrupt about Europe sharing that cost.

The problem appears when I follow the incentive one step farther.

If Europe places a high political value on keeping irregular migration outside Europe, then the government that is capable of helping to accomplish this goal possesses something Europe wants. Geography becomes valuable. Police cooperation becomes valuable. Readmission becomes valuable. Hosting becomes valuable. The ability to make movement harder becomes valuable. And, in the darker version, the possibility that cooperation might disappear becomes valuable too.

Nobody has to sell the migrant. The migrant can still generate leverage simply by being movable.

That’s the distinction I keep coming back to. Under slavery, the person was the commodity. In the modern system, control around the person can become the asset.

The literature already has pieces of this. Scholars write about migration diplomacy, refugee rentier states, remittance dependence, border externalization, and coercive migration. I’m not trying to rename their work. I’m trying to put those pieces beside the historical question that bothered me in the first place: After an economy loses the legal right to trade people, what actually replaces the external income and political structures that trade supported?

My first formulation was too clean. I thought: These countries stayed poor because they never replaced slavery with productive economies. Morocco itself disproves that sentence. It manufactures cars. It exports phosphates and fertilizers. It has tourism, agriculture, logistics, major infrastructure projects, and growing industrial capacity.

The IMF estimated Moroccan real GDP growth at 4.9 percent in 2025

.

In the first four months of 2026, automotive products were its leading export

. This is not an economy that can honestly be reduced to migration.

But that correction doesn’t kill the question. It makes it better.

A country can build a modern productive …

author: anred
title: El podcast de Manuela Santucho: entrega, amor y revolución
content:
El podcast “Manuela Santucho. La vida. Los nombres. El lugar”, realizado por Diego Genoud, publicó su primer episodio el último 7 de septiembre y viene a traernos una historia cargada de emocionalidad y militancia, características que suelen ser disociadas en los vericuetos fetichistas de las lecturas históricas, y más cuando se trata de los setenta.

 Por Nicolás Salas, para ANRed.


“Nenita”, como la reconocen sus familiares y amigos, fue la segunda mujer entre diez hermanos. Nació en la Ciudad Autónoma de Buenos Aires aunque sus raíces y mudanzas siempre orbitaron en dirección a Santiago del Estero.


Esta producción, que puede seguirse en el canal de youtube “Otro periodista”, nos muestra la historia de una militante del Partido Revolucionario de los Trabajadores (PRT) que, como muchos de su generación, se propuso realizar una revolución socialista en la Argentina.


En ningún momento se disimula tamaña ambición. Tampoco se niegan las características de quienes encarnan ese proyecto colectivo. Esta historia nos muestra, a través de “nenita”, que se puede dar la vida por la transformación social y venir de un profundo catolicismo. Que se puede integrar una organización guerrillera sin dejar de lado los gustos por los vestidos y la elegancia. Que sin amor nada importante puede hacerse en la vida.


Su paso por Gramillia, Corrientes, el viaje a Cuba, el diario El Mundo, la defensa de los presos políticos, su amor, el casamiento, el partido, Roby, Perón, Tucumán y los ingenios, el FAS, mil reuniones, “chicho”, Francisco René, Adelita, las primeras caídas, las primeras desapariciones, la disciplina y varios momentos de la vida de Manuela dotan de dinámica a estos primeros cinco capítulos de un podcast que promete mucho más.


Foto: Página 12


El rol de quien asume la narración y la reconstrucción de la historia no es menor. Genoud además de periodista es hijo de Manuela, lo cual imprime una visión humana necesaria y particular. El recorrido por la vida personal de la protagonista no implica en ningún momento el abandono de una lectura política precisa, sino todo lo contrario. Ambas caras de la misma moneda son conjugadas dialécticamente para mostrarnos, a través de una historia individual, un momento trascendental en la lucha de clases contemporánea de la Argentina. Tamaña búsqueda se lleva a cabo sin hacer concesiones a las defecciones que suele generar el paso del tiempo y que, en la actualidad, tiene su expresión en visiones revisionistas tanto por derecha como por “centro”. 


Cabe destacar que es un trabajo sostenido sobre fuentes documentales que incluyen decenas de cintas y grabaciones de entrevistas realizadas durante las últimas décadas. Cada capítulo ronda los 25 minutos, tiempo suficiente para experimentar emociones que van desde la empatía que nos genera una situación familiar particular hasta la bronca por algún acontecimiento político.


Esta producción aparece a 50 años de la desaparición forzada de Manuela Santucho (y gran parte de su familia) a manos de las fuerzas represivas de la última dictadura. El 13 de julio de 1976 la secuestraron en Villa Crespo junto a Cristina Navajas y a Alicia D’Ambra. Se supo que pasó por varios campos de concentración como Orletti, Campo de Mayo, El Vesubio, Coordinación Federal y el Pozo de Banfield. Quienes sobrevivieron a esos lugares y conocieron a Manuela aseguraban que, pese a las torturas y los tormentos, “nenita” se mantuvo fiel a sus principios, dando ánimo al resto de sus compañeros y compañeras, y levantando redes de resistencia en las peores condiciones posibles. Su vida, como lo refleja el podcast, reafirman que las revoluciones las hacen personas de carne y hueso, con sus aciertos y errores, pero ante todo con una entrega sin parangón en el pensamiento enajenado de la sociedad capitalista.

Buon pomeriggio a tutti, tutte e

Ringrazio vivamente i compagni dell’Esercito Zapatista di Liberazione Nazionale, le basi d’appoggio dell’organizzazione, chi ci sta seguendo attraverso le trasmissioni in diretta dai 

puyes

 [NdT: i puyes – in lingua maya tseltal chiocciola o conchiglia di fiume – sono le nuove  zone di organizzazione politica e comunitaria delle comunità indigene zapatiste, che sostituiscono i vecchi “caracol”] e anche chi ci accompagna da altri paesi attraverso internet. Un ringraziamento al Capitano Marcos e al Subcomandante Moisés; oggi per me è un onore essere qui con voi.


Sono molto emozionato, e confesso di essere anche molto nervoso. Dopo tutto quello che si è detto in questo seminario, come anche questa mattina, pensavo di intervenire affermando di essere d’accordo con quasi tutto e chiudere così il mio intervento. Ma nonostante questo vi condividerò alcune questioni che spero possano essere di vostro interesse.


Appartengo ad una generazione che ha visto il Messico sommergersi nella barbarie e il mondo entrare in una profonda e grave crisi. Non fraintendetemi, non penso che il Messico o il mondo in precedenza fossero luoghi migliori, ma è necessario accettare che la guerra del capitalismo nei confronti dell’Umanità e dei Territori ci ha condotto verso un punto di non ritorno. Il 2006 è un anno che ha rappresentato per molti di noi un bivio: è l’anno in cui Felipe Calderón Hinojosa ha diffuso e intensificato la guerra in tutto il Messico. Col senno di poi, possiamo renderci conto che in verità quell’anno rappresenta solamente un tassello di una lunga guerra di sfruttamento e espropriazione. Ciò nonostante, è stato anche l’anno in cui diverse geografie del paese hanno cominciato a vivere la brutalità della guerra. Quella guerra che si viveva, con modi e intensità differenti nei vari territori del Messico, si è diffusa in tutti i boschi, foreste, mari, deserti, strade, scuole e posti di lavoro del paese. 


Dal 2011 in poi ho avuto l’opportunità di visitare diversi stati del paese. Durante questi viaggi ho conversato con membri di organizzazioni sociali, con famiglie in cerca di 

desaparecidos

, con famiglie che hanno sofferto femminicidi, con famiglie di persone assassinate. Durante questi colloqui ho conosciuto la morte nelle sue forme più atroci, nelle modalità in cui è possibile arrivare ad assassinare la memoria stessa. Quei discorsi mi hanno fatto capire che in Messico si puo moriré piu volte: esiste la morte fisica, la morte per oblio e la morte di chi, non più in vita, viene perseguitato e colpevolizzato del proprio assassinio.


La maggior parte delle persone con cui ho conversato denuncia ripetutamente la complicità della polizia, dei governi locali e federali con il crimine organizzato. In alcuni casi hanno segnalato l’esistenza di legami diretti tra presidenti municipali, deputati, membri dei partiti politici e i gruppi criminali. Uno dei casi che ho potuto conoscere da vicino è quello di Melchor Flores Hernández, un giovane di 26 anni che lavorava in strada facendo la statua umana. Il 

Vaquero Galáctico

, il personaggio interpretato da Melchor, è stato arrestato dalla polizia di Monterrey, Nuevo León, e poi consegnato ad un gruppo criminale. E da quel momento non si sa più nulla di lui.


Il caso di Melchor non è l’unico, esistono centinaia di casi simili. È grazie alle ricerche dei familiari delle stesse persone 

desaparecidas

che si è potuto accertare che alcune di queste persone sono state vittima di tratta per essere condotte nei campi, coinvolte nel traffico di droga, utilizzate nella sicurezza dei gruppi criminali o vittima di sfruttamento sessuale. author: Fozzie
title: Chapter 21: Piece Wages
content:
Harry Cleaver's study guide to Karl Marx's Capital volume 1, chapter 21.

Piece wages seem as if workers sell their embodied labor in each piece. Piece wages seem as if the wage is not determined by the value of labor power.

Piece wages and time wages often exist side-by-side:

Marx gives us an example as a point of departure:

1) Setting of piece rates is a source of struggle between workers and capitalists

2) With piece work the need for direct "superindendence" is reduced or even eliminated; workers are forced to work fast and well to meet the going standard of production under the threat of not being fully paid, or losing their job.

3) Piece wages tend to produce hierarchies of wages

4)Piece wages result in workers being willing, or even desirous, of longer working hours.

5) Technological change that increases the productivity of a given time and intensity of labor will:

To illustrate this dynamic, Marx modifies the example previously given on the basis of a doubling of productivity, i.e., total output goes from 24 to 48. As a result:

"Piece-work", to the experienced worker whether in home, factory or field always carries the flavor of exploitation. The subtlety that Marx insists upon - how the form of payment leads workers to drive themselves to high intensity and long hours - is not always immediately apparent to new and naive workers. To them piece-work may seem to provide an opportunity for great achievement: the more you work, the more you get paid. They don't realize at first that the piece rates have been set so that even with their greatest efforts they will earn little in relation to what they produce. They don't realize, because they haven't had the experience, that if they outperform past standards, the piece-rates will be adjusted downward so that their income rises but little, even with increased effort.

In the passage below, from his story "The Apostate", Jack London describes some of this psychological dynamic as well as the physical costs workers may bear under such conditions of exploitation.

After he recovered, he got work in a glass factory. The pay was better, and the work demanded skill. It was piece-work, and the more skilful he was, the bigger wages he earned. Here was incentive. And under this incentive he developed into a remarkable worker.

It was simple work, the tying of glass stoppers into small bottles. At his waist he carried a bundle of twine. He held the bottles between his knees so that he might work with both hands. Thus, in a sitting position and bending over his own knees, his narrow shoulders grew humped and his chest was contracted for ten hours each day. This was not good for the lungs, but he tied three hundred dozen bottles a day.

The superindendent was very proud of him, and brought visitors to look at him. In ten hours three hundred dozen bottles passed through his hands. This meant that he had attained machine-like perfection. All waste movements were eliminated. Every motion of his thin arms, every movement of a muscle in the thin fingers, was swift and accurate. He worked at high tension, and the result was that he grew nervous. At night his muscles twitched in his sleep, and in the daytime he could not relax and rest. He remained keyed up and his muscles continued to twitch. Also he grew sallow and his lint-cough grew worse. Then pneumonia laid hold of the feeble lungs within the contracted chest, and he lost his job in the glass-works.

(Jack London, "The Apostate', in Jack London, Novels & Stories, New York: The Library of America, 1982.

One of the great attractions of piece work and piece wages to capitalists is that with piece rates set low enough, very little supervision is required. In order to earn a living wage workers must work hard, fast and well to produce enough pieces - quite irrespective of whether anyone is looking over their shoulder. The costs of supervision are essentially passed from the capitalist to the workers as they internalize the discipline of piece work and impose work on themselves. This self-imposition of work, of course, goes against workers' instinctive ressentment and resistance to suffering the indignities of alienating work - doing what some one else says to do, they way they say to do it, for their profit and enrichment, and so on. The piece workers, therefore, pay the psychological costs not only of alienation but of the hour-to-hour experience of imposing that alienation on themselves.

author: Erica Malatesta
title: New Stormy Petrel Now Out!
content:
This is the 8th edition of our theoretical magazine in which we discuss issues in more depth. Articles include:


Dossier on AI, Work in the Future Society, Age Verification, the General Strike, Mujeres Libres, and a letter from a reader on veganism.


Editorial


Now and tomorrow


Now: Hope in Every Heart or Business as Usual?


Andy Burnham’s accession to power doesn’t mark any radical change in the direction of the Labour Party. He backs the Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood’s immigration reforms, increasing the wait for indefinite leave to remain from five years to between 10 and 20 years. He supports expanding the use of detention centres. He wrote recently in

The Times

 that “Increasing our national security, in every sense, will be my first priority,” and that arms manufacture would be central in “regenerating and reindustrialising the country.” He threatened that he would “not be squeamish about cutting welfare” to invest more in the arms industry.


He intends to proceed with the £31bn Dreadnought-class boats and with the building of Trident nuclear submarines. He urged EU countries to supply Ukraine with Patriot missiles. He signed a military AI deal with Ukraine, accessing Ukraine’s Avengers AI Labs database. This huge AI database holds data collected by thousands of daylight cameras and infrared sensors across the war zone in Ukraine. They capture footage of millions of objects and the data is then fed back to the Avengers Lab to train new AI models. This will be used to protect military bases from “protesters and hostile actors trying to gain intelligence.” The Burnham administration also will work with Ukraine to explore the development of next-generation low-power AI chips to power drones and robotics.


Burnham appointed Kanishka Narayan as the first AI minister, signalling Labour support for AI, whilst coming out with rhetoric about independence from US Big Tech.


He continues to back Israel and its genocidal policies. Whilst we have experienced the hottest summer on record, Burnham talks about new drilling for oil and gas in the North Sea, exhibiting a complete unconcern about the connection between fossil fuel and climate change. He talks about a “business-friendly socialism”, as if such an obscene coupling was either possible or desirable.


The Future Society


“A map of the world that does not include Utopia, is not even worth glancing at, for it leaves out the one country at which Humanity is always landing… Progress is the realisation of utopias.”


Oscar Wilde


The theme of this issue is ‘The Future Society’. This came about because of our experience of people asking questions about what an anarchist communist society will be like, such as ‘How will it be possible?’, ‘What about crime?’, ‘What about jobs that no one wants to do?’ When many Marxists, and others, envisage a future society it usually involves automation and advanced technology, including AI. While we reject ‘anarcho-primitivism’ (see Issue 7 of Stormy Petrel), we take a critical approach to technology, especially AI. We need to ensure that it will actually enhance our lives as well as be compatible with environmental and resource concerns.


In order to address some of the questions about an anarchist communist society, in each topic we first address the reasons why the status quo is a disaster, both for the working class and the planet. We then also look at the struggles going on today. The attacks on workers’ organisation, surveillance, the insidious insertion of AI into all areas of life, the environmental effects of resource plundering, war, and the drive for growth at any cost, not only have tragic consequences today, but will make it harder for us to create the future we want. We will only be able to collectively create an anarchist communist future if we overthrow capitalism and begin to establish a vision and the foundations for this society.


We have to envision a different future. There has been an ideological onslaught over the past few decades with the capitalist slogan of ‘There Is No Alternative’ advanced over and over again. Any idea of an alternative future is mocked and laughed at. The 19

th

 century vision of a stateless, classless and free society shared by socialists and anarchists is rarely addressed, and dull grey reformism is the order of the day. This was apparent at this year’s Tolpuddle event, where an array of trade union speakers on AI failed to voice any real opposition to it, but just talked …

author: Unknown
title: French Youth Take the Streets against a Bleak Future : A Report
content:
This past week, thousands of teenagers have taken the streets of France, clashing with police as they demonstrate against the deplorable conditions in their high schools and a rapidly collapsing future. This is a promising sign, shifting attention from the seemingly unstoppable rise of the extreme right to the question of what people can do on a grassroots basis to defend themselves. Our correspondents in Paris explore the situation in detail.


Another unprecedented summer of record

heatwaves

,

droughts

, and

wildfires

 throughout Europe underlines the desperate situation we are all facing today, while politicians of all stripes and their techno-industrial sponsors continue to turn a blind eye, forcing us down the path to catastrophe in the name of progress.


Hoping to turn the page on these environmental disasters, the French government has hurriedly shifted focus to other priorities. The coming months represent a crucial transition for Emmanuel Macron and his government, as they will bring Macron’s second term to a close, opening a new political era in France. Candidates are already battling to succeed Macron in power at the beginning of May 2027.


In the midst of this political spectacle, during an increasingly

menacing surge

 in the popularity of the National Rally (formerly, the National Front), the extreme-right party, it is especially meaningful that teenagers have started to organize at a grassroots level to defend themselves. This organizing gained momentum last week, when blockades of high schools, demonstrations, and riots erupted across France, taking everyone by surprise.


Students clash with police forces in Montpellier on October 2, 2026.


Licensed to Kill?


Since Macron was elected President for the first time in May 2017, the political discourse in France has been even more dominated by an emphasis on authoritarian and far-right ideologies in terms of security, immigration, and economic and social issues.


This political shift towards an even more aggressive form of governance has led to increasing state violence targeting the social movements and uprisings that have emerged since. From the eviction of the

ZAD

 at Notre-Dame-des-Landes in 2017 to the

riots

 following the murder of Nahel in 2023, not forgetting the

Yellow Vest

 sequence and the COVID-19 pandemic lockdown experimental

doctrines

, we have experienced a headlong plunge into a world of surveillance, repression, and loss of individual freedoms. This has become today’s new normal.


It was in this already suffocating context that last July, the French government decided to vote on a new bill giving police officers more latitude to use their firearms without consequences—a demand that the far right has promoted for years. If voted through, this legislation could set a

dangerous precedent

, as it would establish “a presumption of ‘legitimate use of arms’ by police and gendarmes ‘in the exercise of their duty’.”


Police arrest a student in Lyons on October 1, 2026.


In other words, not only will police officers be able to freely use their weapons if in any situation they claim to fear for their lives or the lives of others, but authorities will no longer have to prove that the officers acted within the framework of the law, as they are required to do today. It will be up to the victims and their families to provide evidence that the use of firearms was not justified. We can already see how this new law represents a legislative tool enabling law enforcement agents, and therefore, the state, to cover up future murders.


Unwilling to let such a law pass without resistance, political opponents and radicals, who had rightly rebranded this law the “license to kill,” decided to organize massive demonstrations and events throughout France on the weekend of September 18 to 20.

Thousands

 of people took part in these protests in different major cities alongside traditional leftist politicians, rights groups such as Amnesty International and the League of Human Rights, and various lawyers and magistrates’ unions.


In the meantime, another call for action reusing all the codes of the Yellow Vest movement spread online. The origins of this call remain obscure, as some national

newspapers

 have raised the possibility that AI-generated accounts had flooded social media platforms with this rumor on purpose. Nevertheless, media and politicians began commenting on this potential resurgence of the Yellow Vest movement due to the …

author: Mohammed Altaj
title: Israel Above the Law … Palestine Beyond Justice
content:
The world did not lack knowledge of what was happening to Palestinians.

It knew that a people had been living under occupation for decades; that land was being confiscated, settlements expanding, homes demolished, and checkpoints cutting cities and villages off from one another.

The United Nations knew. Governments knew. Parliaments and international courts knew.

The shift now visible across significant parts of Western public opinion did not begin because the world suddenly discovered new facts about Palestine.

What changed was the distance between the news and the human being.

People saw what war means when a child is trapped beneath rubble, what displacement means when a family carries whatever it can and walks away without knowing where it will go.

And the numbers began to acquire names, faces and voices.

One of those names was Hind Rajab.

I do not mention Hind because her story encompasses everything that happened in Gaza. I mention her because some tragedies become windows through which people see what numbers alone cannot reveal.

Hind was trapped inside a car in Gaza in January 2024 after members of her family had been killed. She called for help. Twelve days later, she was found dead inside the car. The two paramedics sent to rescue her were also found dead.

But Hind was no longer a number.

The world also saw seven World Central Kitchen aid workers killed in Israeli strikes while carrying out humanitarian work. And even after the ceasefire announced in October 2025, the killing did not end. According to Palestinian Ministry of Health figures cited by the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs, by September 23, 2026, 1,402 Palestinians had been killed and 4,881 injured since the ceasefire announcement.

Bodies remained beneath the rubble, while families waited to reach loved ones not to save them this time, but to bury them.

But Palestinian history did not begin in Gaza.

And it did not begin on October 7, 2023.

In 1994, Baruch Goldstein, an Israeli settler and member of the Kach movement, opened fire on Muslim worshippers in the Ibrahimi Mosque in Hebron, killing at least twenty-nine people. In 2014, sixteen-year-old Mohammed Abu Khdeir was abducted from Shuafat, beaten and burned alive. A year later, the Dawabsheh family home in Duma was set on fire while the family slept; toddler Ali and later both his parents died.

So when a Palestinian is asked to begin the story on the morning of October 7, he is effectively being asked to erase what came before.

None of this makes the targeting of civilians acceptable, whoever they are.

Justice cannot begin halfway through history.

By September 14, 2026, the United Nations had documented more than 1,600 settler attacks resulting in Palestinian casualties, property damage, or both, across 275 Palestinian communities since the beginning of the year. More than 1,500 Palestinians had been displaced because of demolitions of structures lacking Israeli-issued permits, while more than 2,600 had been displaced in the context of settler violence and related access restrictions.

Between September 15 and 21 alone, the UN documented 51 settler attacks resulting in casualties, property damage, or both. At least 800 olive, fruit and palm trees were damaged, uprooted or burned. In the same week, demolitions displaced 147 Palestinians, including 73 children.

These are not isolated incidents.

This is land being transformed, communities disappearing, families being pushed out.

And this is where the phrase “extremist settlers” is no longer enough.

Who plans the settlements? Who allocates the land? Who builds the roads, extends the infrastructure and provides the protection?

At what point does settler violence cease to be merely the act of an individual and become a problem within the system itself?

In September 2026, UN Secretary-General António Guterres warned that settlement expansion was accelerating, outposts were proliferating and settler violence was rising to alarming levels. He also warned that advancing the E1 settlement plan would deal a “deathblow” to the prospect of a contiguous and viable Palestinian state.

How, then, can the world continue to declare its support for a two-state solution while the geography on which one of those states is supposed to exist is being transformed?

The problem is not confined to land.

In Jerusalem, Christian clergy have repeatedly reported being spat at, insulted and harassed. In April 2026, a Catholic …

Λευτεριά στην Παλαιστίνη, λευτεριά στον Λίβανο.


Η

7η Οκτωβρίου

 ήταν μια πράξη αντιαποικιακής και αντιιμπεριαλιστικής αντίστασης. Μια συνέχεια της αντίστασης που χρονολογείται από τη στιγμή της ίδρυσης του κράτους του “Ισραήλ” το 1948, αλλά και ακόμη νωρίτερα, κατά τη διάρκεια της βρετανικής αποικιακής κατοχής. Ήταν ένας λαός και ένα κίνημα που ξεσηκώθηκαν ενάντια στην κατοχή. Η ημέρα αυτή θα συνεχίσει να τιμάται ως τέτοια για τις επόμενες γενιές, ακόμη και αν οι σιωνιστές και οι ιμπεριαλιστές προσπαθήσουν με κάθε μέσο να ελέγξουν και να αλλάξουν το αφήγημα. Τα αλεξίπτωτα πλαγιάς που πετούσαν πάνω από τον φράχτη προς την κατεχόμενη Παλαιστίνη, ο φράχτης που περιέκλειε τη Γάζα και γκρεμίστηκε από τους ανθρώπους που εκδιώχθηκαν από τη γη τους πριν από δεκαετίες: αυτές οι εικόνες δεν θα ξεχαστούν και θα παραμείνουν στη μνήμη μας ως σύμβολα της αντίστασης του Παγκόσμιου Νότου.


Η απάντηση της σιωνιστικής οντότητας, με την υποστήριξη των ΗΠΑ, υπήρξε ανελέητη. Από τον Οκτώβριο του 2023 γινόμαστε μάρτυρες μιας γενοκτονίας που μεταδίδεται ζωντανά και πολλών φρικαλεοτήτων που διαπράττονται από τη σιωνιστική οντότητα και τους ιμπεριαλιστές των ΗΠΑ (με την υποστήριξη ευρωπαϊκών κρατών). Η Γάζα έχει ισοπεδωθεί από τους βομβαρδισμούς και, παρόλο που γίνεται λόγος για κατάπαυση του πυρός, συνεχίζουν να βομβαρδίζουν και να πυροβολούν αδιακρίτως. Ο Λίβανος και η Συρία τελούν υπό κατοχή και δέχονται συνεχείς επιθέσεις από τη σιωνιστική οντότητα. Οι κυβερνήσεις αυτών των περιοχών καταστέλλουν την αντίσταση και την εναντίωση στη Δύση και το “Ισραήλ” στα εδάφη τους, ενεργώντας ως εντολοδόχοι των ΗΠΑ. Όλα αυτά συμβαίνουν ενώ το “Ισραήλ” καταλαμβάνει όλο και περισσότερα εδάφη, αποσταθεροποιώντας περαιτέρω την περιοχή.


Το κράτος του “Ισραήλ” και οι ΗΠΑ καταστρέφουν ορισμένες από τις αρχαιότερες περιοχές με συνεχή κατοίκηση στην ιστορία του πολιτισμού, στην Παλαιστίνη, τον Λίβανο, τη Συρία και το Ιράν. author: heinhtetkyaw
title: Simone Weil: The waning of the working class, technique and the rise of fascism
content:
The only hope of socialism resides in those who have already brought about in themselves, as far as is possible in the society of today, that union between manual and intellectual labour which characterizes the society we are aiming at. ~ Simone Weil

The long-foreseen moment has arrived when capitalism is on the point of seeing its development arrested by impassable barriers. In whatever way we interpret the phenomenon of accumulation, it is clear that capitalism stands essentially for economic expansion and that capitalist expansion has now nearly reached the point where it will be halted by the actual limits of the earth’s surface. And yet never have there been fewer premonitory signs of the advent of socialism. We are in a period of transition; but a transition towards what? No one has the slightest idea. All the more striking, therefore, the carefree security with which we settle down in this transition period as though it were a definite stage, so much so that considerations concerning the crisis of the system have almost everywhere become commonplaces. Certainly, we can always go on believing that socialism will arrive the day after tomorrow, and make a duty or a virtue of this belief; so long as we go on taking, day by day, the day after tomorrow to mean the next day but one after today, we shall be sure not to be disappointed; but such a state of mind is difficult to distinguish from that of those worthy people who believe, for instance, in the Last Judgment. If we want to traverse this sombre age in manly fashion, we shall refrain, like the Ajax of Sophocles, from letting empty hopes set us afire.

Throughout history men have struggled, suffered and died to free the oppressed. Their efforts, when they did not remain sterile, have never led to anything except the replacing of one oppressive régime by another. Marx, who had observed this, thought he was able to demonstrate scientifically that things were different in our day, and that the struggle of the oppressed would now lead to a true emancipation, not to a new oppression. It is this idea, which we have preserved as an article of faith, that we need to examine afresh, unless we mean systematically to close our eyes to the events of the past twenty years. Let us spare ourselves the disillusionments of those who, having fought for Liberty, Equality, Fraternity, discovered one fine day that what they had got was, as Marx says, Infantry, Cavalry, Artillery. But they at any rate were able to draw some lesson from the surprises of history; sadder is the lot of those who perished in 1792 or 1793, in the street or on the frontiers, fully convinced that with their lives they were purchasing the freedom of mankind. If we are to perish in the battles of the future, let us do our best to prepare ourselves to perish with a clear vision of the world we shall be leaving behind.

The Paris Commune was an example not only of the creative power of the working-class masses in movement, but also of the fundamental impotence of a spontaneous movement when it comes to fighting against organized forces of repression. August 1914 marked the bankruptcy of proletarian mass organizations, both on the political and the trade-union planes, within the framework of the system. From then onwards it became necessary to abandon once and for all the hopes placed in this mode of organization not only by the reformists, but by Engels. On the other hand, October 1917 ushered in new and radiant prospects. At last the means had been found of combining legal with illegal action, the systematic labours of disciplined militants with the spontaneous seething of the masses. All over the world communist parties were to be formed to which the Bolshevik party would pass on its knowledge and technique; they were to replace social democracy, already described by Rosa Luxemburg, in August 1914, as a “stinking corpse”, and very soon to disappear from the stage of history; and they were to seize power within a very short time. The political régime set up spontaneously by the workers of Paris in 1871, then by those of St. Petersburg in 1905, was to become solidly entrenched in Russia and so on to embrace the entire civilized world. Of course, the crushing of the Russian Revolution by the brutal intervention of foreign imperialism might blast these brilliant prospects; but, unless such a thing occurred, Lenin and Trotsky were certain of introducing into history precisely this particular series of …

title: Online ACG public meeting on the Organisational Platform of the Libertarian Communists 7pm, Wednesday October 21st
content:
Notice on forthcoming ACG meeting

The Organisational Platform of the Libertarian Communists, popularly known as The Platform, was published by exiled Russian and Ukrainian anarchist communists in 1926. This short, draft, pamphlet shook the anarchist world and divided opinion with its call for a General Union of Anarchists, tactical and theoretical unity and collective responsibility. It has continued to inspire many anarchist communists across the globe. The meeting will discuss the (in)famous Platform and consider what it offers us 100 years after its publication. Get your free tickets here: https://www.eventbrite.com/e/the-organisational-platform-of-the-libertarian-communists-tickets-2003055825896?aff=oddtdtcreator

Anarchism and Insurrectionary Anarchism

Hacktivism as Digital Insurrection

Examples of Hacktivist Resistance

The essay you are about to read was written in the past when I was an early grad student still becoming a realized writer of anarchism’s ideas. Some of the information may be overly moralistic and other points may be overly empirical. Some of the writing may be overly casual while other areas may be overly academic. Some information that should be cited may not be, and some information that is cited may not have to be. My standpoints and interpretations of ideas throughout this piece may have changed since its writing, but it was my analysis at the time that I stood behind and defended. For any questions on the information presented, my updated perspectives and beliefs, or anything of the like, feel free to message me directly. If you believe the question you are asking is of good faith and may encourage a fruitful conversation including others, feel free to comment below to start the conversation. Be kind.

On December 29, 2025, a hacker known as Martha Root took the stage at an annual hacking convention in Hamburg, Germany. Dressed in a pink Power Rangers outfit, she shared how for months, she had been infiltrating three white supremacist dating websites by creating AI chatbots to interact with users while collecting their personal information. In the panel’s final fifteen minutes, she remotely accessed and deleted all three websites, much to the neo-Nazi website creator’s disapproval, which he described in a tweet as “cyberterrorism.” Root noted how easy it was to hack into the websites, citing “poor cybersecurity hygiene that would make even your grandma’s AOL account blush.”[1] Root’s actions can arguably show how the principles of insurrectionary anarchism, such as direct, autonomous, and disruptive intervention, can extend from physical spaces into the digital realm. Such actions can include Root’s hacking/hacktivism as well as DDoS attacks and the targeted takedowns of extremist, corporate, or state-controlled websites. Cyberspace itself can be seen as a loosely-governed libertarian space that offers hackers near-total freedom to translate traditional anarchist tactics into digital actions. Insurrectionary anarchism can take form in contemporary digital spaces through autonomous hacktivism, the disruption or removal of oppressive online networks, and decentralized digital interventions.

Anarchism can be defined as a sociopolitical philosophy that is against hierarchies wherever they may be found. Such hierarchies can include political ones such as the state and representative democracy, economic ones such as capitalism and wage labor, and social ones such as patriarchy, homophobia, and organized religion.[2] It is widely seen as one of the only ideologies that fully confronts and wishes to dismantle all forms of capitalism along with the state and its power without utilizing either for personal benefit. Anarchie, Femmes, Émancipation

https://radio-libertaire.org/accueil.php


Depuis le 150

e

Ce fut le cas avec l'autogestion, l'art et la culture, la place des idées anarchistes dans la Commune… En 2026, quatre groupes de la région parisienne, les Groupes Louise Michel, Salvador Segui, Pierre Besnard et Commune de Paris organisent une journée destinée aux femmes, à leur rôle pendant la Commune, en projetant leurs revendications dans les luttes actuelles en France et dans le monde.


Aujourd'hui, comment les luttes des femmes participent à la perspective anarchiste

 

?


Sur tous les continents, les femmes luttent malgré les guerres, les dictatures, les emprisonnements, les déplacements forcés, les violences sexuelles. La situation des femmes relève aussi de l'apartheid de genre et, les féminicides ne cessent. Mais les combats pour le droit à l'avortement, à la scolarisation, à l'accès à l'emploi, à l'égalité des salaires se rejoignent contre le patriarcat et le capitalisme. De même du côté du genre et de la pensée queer, ou dans le champ culturel, apparaissent des revendications contre l'invisibilisation des femmes, sur la liberté du corps, le respect de chacun et chacune, être libre. Il reste à continuer de définir et de faire vivre l'anarcha- féminisme.
