title: CPT report documents overcrowding, ill-treatment and isolation in Turkish prisons
content:
The Council of Europe’s Committee for the Prevention of Torture (CPT) has published two long-withheld reports on conditions in Turkish prisons and police detention facilities. The findings are based on visits conducted in January 2021 and February 2024. The reports were not made public until October 6, 2026, after the Turkish authorities agreed to their publication. The findings range from severe overcrowding and allegations of physical ill-treatment to years of de facto isolation in high-security prisons. The CPT paid particular attention to prisoners serving aggravated life sentences, as well as women and LGBTIQ+ prisoners.


During its 2021 visit, the delegation inspected 13 police and gendarmerie facilities, including police headquarters and counterterrorism units in Ankara, Diyarbakır and Istanbul. It also visited eight prisons, including women’s prisons in Istanbul-Bakırköy and Kayseri, a juvenile prison in Istanbul-Maltepe and a high-security prison in Diyarbakır.


The special visit in February 2024


focused on four high-security prisons in Antalya, Iğdır and Van, as well as two L-type prisons in Antalya and Maltepe, Istanbul. Particular attention was paid to the detention conditions of prisoners serving aggravated life sentences, as well as the situation of women, LGBTIQ+ prisoners and people held in solitary confinement for administrative or disciplinary reasons.


338,000 people in prison


The growth of the prison population has been particularly dramatic. At the end of 2019, around 290,000 people were imprisoned in Turkey. By January 2021, the number had fallen to around 192,000, largely against the backdrop of the COVID-19 pandemic. Even then, however, the CPT found overcrowding in most of the prisons it visited.


The trend subsequently reversed. According to official figures, around 338,000 people were in prison as of June 2024. This corresponded to approximately 395 prisoners per 100,000 inhabitants, making it the highest incarceration rate among Council of Europe member states at the time. The CPT calls on the Turkish authorities to give the highest priority to reducing the prison population and addressing the structural causes of overcrowding.


Allegations of beatings and falaka


At Antalya S-Type Prison, the CPT delegation encountered several allegations of physical ill-treatment in 2024. Prisoners reported being slapped, punched, kicked and beaten with batons. The Committee considered several of these accounts credible. In two cases, prisoners also reported being beaten on the soles of their feet with batons—a method of torture known as “falaka” (bastinado). In one case, the delegation observed injuries that were consistent with the prisoner’s account of ill-treatment.


The CPT calls for prison management and staff to be unequivocally informed that physical ill-treatment and the disproportionate use of force are unlawful. Public prosecutors, it says, must also investigate cases involving the use of force by prison staff more thoroughly.


Years of de facto solitary confinement


The CPT also sharply criticizes the conditions of prisoners serving aggravated life sentences. In the high-security prisons visited, a significant proportion of them had been held in de facto solitary confinement for months or even years. Some prisoners spent at least 21 hours a day alone in their cells. In some cases, regular out-of-cell activities were limited to daily outdoor exercise, which was also taken alone.


The CPT warns that prolonged isolation can have serious consequences for mental, somatic and social health and, under certain circumstances, may amount to inhuman or degrading treatment. The Turkish authorities are therefore called upon to take urgent steps at the prisons visited to ensure that all aggravated life -sentenced prisoners (and any other prisoners held alone in their cells) are offered meaningful human contact for at least two hours every day and preferably more. More generally, the Committee emphasises once again that the very concept of the detention regime of persons sentenced to aggravated life imprisonment, as defined in the law, is fundamentally flawed and should be subject to a complete overhaul.


Women and children held in unsuitable conditions


The CPT also found significant overcrowding in the L-type prisons in Antalya and Istanbul-Maltepe. In Antalya, some areas accommodating women were in poor structural and hygienic condition. Conditions for imprisoned mothers and their …

author: Soraya Kishtwari
title: French Teen Loses Hand After Police Use Grenade Amid Student Protests
content:
A teenager lost his hand in France after a police grenade exploded during widespread student protests on Monday, amid mounting reports of violence by officers. 


The 15-year-old boy was injured outside Auguste-Béhal high school in the northern town of Lens, in Pas-de-Calais, where riot police had been deployed after protesters reportedly threw objects at officers.


It is not yet clear what type of grenade it was or exactly how it caused the injury. A police union source told AFP the boy

appeared to have picked it up

, but a

girl reportedly standing nearby

 told regional newspaper La Voix Du Nord this was false. 


“I was there, I saw it. He didn’t pick it up,” she said. 


Witnesses told

Le Monde

 that riot police had pushed protesters back before throwing the grenade. 


On 28 September, a police officer shot a tear gas grenade and struck a 14-year-old boy named Eden in the face at close range,

Le Monde reported

. 


“Eden has a double jaw fracture, several of his lower teeth have been pulled out, and all his upper teeth are broken,” his lawyer, Elsa Marcel, told a press conference. His mother added that he can only consume liquids: “His jaw is sealed shut with just enough space for a straw.” 


In another incident, a 16-year-old lost sight in one eye after reportedly being hit with a rubber bullet. An investigation is underway to clarify what happened.


In total, six judicial investigations into alleged police violence have been opened since a wave of student protests erupted at the start of the academic year over teacher shortages, overcrowded classrooms and poor school conditions. Students have described leaking classrooms, deteriorating buildings and going months without teachers.


Education minister Édouard Geffray said 190 students had been injured since the protests began, while the Interior Ministry reported 650 injuries among police officers, including a female officer who was chased and kicked. Seventy-eight school staff members have also been injured. The figures do not distinguish between serious and minor injuries. 


Prime minister Sébastien Lecornu said student grievances were

“legitimate” and promised action

 on teacher shortages, school repairs and overloaded timetables, with some pupils starting as early as 8am and finishing as late as 6pm.

Unions

 say the government needs to reverse cuts to education rather than offer limited measures.


As many as

200,000 people

 were expected to join a national day of action on Tuesday, with 1,800 schools due to be blockaded as teachers, trade unionists and parents join demonstrations.


Parent groups, led by the Fédération des Conseils de Parents d’Élèves, the largest federation of public school parent associations, have also

called on parents to join the protests

.


The Union Syndicale Lycéenne, which represents high schools, said Tuesday that the number of people mobilising had reached a “

new record

”.


Amnesty International

said

: “Protests have been met with unnecessary and disproportionate force by police, including the unlawful use of tear gas grenades and rubber bullets. The Ministry of Interior announced that there have been more than 5,000 arrests of protesters and stated that 85% of those arrested have been children.”

author: dev
title: Ritchy Thibault, premier prisonnier du mouvement lycéen
content:
Interpellé en pleine rue jeudi dernier, l'écrivain et voyageur Ritchy Thibault a été emprisonné. Il lui est reproché un discours prononcé à Saint-Denis lors d'une assemblée générale de lycéens. Une audience se tiendra ce lundi à 13h au tribunal de Bobigny qui statuera sur sa libération dans l'attente d'un procès ou son maintien en détention, ce qui serait un très mauvais signal envoyé aux lycéens plus que jamais mobilisés.


Il y a des fabricants de destins qui l'aimeraient clandestin.


Certains commencent dans des amphithéâtres, d'autres dans les caravanes ou sur des rond-points de campagne. Celui de Ritchy Thibault semble, lui, avoir trouvé un drôle de raccourci : viré de l'hémicycle en tant qu' attaché parlementaire, on le retrouve forcément dès le premier jour de la mobilisation aux abords d'un lycée de banlieue et de nouveau devant les tribunaux pour sa prise de parole.


Le voilà érigé en quasi responsable de la contestation, incarnation autocentrée pour le Parquet - proclamée d'une jeunesse qui ne supporterait plus rien — ni l'ordre, ni l'autorité, ni les institutions, et encore moins ceux qui prétendent les représenter. À chaque mobilisation son cortège, à chaque polémique sa réponse proportionnée, à chaque interpellation sa détermination sauf qu'à chaque fois ou presque il y a un mort, qui un voyageur traîné sur 100 m par la Municipale qui un maire véreux cloitrant une aire de « gens-du-voyage ».


Voir en Ritchy Thibault une sorte de porte-parole naturel des populations opprimées semble se dessiner assez fiablement au fil des mois et parfois des semaines, au fil des émeutes, et manifestant en première ligne pour la fin des coups et des étranglements sur la voie publique jusqu'au fond des mitards.


Chatgpt dirait : c'est là que le personnage devient intéressant. Il se retrouve quasiment à chaque procédure a établir un rapport de force - comme un rapport de farce - une variante de la fameuse Défense de rupture. On le voit à chaque fois argumenter - dans ce régime de parole qui est le sien à des joutes assez réussies et brillantes de tentatives d'auto-désarrestations (désarrestation = lorsqu'un groupe de personnes tentent de libérer physiquement un•e camarade au prise avec la Maréechaussée.) Dans cette nouvelle économie de la contestation, l'arrestation devient parfois une ligne de CV, la convocation une médaille et le passage devant la justice un épisode supplémentaire dans le récit héroïque du rappel historique - à chaque fois situé des personnes, persécuté (génocide des voyageurs, parquages, apartheid de l'Etat français envers des populations).


L'atout de Ritchy Thibault, ce n'est pas qu'il parle trop. C'est qu'il a fait de la confrontation avec le pouvoir une méthode, un médium — et que le pouvoir judiciaire, lui, a les moyens de transformer chacune de ces confrontations en procédure, le transforme en tribune.


La vraie question devient : justice qui protège l'ordre public ou justice qui finit, volontairement ou non, par devenir un instrument de mise au pas d'une parole et se prendre les pieds dans le tapis d'une bienséance confinant à l'absurde du droit commun en sytème politique. Ritchy Thibault nous montre avec délices, les affres de toute assignation - et autres rapports de dominations - qu'ils soient éducatifs, issus du monde les ronds de serviettes et des pantoufles, voire des patins pour cirer les Parquets. Blague à part, la bascule judiciaire, voire carcérale peut vite arriver, une incarcération, des amendes, des menaces de mort à la pelle montrent que le fil est ténu mais il tient la ligne. A nous tous de le sortir de là.


#FreeRitchy

title: Yıldız Teknik Üniversitesi'nde siber saldırı duyurusu: 140 bin öğrencinin verisi çalınmış olabilir
content:
Yıldız Teknik Üniversitesi'nde (YTÜ) 1 Ekim'den bu yana yaşanan sistem aksaklıklarının arkasından siber saldırı çıktı. Kişisel Verileri Koruma Kurulu'nun (KVKK) 7 Ekim tarihli kararıyla üniversitedeki veri ihlali resmi olarak kamuoyuna duyuruldu. Yaşanan siber saldırı ve veri ihlalinden yaklaşık 140 bin öğrenci ile 4 bin 500 personelin etkilendiği belirtildi.

Yıldız Teknik Üniversitesi'nde altyapı sorunu: Öğrenciler çevrimiçi derslere erişemiyor

Üniversitenin resmi internet sitesi, Öğrenci Bilgi Sistemi (OBS), Online Yıldız ve çeşitli başvuru sistemlerine günlerce erişim sağlanamazken, üniversite yönetiminin yaşanan aksaklıklara ilişkin ilk etapta kapsamlı bir açıklama yapmadığı görüldü. Yönetim, 3 Ekim'de yaptığı ilk duyuruda süreci yalnızca "teknik çalışma" olarak nitelendirmişti. Ancak KVKK'nın devreye girmesiyle birlikte sistem kesintilerinin arkasında bir fidye yazılımı saldırısının olduğu netlik kazandı.

Kişisel Verileri Koruma Kurulu’nun yayımladığı duyuruda "Veri sorumlusu sıfatını haiz Yıldız Teknik Üniversitesi tarafından Kurula iletilen veri ihlal bildiriminde özetle; ihlalin 01.10.2026 tarihinde başladığı ve aynı gün tespit edildiği, veri sorumlusunun sanallaştırma altyapısı ve üzerinde çalışan sunucuların fidye yazılımı saldırısından etkilendiği, ihlalden etkilenen ilgili kişi grubunun öğrenci, personel ve ziyaretçiler olduğu, mevcut kayıtlara göre ihlalden etkilenmiş olabilecek ilgili kişi sayısının yaklaşık 140.000 öğrenci ve 4.500 personel olduğu, ziyaretçilere ilişkin sayının henüz belirlenemediği, ihlalden etkilenen kişisel veri kategorilerinin belirlenemediği bilgilerine yer verilmiştir" ifadeleri kullanıldı.

Öğrencilerin hangi kişisel verilerinin siber saldırıdan etkilendiği ve dışarı sızdırıldığı konusundaki belirsizlikler ise hâlâ devam ediyor.

31 yıldır emeğin sesi olan Evrensel, gücünü sadece okurlarından alıyor. Emeğin sesinin daha gür çıkması için sen de güç ver.

author: Mike Ludwig
title: Progressives and Republicans Introduce Competing Bills to Rein In Flock Cameras
content:
The Ban Flock Act aims to slow the rise of Flock-style cameras amid rising fears about AI mass surveillance.

Honest, paywall-free news is rare. Please support our boldly independent journalism with a donation of any size.

Republicans and Democrats in Congress have introduced competing legislation to rein in the government’s use of Flock cameras and other automated license plate readers (ALPRs) following widespread abuses by police and intense public backlash to the powerful surveillance technology.

ALPRs allow police to track vehicles and their drivers across expansive areas by using a variety of easily searchable data points from images captured by the cameras. The Ban Flock Act, backed by some Democrats and progressives, would halt federal funding to slow the rise of AI-powered surveillance nationwide. A competing GOP bill creates legal guardrails for police when using ALPR data but would not “ban” license plate surveillance by the federal government.

Introduced on October 2 by Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vermont), Sen. Jeff Merkley (D-Oregon), and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-New York), the Ban Flock Act would prevent federal funds from being used to purchase ALPRs, including but not limited to Flock cameras. In order to incentivize a “moratorium” on the use of ALPRs by local police, only state and local governments with laws or policies in place to prohibit the use of ALPRs could continue receiving financial assistance from several federal entities, including from the Departments of Justice, Homeland Security, Transportation, Housing and Urban Development, and Health and Human Services.

The bill would also ban the use of both ALPRs and the data gathered by them at the federal level while creating a legal avenue for lawsuits against the federal government over privacy violations.

However, the legislation would not place an outright ban on the use of Flock and similar cameras attached to license plate analytics software, nor would it ban the use of AI-powered surveillance systems by local governments and private actors. The Ban Flock Act would also allow Congress to pass legislation allowing police to use ALPRs for a specific purpose with privacy restrictions, including deleting data after 48 hours. ALPRs used to collect tolls are exempt from the bill.

Speaking at an event in Bakersfield, California, on October 5, Sanders linked Flock cameras to the controversial rapid advances in AI. While the AI systems that enhance ALPR surveillance are not the most controversial frontier models still in development, AI-powered search engines made by Flock Safety and its competitors to analyze data collected by ALPRs make the systems much more powerful.

When asked by Sanders if they had heard of AI data centers and Flock cameras, the crowd booed.

“We are looking at the possibility [of] the evisceration of privacy rights in America,” Sanders said.

Flock Safety is the leading manufacturer of ALPRs along with competitors such as Axon and Motorola Solutions, which some cities are turning to as the Flock brand becomes increasingly controversial. With an estimated 120,000 ALPRs installed nationwide, Flock’s cameras alone record and analyze about 20 billion images of vehicles each month. The anti-surveillance group DeFlock has mapped more than 143,000 ALPR cameras across the lower 48 states.

ALPRs are not new, but the technology has advanced rapidly in recent years and is often integrated with AI, allowing police to effortlessly search for vehicles and people without needing to enter a license plate number. ALPRs capture images of each passing vehicle, recording location, date, and time, as well as the vehicle’s make, model, color, and identifying features such as dents, roof racks, and bumper stickers, and then turn these into searchable data points.

For example, when police in Lenexa, Kansas, put a local activist under ALPR surveillance in 2025 after he wrote an op-ed criticizing city officials and was investigated in connection to a petty vandalism case, they were able to easily track his grocery shopping habits and even identify his shoes, according to internal records.

In a statement, Ocasio-Cortez said the widespread integration of AI-powered cameras into everyday life is “unconscionable.”

“Across the country, Big Tech companies like Flock Safety have built a mass surveillance system to harvest Americans’ private and personal data without their consent,” Ocasio-Cortez said on October 2. “AI-powered cameras are …

author: Isaac Nellist
title: Lizzie O’Shea: ‘Surveillance technology is a threat to democracy’
content:
Lizzie O’Shea, a writer, lawyer and founder of Digital Rights Watch, told the New South Wales Council for Civil Liberties’ (NSWCCL) annual fundraising dinner and journalism awards on October 1 that rapidly developing surveillance technology is throwing up many challenges.

Digital technology and democracy are in a “significant amount of tension”, O’Shea said. She added that defending civil liberties is not about “clever people working to impose civil liberties on everybody else”, but that campaigners “have to convince a critical mass that they have to defend their own rights”.

Referencing the origins of professional policing in London in the late 18th century, she described it as “a period of immense technological disruption”, as the Industrial Revolution was reshaping society.

The new police force, O’Shea said, was used to “monitor, enforce and impose the new conditions of social order”. Specifically, it ensured merchants’ profits and prevented dockworkers from supplementing their wages by pilfering stock. The idea was to get the state and industry to collaborate, with a “form of surveillance of everyday people”.

“Policing was talked about as a new science in the detection and prevention of crime,” she said. The spectacle of force “offered an economical and effective way of maintaining order”.

O’Shea said it helps explain the state’s decisions in the digital age. “Like their historical counterparts, modern police understand the power of surveillance in enforcing a form of discipline.

“‘Safety’ is about preserving social order, rather than reducing harm. By allowing law enforcement and intelligence agencies to tell us what is safe, we allow them to use technology in increasingly oppressive ways.

“Rapid technological advances have been accompanied by disruptive transformations in social relations, and an acceleration of policing has often been a response.”

O’Shea described advances in technology in the 21st century as being “a fundamental threat” to democracy. She said more than 100 “security” bills have been passed over the past two decades, connected to surveillance, national intelligence agencies and law enforcement, and 875 new offences have been created.

Many have sought to repurpose existing systems of corporate surveillance for state surveillance, while surveillance technology companies receive lucrative government contracts.

O’Shea also said Labor has “effectively abandoned” regulation of artificial intelligence (AI) and facial recognition technology.

“Less than 10% of Australians think it’s reasonable for a retailer to ask for your biometric information to access their services, but on an almost daily basis they will experience this.

“Everyone is telling us that AI is fundamentally important — politicians, the financial markets, a media that takes industry sources as truth — but a study by the University of Melbourne found that Australians are among the least optimistic in the world about artificial intelligence.

“More people are concerned about the negative outcomes than the benefits … 87% would be more inclined to trust and use AI products if international standards were in place to protect them.”

O’Shea pointed to the campaign to remove Palantir from Coles stores and the defeat of a data centre proposal in Lane Cove as examples of where most people’s attitudes lie.

“The hand of power is seeking to crush us, but we have the capacity to land a counterpunch,” she said. “This is the time for organisers, agitators, lawyers, ratbags and policy nerds to work together to build an alternative future where civil liberties are protected and our democracy can flourish.”

NSWCCL president Timothy Roberts told the gathering that the NSWCCL aimed to be an “ever-watchful guardian” of civil liberties, noting the huge challenges. He referenced last year’s March for Humanity, across the Sydney Harbour Bridge, when 300,000 people marched to protest Israel’s genocide in Gaza and demand that Labor act.

“It felt like the flame of liberty could not burn brighter or stronger — we must continue to celebrate that occasion as an example of the collective exercise of our human rights,” Roberts said.

The NSWCCL’s journalism awards went to Guardian journalists Ariel Bogle and Nino Bucci for uncovering the use of “less-lethal” weapons by police. Star Observer journalist Jacques Nieuwoudt won the young journalist award for his coverage of police raids of LGBTIQ spaces on Oxford Street.

author: groundxero
title: Barricades, Internet Shutdown, Mass Detentions: Delhi Police Violent Crack Down on Protest against CEC Gyanesh Kumar and SIR
content:
Thousands of protesters gathered around Delhi’s Jantar Mantar on 2 October, defying the denial of police permission and a sweeping security clampdown imposed to prevent the protests from taking place. Barricades sealed the designated protest site from all four directions, mobile internet was suspended across central Delhi, several Metro stations were shut, and riot-control forces were deployed in large numbers. What followed was a day of mass detentions, many involving the use of force against women, students, journalists and other protesters. The violent crackdown came amid a renewed call for mobilisation for a ‘Jail Bharo Andolan’ and ‘Jantar Mantar 2.0’ against the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls and demands for the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar, with organisers calling the 2 October action only the beginning of a wider protest movement.


 


New Delhi, 2 October 2026


by

Mouli Sharma


 


“Thousand is a lowballed estimate,” said a lawyer’s group called

Lawyers for Detainees

, one of several such collectives formed after the historic protests that shook the national capital a mere three months ago after uproar against repeated failures and irregularities in the conduct of public examinations under the tenure of former Union Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan. Now, recent history is attempting to recreate itself as a similar uproar against the government’s Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls, and the recent revelations of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar’s alleged role in the same has led to widespread national outrage.


 


“85 people have been detained in this station alone,” said Adv. Surya Prakash, who was present at the Badarpur police station. “We have reports that at least 20 buses filled with detainees left the protest site during the day. Many detainees were released informally at random locations far away from the centre of the city, while still more were taken to stations like this one. The actual number of detentions is much higher than whatever numbers will be produced here at the stations,” he said.


 


The figure, though, may include repeat detentions, the most prominent case being of AISA president Neha Bora herself, who was detained at least three times from the same location outside the Royal Plaza Hotel, near the East entrance of the protest site near the Kerala Bhawan canteen, first alongside psephologist and activist Yogendra Yadav, a second time with several student protesters of other parties, and a third time again with fellow AISA leader Anjali of the Delhi University. Former Delhi CM Atishi, independent journalist Harsh Yadav, and at least 700 more students were detained through the day.


 


“700 is the count we have so far from police stations taken across the city,” said Adv. Vertika Mani, also a part of the lawyers’ collective. “But that obviously cannot account for the many detainees who were released at unofficial locations.”


 


The CJP’s ultimatum to the government of witnessing a ‘Jantar Mantar 2.0’ should Gyanesh Kumar fail to resign within 48 hours (given on 25 September, the deadline for which had long since passed) kicked off with a bang on Friday, as an identical call for the police-defying protest in Shivaji Park, Mumbai was given by countless student, labour, farmer and other political organisations at the eponymous Jantar Mantar in New Delhi, led by prominent activists including Neha Bora, Yogendra Yadav, Nandita Narain, and Prashant Bhushan. Hundreds of civilians took to the streets on the morning of 2 October, on the occasion of Gandhi Jayanti, only to be met with armed state forces deployed in massive numbers and a once-designated protest site cut off from their access through curfews (Section 163 of the BNS was declared in the region, without any justification beyond prevention of a ‘crowd forming’) and police barricades blockading entrances to the site from all four directions, dispersing protesters across a wide 2km radius.


 


What followed was a circus of media, police, and protester, as for four hours following the 11 am time given for the assembly, bus after bus was filled with peaceful protesters ‘detained’ under the simple justification of following ‘orders from above’. At least one protester, a young man named Roveen from the All India Students’ Association (AISA) (of whom Neha Bora is national president), was grievously assaulted by the police and had to be taken to a …

author: Katharine Trendacosta
title: Site-Blocking Will Not Defend IP, No Matter the Bill’s Name
content:
There has been a raft of site-blocking bills in the latest Congress, and the latest is called the “Deterring Extraterritorial Foreign Exploitation of Networks Damaging Intellectual Property” aka the “

DEFEND IP Act

.” The problem is that instead of “defending IP,” this bill will incentivize censorship, overblocking, and bad faith attempts to block access to a website. DEFEND IP Act, and all of these site-blocking proposals, threaten the open web.

 


We keep seeing attempts to pass site-blocking legislation–from SOPA/PIPA in 2012 to

Block BEARD

,

FADPA

, and

ACPA

 this year. Every one of them has at its core the rotten idea that enforcing copyrights requires building a censorship machine for websites into the architecture of the internet. This is, of course, a disaster for a free and open web. There is no way to create a mechanism for blocking access to an entire website that does not invite both deliberate abuse and lots of collateral harm to free and lawful speech.


DEFEND IP deputizes every service provider into a copyright cop, so long as a rightsholder has accused a website of copyright infringement. Let’s be clear: this isn’t about removing access to an infringing work–that already exists via the DMCA. This isn’t about getting damages from the website or the uploader. It is about making an entire website inaccessible for everyone trying to visit it.


DEFEND IP lets any rightsholder go to a court and get an order requiring service providers to block access to an entire website after alleging copyright infringement. What DEFEND IP does not have is any deterrent for someone seeking to block a website in bad faith. There are no punishments for getting a website blocked for protected speech. There are no meaningful remedies for those whose speech is vanished from the internet due to an entire website being disappeared. It creates a one-stop shop for getting an entire website–again, not an instance of infringement but an entire site hosting all sorts of user content–removed. But for those whose business, speech, or access to information is affected, there is no easy way to get the site restored.


DEFEND IP scales up the extraordinary legal structures that already exist for copyright enforcement. In doing so, it likewise scales up the problems those regimes pose to protected speech.

 


We see this with DMCA takedowns all the time. We see it with bad faith

takedowns

 used to silence criticism or commentary. We see it with the voluntary use of copyright filters by sites like YouTube, where seconds of sound matching seconds of sound in another video can prevent an entire work from reaching its audience. In these existing systems, there are at least some mechanisms of challenge available to the targeted creator. DEFEND IP has none. Instead, site owners, users, or readers will have to find a lawyer and go to court and hope to challenge the order, a slow, expensive, and daunting process


Those existing systems are already frustrating for the targeted creators and users, but under DEFEND IP a whole class of people doing protected speech will find themselves deplatformed because of the actions of others


This bill is not a defense of creativity or creators. It is a way to reshape the internet by building a vast new infrastructure of censorship. Congress should put aside DEFEND IP and the failed idea of site-blocking laws, for good.

author: Sofia Little
title: Get the Flock Out
content:
On September 23rd, the Senate Judiciary Subcommittee on Crime and Counterterrorism held a hearing titled “Always Watching: Flock’s Nationwide AI Surveillance Network,” examining the privacy risks, data sharing, and misuse of private automated license plate reader (ALPR) networks.

The hearing was chaired by Sen. Hawley (R-MO) and featured five witnesses, including Lindsey Isaacs, a wrongfully accused driver, Alasdair Whitney from Legislative Counsel Institute for Justice, Sheriff Ross Teeple, Benn Jordan, a self-proclaimed “hacker”, and policy counsel analyst Chad Marlow from the ACLU, where they have coined a campaign called “Get the Flock Out.”

The hearing highlighted pertinent concerns about how ALPR technology can be used and shared. Public concern about Flock cameras has also grown in recent months. A September 2026 Navigator Research survey found that 62% of registered voters were concerned about Flock camera use, including 66% of Democrats, 55% of Republicans, and 70% of Independents.

Flock Safety was founded in 2017 by CEO Garrett Langley, operating as a small startup meant to provide ALPR cameras to homeowners associations and neighborhoods looking to reduce petty theft and local property crimes. Now, it has grown into something alarmingly dystopian: an AI powered network of over 120,000 cameras across 49 states that photograph, scan, tag, and log every driver that passes, whether or not they are suspected of any crime.

License plate reader technologies have existed since the 1970s, in the form of speed, toll, and red-light cameras. These are only triggered by a specific action, such as running a red-light or driving through a toll booth, and only track license plate numbers. The entry of venture capitalist funding and advanced AI technology into the mass surveillance industry has transformed these automatic traffic enforcement cameras into a complex web of invasive surveillance tools.

During the hearing, ACLU’s Mr. Chad Marlow argued that companies operating ALPR systems are profiting from the collection and sharing of information about people’s movements. The ACLU has called for greater limits on how ALPR data can be collected, accessed, and shared.

Privacy concerns extend to how ALPR data can affect people seeking reproductive health care. During the hearing, Sen. Booker (D-NJ) raised concerns that states could use ALPR technology to track people traveling to obtain reproductive care. The concern comes amid documented cases of law enforcement using vehicle surveillance systems to investigate people seeking or suspected of seeking abortion care.

Unfortunately, this ‘hypothetical’ scenario has become the reality for women across the country.

Witnesses Alaster Whitney and Sheriff Ross Teeple both testified about the overreach of Flock’s ALPRs, with Whitney highlighting jurisdiction concerns which police officers have already been accused of taking advantage of.

In Texas, a sheriff’s deputy used 83,000 Flock ALPRs to track a woman who allegedly performed a self-administered abortion, at the behest of her abusive partner. In Massachusetts, a police officer used Flock networks to stalk a former romantic partner who said she had changed her identity to escape from his abuse. In Kentucky, a police officer was accused of searching his child’s mother 1,000 times through Flock’s network, though she has a protective order. The Institute for Justice has catalogued more than 200 incidents of these ALPR abuses, including romantic stalking, wrongful stops and detentions, non-law enforcement use and other types of misconduct.

These encroachments do not just stop here, as Sen. Padilla (D-CA) spotlights the use of loopholes within Flock, which ICE officers take advantage of to track immigrant communities. While Flock has guaranteed no direct access to the Border Patrol subagency, Witness Marlow points out all it takes is one sympathetic person connected to ICE for the agency to obtain access to billions of pictures of citizens, including facial properties.

Concerns about ALPR surveillance have crossed traditional political lines. During the hearing, Sen. Hawley noted that supporters of the Second Amendment have “long feared national databases of any kind.” This has drawn criticism from across the political spectrum highlighting the bipartisan opposition.

While Flock operates as a leading company which produces ALPRs, they are not the sole producers. Companies like Axon and Motorola have slowly begun increasing …

author: EDRi
title: The KIDS Act will make the internet less safe
content:
On 16 September, the European Commission presented the KIDS ACT, its plan for making online experiences safer for young people. Far from being a move to lead the EU towards better digital environments, this move is a missed opportunity to address the root cause of why online platforms are harmful to children – and everyone else. This blog analyse the proposal’s shortcomings.

During her annual address to the European Parliament, the President of the European Commission announced her intention to protect young people from platforms and services that deprive children of their childhood and of their focus. The next day, the Commission published the KIDS ACT (an acronym for ‘Keeping Internet Digital Spaces Accountable and Trustworthy’). This announcement arrives after a period of much debate around protecting young people online, and even announcements of social media bans from countries across Europe. As a response to this discussion, on April 22, youth organisations across Europe came together to demand real change, instead of exclusions and bans, from EU lawmakers.

The Commission had the opportunity to change the rules of the dangerous game that makes people unsafe online. Instead, it’s mostly restricting who gets to play. Not only is the KIDS ACT a terrible proposal, it’s also a missed opportunity for the European Commission to lead the EU towards a safer digital environment for children and everyone else. The proposal instead determines who is allowed to use services built upon harmful design choices, and clumsily tries to make some of these choices safe for a narrow age bracket, rather than addressing why they can be harmful in the first place. In doing so, it leaves largely untouched the business models that put us all at risk, and sets complex standards for safety which will cement Big Tech dominance. Let’s unpack the proposal.

The KIDS ACT mostly delays young people’s exposure to online harms. On the one hand, it would ban social media accounts for those under 15*. On the other hand, it would require companies to apply certain protections to minors’ accounts against pervasive exploitative tracking, intrusive default settings, and AI companions designed to create emotional dependencies, among other risky features.

What is striking is that these protections apply only to people aged 15*-18. It’s as if these services, practices and functionalities will magically cease to be harmful on someone’s 18th birthday. We all remain vulnerable to manipulative design and unfair personalisation even as adults: not even the most digitally literate person can examine every single default setting, decode every recommendation system, or resist every strategically timed prompt designed to get us to keep clicking. Fairness must be built into the environment itself, not left to the skills of the people using it. Many of the measures proposed in the KIDS ACT address harms that are not specific to childhood and were therefore meant to be tackled through the forthcoming Digital Fairness Act (DFA), which the Commission said will address addictive design for all consumers. The risk is that by treating these practices primarily as child-safety problems, the Commission is lowering the ambition of the rules still to come. Under the appearance of acting on online harms, the KIDS ACT may rob us of stronger protections for ALL of us, including children.

The underlying logic of the KIDS ACT is that, while some risks can be mitigated for people aged 15-18, those under 15* years old should be banned from social media altogether. This blanket age-based exclusion treats children’s online presence as the problem, rather than following young people’s own call to examine the conditions under which digital services expose them to harm. Under the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child, young people — including those under 15 — have the fundamental right, online and offline, to participate in society, access information, communicate with others, play, and develop their identities. Age-gates undermine these rights.

They would also fundamentally change the open nature of the internet: services would have to treat users as children by default unless they prove their age. The Commission’s approach would create a two-tier internet in which children but also adults who cannot or do not wish to pass an age check are excluded from spaces that have become important for education, socialisation, access to information and participation in public life. People …

Open Source Is Not the Same Thing as Liberation

Open Source Is a Tool, Not a Commandment

There is a peculiar form of ideological dogmatism that has emerged within parts of the FOSS movement. Even in anarchist circles, some people seem to believe that opposition to intellectual property must take precedence over virtually every other ethical consideration. After all, if copyright, patents, and other forms of intellectual property are inherently illegitimate, then any attempt to place limits on how the things we create are used or distributed must necessarily be reactionary, right? Even when those limits are intended to protect workers, creators, and wider communities from exploitation by capital?

Anarchists do not seek to abolish one particular category of property while leaving other relations of domination untouched. Nor do we advocate stripping workers of control over the fruits of their labor in the name of an ideological dogma that ultimately has little to do with fostering anarchism.

The rise of so-called “generative AI” has made this contradiction impossible to ignore. My recent essay on this technology was criticized by some open-source diehards because, in their view, no one has the right to restrict the flow of information — even when that flow gushes directly from the minds and labor of workers and creatives into the bulging bank accounts of Silicon Valley billionaires.

To be clear: I am not opposed to free and open-source software. The forum I run (Raddle.me) was built on software (Postmill) that my cofounder released into the commons from the outset under a FOSS license. Even when fascists forked her code to spread hate and harassment, and when a scummy developer violated the license and tried to pass her work off as his own for profit, we did not respond by retreating behind a closed-source license. As anti-authoritarians and anti-capitalists, we certainly could have justified doing so when her work was being used to harm marginalized communities and enrich capitalists, but the license was kept open.

The same principle applies to my own writing. I release all of my essays freely, and I give zine-makers permission to reprint them without restriction. I believe in sharing knowledge and making creative work accessible. People have the option to donate to support my work if they want to. What I oppose is capital taking that generosity, enclosing it within a for-profit ecosystem, and turning it into another mechanism for extracting wealth from the people who created it.

This is not an argument that copyright is inherently liberatory. It is an argument that the abolition of intellectual property is not, by itself, liberation.

I feel compelled to take a stand against the increasingly rigid open-source absolutism that has taken hold in parts of the milieu: against the ruling class taking our collective knowledge, privatizing it, and selling it back to us. I do not consider this a pro-IP argument, but I’m sure plenty of people will disagree. It is an argument against AI slop …

author: Slingshot robot #1
title: Live in the Real World
content:
Our dependence on our phones isn’t an accident. We depend on them logistically for our navigation, payment, and communication. But our phones and the apps they contain are also designed to build emotional dependence — there are entire teams of top-of-their-field psychologists, engineers, sociologists, and designers getting paid hundreds of thousands of dollars a year to make apps even just a little bit more addictive. The emotional and logistical dependence on our phones intertwine in a mutual feedback loop, making it difficult to reduce either.

Every interaction we have with our phones deepens opportunities for state surveillance. Our online activity creates a database of our interests, purchase history, friend networks, location, and activism that the FBI of yesteryear could only have dreamed of. But the biggest problem, as with any addiction, is how something that is fun and useful in small doses can start to take more and more of our time and attention, preventing us from doing other things that we value. So what is there to do?

For most of us, the apps that most deeply build psychological dependence on our phones are social media apps and games. These often take, in some ways, the place of cigarettes in our society today — we do them on a quick break, or when we need to ‘unwind’. But like nicotine, they mostly sate the need that they themselves create. After unwinding in this way, do you feel deeply rested and reset?

If there is an app that you feel wastes your time, or you dislike how much you use, just delete it! You can always re-download it. Note down in your organizer the date and time you deleted the app, and why. If you redownload the app, note that down too. It’s helpful to understand our own patterns of use, to help us understand where we use “tools” or “toys” out of necessity or fun, versus out of psychological dependence.

Think about other activities you can do when you would have used your phone. If you delete an app, it’s easy for some other app to quickly replace it. Be realistic about what might feel fulfilling and restful while deprogramming, in those times and in that headspace. Watching landscapes slide past, noticing the people around you, thinking about your present, past or future, having a conversation with a friend or stranger, reading: each of these might feel more wholesome or restful than your phone. Your Slingshot organizer may be able help you… Don’t you think the edges of the date pages could use additional intricate doodles? Or perhaps you can journal a bit, filling in past date entries with what you remember doing, seeing, eating, or thinking on that day? Use the blank pages in the back to write poetry or outline a manifesto or draw art. Let your boredom be a canvas, a portal to discovery, not something to avoid.

These activities won’t feel as stimulating or give you the same dopamine rush as the apps you’re used to. It’s normal to feel a sense of confusion or loss in this process. Perhaps at some deep level the bright, shifting light of the screen feels like a flickering fire: a thousand generations of finding safety and community in campfires draws us inexorably to this bright cold flame. Try changing your phone’s settings to have the display be in black and white, or switch to a dimmer, less attractive color palette.

We can also feel emotional dependence on the instant knowledge and communication phones provide. What if we can’t respond right away to a friend or loved one? It’s so easy to ask a question to AI like Siri or Google and get an affirming answer! Like puppies or young children, we become anxious without the constant presence of that communication or knowledge. Try consciously pushing your limits more often — if you don’t know something, discuss it rather than looking up ‘the answer’ right away. Delete search bars and AI assistants from your phone and download the Wikipedia app, so if you do need to look something up, you will break that instant gratification loop, finding your own answer and giving yourself context along the way. And try setting aside a specific time of the day to answer your messages. Let friends or loved ones know you might not respond quickly outside of that time.

Logistical dependence is hard in a different way. Practical uses for our phones are often the most problematic sites of government and corporate surveillance, and reinforce emotional dependence by repeatedly forcing us back to our screens.

Try leaving your phone on airplane mode …

author: Monica Atieno, Angela Chukunzira and Athandiwe Saba
title: Inside Kenya’s Hidden Deals with Big Tech
content:
When an outsourcing company working for Meta found itself being sued in Kenya, it took its problem to the President.


The dispute had begun in May 2022, when former Facebook content moderator Daniel Motaung sued Sama and Meta over working conditions. Another 43 moderators brought a case in March 2023. The workers had been employed by Sama to moderate Facebook content, work that required them to repeatedly view disturbing material. They argued that Meta, which ultimately benefited from and controlled aspects of their work, should also be held responsible.


Sama was not a minor contractor in Kenya. It was part of the labour pipeline that allowed a global technology company to outsource some of the most harmful work of the internet to Kenyan workers. Meta fought to remove itself from the litigation, arguing, among other things, that Kenyan courts did not have jurisdiction over the foreign company. But on 20 September 2024, the Court of Appeal rejected that argument.


Then on 11 November 2024, less than two months after that ruling, the Business Laws (Amendment) Bill was published. It proposed new rules for Kenya’s outsourcing industry, including provisions dealing with who should carry responsibility for workers employed by outsourcing companies.


Less than a month later, on 9 December, President William Ruto publicly said Sama had approached him about its legal troubles. “Now I can report to you that we have changed the law,” he said, adding that “nobody will take you to court again on any matter.”


But the bill was still before Parliament, where a fight was unfolding over who should be held responsible for outsourced workers. Business groups including KEPSA and the Kenya Association of Manufacturers

argued

 that responsibility should largely remain with the outsourcing company. Tech workers argued that companies that control or benefit from their work should also be held responsible. This was very important for workers trying to sue companies such as Meta rather than only their local contractors.


Figure 1: Africa Tech Workers Movement members during a joint press conference in August 2025, raising concerns about the Business Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2024.


The workers also went to court to try to stop the bill. In June 2026, the High Court

declined

 to intervene. On 19 August 2026, the National Assembly passed the amendments. It now awaits for presidential assent. 


For James Oyange, a former content moderator, Ruto’s statement sent a clear message about whose side the government was on. Workers had gone to court seeking protection from some of the world’s most powerful technology companies; instead, he said, the government appeared to be changing the rules in the companies’ favour.


“We are on our own. It is the responsibility of the government to protect us, but they are taking Big Tech’s side. It means the companies can do what they want.”


Oyange fears that if technology companies can turn to the government when workers sue them, while workers are left with fewer ways to hold those companies responsible, the balance of power shifts even further away from workers.


The Sama case is one part of a much wider relationship between Kenya’s government and global technology companies.

The Continent

 identified at least 12 publicly documented meetings, agreements, regulatory engagements and partnerships between the Kenyan government and Microsoft, Google, Amazon, TikTok and Starlink since 2023.


The investigation also found a pattern across these relationships. Major technology companies are being brought into public services, infrastructure and policymaking, often through agreements the public cannot see. At the same time, laws and policies are being developed that can make it easier for these companies to operate. What is much harder to find is who negotiated these arrangements, what Kenya agreed to in return, and who is checking whether they serve the public interest.


Agriculture is one example. In 2020, the Ministry of Agriculture signed an agreement with Microsoft to use technology to

improve farming and food security.

 Microsoft would provide cloud technology for digital tools using information about weather, pests, farming inputs and production.


The partnership expanded in 2022, when AGRA joined Microsoft on a digital agriculture programme that included Agribot known as Kuzabot, a service that sends farmers advice by SMS and WhatsApp. According to the

Community Alliance for Global Justice’s …

author: webdev@democracynow.org (Democracy Now!)
title: Three Years into Genocide, "The IDF Is Still Hunting Gazans": Palestinian Journalist Akram al-Satarri
content:
In Gaza, October 7, 2023, is viewed as the beginning of the genocide. Over the past three years, Israel killed over 74,000 people, according to the Gaza Health Ministry, but many believe that number is a vast undercount. The killing continues despite a so-called ceasefire that took effect about a year ago.


“Every single aspect of the life of the people of Gaza has changed once and forever,” since October 7, says Akram al-Satarri, a Gaza-based journalist. He points out that a large majority of structures in the Gaza Strip have been reduced to rubble and that Israel controls around 70% of Gaza. “The Israeli Air Force is still hovering all around different parts of the Gaza Strip, and the

IDF

 is still hunting Gazans, disturbing the already disturbed life, spreading death and displacement once and once again.”

author: Fozzie
title: Why we should not take sides in war - Devrim Valerian
content:
From Dope Magazine #35, Autumn 2026.

The Prime Minister wears a T-shirt now. It costs 80 quid, and his jeans cost £295. The very nice Harrington jacket he’s often seen in costs £695. Looking like an ordinary bloke is expensive these days.

He’s apologised over Gaza too. He said that Labour “didn’t get it right” and “needs to do better”. It sounded like the British government was finally going to take a position on genocide. Even the climb down sounded a bit more radical than the days of Keir Starmer; “There’s increasing evidence that war crimes appear to have been committed.” But then he told us that it's not a matter for him to decide upon. Instead, it “must be for the international courts to determine, rather than politicians.”

Words matter. If the UK government declared that war crimes were being committed in Gaza, let alone a genocide, it would trigger a legal obligation to stop arms sales. The new policy then is to smile, apologise, and go on selling Israel the weapons, including components for F-35 aircraft, that it needs to continue its mass slaughter of an unarmed civilian population. Little appears to have changed at all. The sales of arms continue, and those who object to this are still arrested and charged under terrorism laws. It should come as little surprise from someone who has been a member of Labour Friends of Israel since 2015.

He also appeared alongside Volodymyr Zelensky at his first meeting with a foreign leader and assured him that the UK was 100% with Ukraine for as long as it takes. On the surface, the situation in Ukraine has similarities with that in Palestine. Russia invaded Ukraine and is committing atrocities there, just as Israel is in Palestine. The first difference is in the British response. Britain is 100% with Ukraine. In Palestine, it is selling Israel arms with which to commit genocide. That would be the equivalent of selling Russia bombs to commit massacres in Ukraine.

There must, then, be some difference between the two situations. It’s certainly not one of morality. The horrors inflicted by the Israeli army upon the civilian population have been far worse than those committed by Russia in terms of people killed. Why then is the UK 100% behind Ukraine, yet arresting people on the streets for saying that they oppose genocide in Palestine?

The answer lies not in the field of morality, but in that of geopolitics. Britain sees it as in its interests to support Israel. It also sees it as in its interests to support Ukraine. The dead have no voice in this. Nor is there anyone speaking up for any moral imperative. It’s national interests that speak loudest.

We should look at the causes of the war in Ukraine. This war is not the act of some ‘irrational actor’. Putin did not start this war because he is ‘crazy’. This war is part of a long struggle played out between America and Russia since 1945. It seemed that after 1989, Russia had been historically defeated in this struggle. Certainly, it suffered a huge defeat. The Warsaw Pact and even the Soviet Union itself were broken up. NATO and the EU expanded rapidly to incorporate many of the newly ‘independent’ states. Now, with America’s role as the single world power diminishing, Russia has seen its chance to reassert its power over Ukraine. It’s not some act of a single ‘madman’. It’s an expression of the interests of Russian capitalism. This is how imperialism works.

So in the midst of this struggle between two imperialist giants, Ukrainian workers are being asked to defend ‘their’ country, and in Britain everybody is being asked to back them. The great powers, as ever, are not clashing directly. This struggle is being carried out by a series of small wars, either between proxies or involving one of the major powers directly intervening in a country. We’ve seen all this before, in Korea, Vietnam, Afghanistan, and a host of proxy wars across the ‘third world’.

Workers in Ukraine are being rallied to this slaughter with all sorts of propaganda. Many of the slogans sound ‘left’. Both sides rally behind slogans of ‘anti-imperialism’. However, this is just a cynical ploy to rally the populace to die on behalf of one imperialism against the other. ‘Anti-fascism’ has become the rallying call of the warmongers on both sides. The West accuses Putin of being ‘worse than Hitler’, and the Russians accuse the Ukrainians of being Nazis.

Then we have patriotism. In times of war, nation-states always rely on patriotism. Russia is using it …

author: Redazione_web
title: A volte ritornano. Opporsi alla ripresa del nucleare
content:
In questo mondo di ladri e ciarlatani, i governanti italiani non possono permettersi il lusso di non essere alti rappresentanti, nella prima categoria, ma anche della seconda! Così, come nei più famosi film dell’orrore, quelli che sembravano definitivamente sepolti da anni, escono dalle loro tombe con un nuovo vestito, ma con l’inconfondibile nefasto lezzo di sempre. Escono dalla tomba idee fasciste di patria e razza, e, per non sbagliarsi, riaffiorano anche tecnologie bocciate da 40 anni per mezzo di ben 2 referendum. Parlo del nucleare.


I ciarlatani parlano di crisi energetica, del petrolio che non abbiamo, per cui dobbiamo assolutamente stringere accordi con governi a dir poco criminali; parlano del gas da comprare a tutti costi, di terre rare e poi – ciliegina sulla torta – della recente guerra innescata da Stati Uniti e Israele con l’attacco all’Iran e il conseguente blocco dello stretto di Hormuz. In questo contesto, caratterizzato dalla retorica di giornalisti prezzolati e di politici, si ritira fuori il nucleare.


Queste chiacchiere nascondono una realtà ancora peggiore. Prima di tutto chiariamo che la politica energetica in Italia, ma anche le scelte politiche dei governanti italici e il posizionamento delle truppe italiane nei vari paesi del mondo, è dominata dagli interessi finanziari dell’ENI, la multinazionale nostrana, la compagnia energetica integrata in decine di paesi, che abbraccia tutti i settori, compreso quello della transizione energetica, della ricerca chimica e dello sviluppo di tecnologie innovative. Il governo italiano non fa nessuna scelta senza il suo beneplacito, in particolar modo oggi che la geografia mondiale sta cambiando radicalmente, e che le guerre sono solo l’aspetto più tremendo e spettacolare dello sfruttamento dei territori e non solo.


A questo va aggiunto che il boom dell’intelligenza artificiale, in tutti i campi, compreso quello militare, richiede molta energia. Si pensi che, secondo quanto indicano le proiezioni, entro la fine del decennio i data center per L’IA arriveranno ad assorbire circa 945 terawattora all’anno, una cifra che eguaglia l’intero fabbisogno energetico di una nazione fortemente industrializzata, come il Giappone.


In Italia le attuali forniture energetiche sono oggi appena sufficienti al fabbisogno nazionale.


Dovendo necessariamente limitare le emissioni di anidride carbonica dunque si deve eliminare o almeno diminuire l’uso di combustibile fossile, e in maniera folle ci si è rivolti al nucleare.


Questa scelta nasce da una parte dall’immenso spreco energetico in atto, imposto da questo sistema capitalista, dall’altro dal limite dettato inevitabilmente dalla strategia politica adottata anche per le rinnovabili, quella di non utilizzare le case e gli edifici esistenti, ma, per mantenere il monopolio e la proprietà dell’energia, si preferisce installare immensi campi eolici e fotovoltaici, finanziati per altro anche da chi propone il nucleare, perché il business deve essere in tutti i settori.


Ancora tu…ma non dovevamo vederci più?


Il Parlamento il 23 settembre 2026 ha approvato la legge delega al Governo in materia di energia nucleare. Tutto questo anche se c’erano già stati ben 2 referendum che avevano detto no al nucleare.


Quando in tempi non sospetti noi anarchici sostenevamo che il referendum non era la panacea di tutti i mali, che dietro questo strumento, apparentemente di democrazia diretta, si poteva effettuare una truffa, indubbiamente avevamo ragione! Vediamo perché.


Una delle cose fondamentali della Costituzione era, ed è,

 la s

ovranità del Parlamento; s

econdo il principio della democrazia parlamentare, il Parlamento mantiene il potere di legiferare su qualsiasi materia non vietata dalla Costituzione, approvando nuove norme e cornici di regole (come le recenti leggi delega sulla fissione sostenibile).


I referendum sul nucleare, in entrambe le occasioni, erano

referendum abrogativi,

regolati dall’Articolo 75 della Costituzione italiana. D’altronde in Italia i referendum possono essere solo abrogativi – qui sta l’inganno! – sono cioè uno strumento che permette ai cittadini solo di cancellare leggi esistenti, non di scriverne di nuove o di inserire divieti assoluti in Costituzione.


I tre quesiti del 1987


Nel Referendum del 1987 nessuno dei quesiti chiedeva esplicitamente “Volete vietare il nucleare?”


I cittadini furono chiamati a cancellare i meccanismi normativi che ne facilitavano lo sviluppo.


Il primo quesito …

author: Unknown
title: Torino è contro il riarmo: corteo 24 ottobre “Noi la guerra non la paghiamo”
content:
Nasce dal percorso cittadino che ha visto una

tappa il 19-20 settembre

 scorso una data di mobilitazione cittadina con respiro regionale per sabato 24 ottobre: contro il riarmo, contro il caro-benzina, contro i data center e per rivendicare risorse per salute, formazione e casa. Sulla pagina

torinocontroilriarmo

 si trovano il lancio e gli appuntamenti in avvicinamento.


Di seguito ripubblichiamo l’indizione.


La crisi della città di Torino e della regione Piemonte non vedrà alcuna possibilità di fuoriuscita con la conversione dei territori, delle industrie, delle scuole e della ricerca in chiave bellica.

Le poche risorse esistenti oggi non devono andare alle armi ma a sanità, formazione, casa e reale presa in carico e gestione dei territori a livello energetico e ecologico. 


Assenza di pianificazione, processo di privatizzazione, consumo di suolo e speculazione energetica, oltre alla

svendita a big tech americane

 di intere porzioni di territorio cittadino e piemontese per la corsa all’oro dei data center, sono le questioni da contrastare. Non pagheremo i costi della cosiddetta transizione green, che impone

il ritorno al nucleare, truffa del governo

, insostenibile sia economicamente che ecologicamente.

Basta con grandi opere inutili come il tav

, vogliamo investimenti nella cura e manutenzione del territorio oltre che per il trasporto pubblico. Non vogliamo la

militarizzazione dei quartieri

, da Barriera di Milano a Vanchiglia. Quest’ultimo  segnato dalla presenza costante e inutile di forze dell’ordine a seguito dello sgombero del centro sociale Askatasuna, spazio che vogliamo venga restituito al quartiere e che possa ritornare a vivere. Così come rifiutiamo  la svendita di pezzi di città a fondi speculativi come BlackRock e patrimonio abitativo pubblico ridotto in briciole, sono dinamiche da fermare immediatamente. 


Le scuole e le università diventano il terreno di propaganda militarista, bellica e patriottica, contaminando saperi e trasformando gli istituti scolastici in caserme. Mentre le scuole crollano, le Università cullano la rivoluzione tecnologica utile ad alimentare il complesso accademico-militare-industriale.

Il riarmo erode le briciole destinate alla formazione e a una sanità in completa crisi

: liste d’attesa, privatizzazione, chiusura di poliambulatori in favore di case di comunità inesistenti, aumento del ticket sanitario a seguito della cancellazione del bollo auto, sono solo alcuni aspetti. Ma i soldi per la costruzione di mega ospedali come quello che dovrebbe sorgere nel parco della Pellerina si trovano, mettendo in contrapposizione ambiente-salute.


Oggi

la propaganda dell’amministrazione si piega alle necessità delle industrie belliche e dei capitali privati

, unici investitori nella crisi perché è proprio nel processo di finanziarizzazione che i grandi fondi o monopoli possono ancora fare profitto. Il lavoro non è in crisi soltanto perché a Torino non esiste più la FIAT, ma perché si muore per lavorare, perché chi studia e si forma non ha alcuna garanzia e lavora in condizioni pessime, perché il lavoro è organizzato in funzione di rendere la popolazione disponibile e ricattabile.

La fuoriuscita dalla crisi è possibile solo se insieme ci si organizza dal basso per riappropriarsi di ciò che è utile ad una vita dignitosa, senza guerra e in cui le nostre poche ricchezze non vengano espropriate. 


In questa città abbiamo saputo porre delle questioni fondamentali sul piatto:

il terreno del dibattito pubblico lo vogliamo dettare noi a partire da un percorso di partecipazione collettiva e dal basso, a partire dalle esigenze delle lotte.

 La vivacità dei giovani, il riscatto collettivo che la Palestina ci ha dato, la possibilità di vivere bloccando la logistica di guerra di una città dove ogni arteria è complice di un futuro di morte e genocidio, la vittoria di essere in piazza ogni giorno liberandosi dal lavoro e di riconoscersi nelle dimensioni di confronto e di incontro è un patrimonio prezioso che sarà la bussola per andare avanti. 


Torino è partigiana perché ha saputo e continuerà a schierarsi dalla parte giusta della storia.

author: Dominic Gutoman
title: ‘Army use of child a violation of int’l humanitarian law’
content:
MANILA – The Philippine Army’s publication of child pictures to pressure a New People’s Army (NPA) member to surrender is a violation of international humanitarian law (IHL), a human rights group said in a statement.

“Posting the child’s name, photograph and location while giving her mother an ultimatum to surrender was not only inhumane and exploitative, it was tantamount to holding the child hostage to compel her mother to do something against her will,” said human rights lawyer Maria Sol Taule, deputy secretary-general of Karapatan, in a statement on October 5.

In a deleted post, the 93rd Infantry Battalion of the Philippine Army published photos of a seven-year-old child with personal details under the pretext of a “birthday party” celebration to urge their NPA mother to surrender.

The Philippines is a signatory to the Geneva Conventions and is obligated to follow the rules of war under IHL. “Children shall be the object of special respect and shall be protected against any form of indecent assault. The Parties to the conflict shall provide them with the care and aid they require, whether because of their age or for any other reason,” the Fourth Geneva Convention stated.

The Philippines also ratified the United Nations (UN) Convention on the Rights of the Child. Under this binding treaty, children should also not be subjected to any arbitrary or unlawful interference on her privacy, family, home or correspondence, or unlawful attacks to their reputation as outlined in the Article 16.

“What the 93rd Infantry Battalion did is equal to hostage-taking,” said Elle Buntag, secretary-general of child rights group Salinlahi. “Basically, it is exploitation to force their mother to surrender.”

The group also recalled the case of certain “Baby Rhea”, a two-month-old infant held hostage along with two pregnant Red fighters in November 2022.

On September 19, Karapatan reported that military agents shot Arnida Cuaton Maguiguilid as she was about to enter the gate of the boarding house in Tagum City.

Maguiguilid was seven months pregnant, a member of New People’s Army on medical leave, and unarmed when she was seized by the elements of the 603rd Infantry Brigade and 6th Infantry Division of the Philippine Army.

“The pregnant NPA member, also vulnerable due to her condition, clearly had hors de combat status. Despite this, she was shot in the back, which crippled her and endangered her unborn child as well,” Taule said.

Rule 47 of the International Humanitarian Law prohibited attacking persons who are recognized as “hors de combat” or anyone who is defenseless because of unconsciousness, shipwreck, wounds or sickness.

“We are calling on the Filipino people, defenders of children’s rights, human rights and international humanitarian law, to help the victims attain justice and hold the AFP accountable,” Buntag said. (DAA)

author: Joshua Carroll
title: Israel at Risk of Civil War and State Collapse, CIA Report Says
content:
A CIA report has said Israel is at risk of civil conflict and state collapse as its genocide in Gaza and attacks on Iran and Lebanon take their toll.


The unpublished August assessment, uncovered by

Drop Site News

 and

Capital & Empire

, found that Israel’s ongoing military campaigns have degraded the political, economic and social fabric of the country.


Titled Fracture From Within, the report was compiled by the spy agency’s Red Cell, which is tasked with challenging prevailing assumptions within the organisation. The CIA did not respond to a request for comment from the outlets. 


It points to deepening anger over the exemption of Haredi men – often referred to as ultra-Orthodox – from military service, large numbers of heavily armed ex-soldiers returning from committing atrocities in Gaza and a cost-of-living crisis as factors that could converge into conflict. 


An intelligence source told the publications: “Famously the Freikorps of Germany were PTSD-addled veterans with weapons and bloodthirst. I’m not saying Israel post-Gaza is Germany post-WWI but there are certainly aspects of this that ring similar to me.”


A

2018 rule change

 made it easier for ex-Israel Defense Forces soldiers to obtain and keep guns, and after 7 October 2023 the government allowed

further mass expansion

 of firearm permits.


Ahead of elections on 27 October, the report also highlights political fractures within Israel, where prime minister Netanyahu is under fire for his failure to prevent the Hamas attacks – amid accusations that he was

warned about them

 in advance. 


Netanyahu’s government was accused of triggering a constitutional crisis in July by openly refusing to comply with a supreme court ruling that allowed the country’s broadcasting regulator to continue operating. The government

reportedly wanted to prevent the regulator

 from letting an anti-government critic purchase a major TV channel. 


A previous attempt by Netanyahu’s government to curb the supreme court’s power led to mass protests ahead of October 2023.  


The CIA’s report was written by “Israel experts,” an intelligence source said: “With the upcoming election and the fissures in Israel we should take seriously their conclusion that Israel is one spark away from real internal conflict.”


One scenario in the report involves Hamas or Hezbollah exploiting domestic weakness, while another mentioned tech companies pulling out of Israel, causing more economic strain.

author: kinder des zorns
title: Feuer der KI-Kriegsindustrie! CleanTech Business Park Marzahn sabotiert
content:
„

Was haben die Zielauswahl durch die israelischen Streitkräfte (IDF) im Gaza-Krieg, die Verschleppungen durch die US-Migrationsbehörde ICE und die sogenannte Abwendung drohender Gefahren durch deutsche Landespolizeien gemeinsam? Sie setzen ein neues Modell datengetriebener Herrschaft über Menschen durch, ein Modell, das von wenigen Tech-Konzernen kontrolliert wird. Es basiert auf den Daten, die wir alle täglich bei der Nutzung der Systeme von Unternehmen wie Meta, X, OpenAI und Google erzeugen. […] Unsere zivilen Daten sind notwendiger Bestandteil dieser zivil-militärischen Infrastruktur – oder andersherum: Es gibt keine rein zivile Nutzung zivil-militärisch entwickelter Technologien! Wir sind Teil der KI-Kriegsindustrie und Teil der Zerstörung! […] Es ist an der Zeit, […] aus der Architektur des Krieges zu desertieren, verbunden mit der konsequenten Sabotage der vielfältigen Prozesse und Knotenpunkte, in denen sich das Zivile ins Militärische einwebt.“


Wir haben uns den Aufruf „

KI beginnt hier

“ zu Herzen genommen und einen der sensibelsten Bereiche zivil-militärischer Technologien angegriffen. Durch gezielte Brandlegungen¹ an dutzenden Starkstromkabeln haben wir die Stromzufuhr des CleanTech Business Parks am Stadtrand von Berlin-Marzahn unterbrochen und damit mehreren Unternehmen, die mit ihren Halbleitern/Mikrochips, Präzisionsmaschinen und elektronischen Hochleistungsbauteilen das Gehirn und das Herz des technologischen Angriffs bilden, die Lebensadern durchtrennt. Konkret gilt unsere Sabotage den Produktionshallen von Swissbit Germany AG, Finetech und Emerson/Flexim. Alle drei Firmen fertigen Dual-Use-Produkte. Diese finden sowohl in vermeintlich zivilen Bereichen wie Rechenzentren, der Luft- und Raumfahrt, der Öl- und Gasförderung, in Atomreaktoren, Windkraftanlagen oder im Bergbau Anwendung als auch in nahezu allen modernen Waffensystemen. Zu ihren Abnehmern zählen Sicherheitsbehörden, das Militär und Unternehmen der Rüstungsindustrie. Bereits ein kurzzeitiger Stromausfall kann ihre hochspezialisierten Fertigungsanlagen erheblich beschädigen und zu wochenlangen Verzögerungen führen. Genau das war unsere Absicht.


Wir haben lange abgewogen, ob die Sabotage von Stromleitungen derzeit ein angemessenes Mittel im Kampf für eine andere, gerechtere Welt ist. Angesichts der Auswirkungen des Stromausfalls im Januar infolge der Sabotage des Gaskraftwerks Lichterfelde haben wir diese Entscheidung nicht leichtfertig getroffen. Dass wir uns trotzdem dafür entschieden haben, ist in erster Linie eine Konsequenzen aus dem Scheitern anderer Protest- und Aktionsformen. Diese haben sich in Anbetracht der globalen Eskalation von Kriegen, Wettrüsten, Artensterben, Umweltzerstörungen, Flutkatastrophen, Waldbränden, Hitzetoten und einem erstarkenden Faschismus vielfach als unzureichend erwiesen. Wir sind der Meinung, dass die Zeit der Symbolpolitik und des guten Willens ein Ende haben muss. Wir wollen die Abläufe kapitalistischer Ausbeutung wirksam und unmittelbar unterbrechen und den Profiteur:innen von Krieg und Umweltzerstörung spürbare wirtschaftliche Verluste zufügen. So wie es andere in den vergangenen Monaten getan haben. Außerdem soll die Aufmerksamkeit, die eine solche Aktion erzeugt, dem Image Berlins als Investitionsstandort für Technologie- und Rüstungsunternehmen nachhaltig schaden. All dies halten wir aktuell für dringend notwendig und ist erklärtes Ziel dieser Unterbrechung. Aber auch in Sachen Repression und staatlicher Gewalt scheint uns der Weg der nächtlichen Sabotage sicherer zu sein als z. B. Demos, die zunehmend von Schikanen, Einschüchterungen und brutalen Festnahmen geprägt sind. Sich bei Aktionen vor Ort festnehmen zu lassen, – wie es andere aus der Klimagerechtigkeits- und Antikriegsbewegung praktizieren – um Gerichtsprozesse als Bühne zu nutzen und an das Gewissen der herrschenden Rechtsprechung zu appellieren, oder bei der Räumung von Sitzblockaden auf die Nachsicht der Cops zu hoffen, halten wir angesichts einer zunehmenden Faschisierung jedoch für gefährlich und naiv. Trotzdem gilt allen Repressionsbetroffenen natürlich unsere volle Solidarität.


Ein weiteres Kriterium für die Ausführung unserer Tat war, dass ein Stromausfall, dessen Ausmaß wir im Vorhinein nicht vollumfänglich abschätzen konnten, bei spätsommerlichen Temperaturen für mögliche Betroffene, die nicht das eigentliche Ziel unserer Aktion sind, weniger einschneidend ist.
